chunks.heading: Abnormal & Clinical Psychology — the full book, disorder by disorder (Ahuja + DSM-5-TR + ICD-11)
chunks.text: Abnormal & Clinical Psychology — the full book, disorder by disorder (Ahuja + DSM-5-TR + ICD-11) Not a summary. The Abnormal section the library was missing, built the way the exam actually asks it: off Niraj Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry (the standard Indian psychiatry text), walked disorder by disorder, with each disorder's classification pinned to both coding systems — DSM-5-TR (APA, 2022) and ICD-11 (WHO, in force Jan 2022) — because MET / NIMHANS / RCI fish in the gap between them. Each disorder keeps one recurring frame: (1) what it is / core clinical picture · (2) the diagnostic criteria (DSM and ICD, with the cut-offs) · (3) subtypes & course · (4) etiology in one line · (5) treatment · (6) the trap it's tested through . The "this-vs-that" distinctions MCQs live on are flagged in red trap boxes; where NIMHANS pushes past Ahuja it's in purple . Built 2026-06-07. chunks.heading: Ch 1. What counts as abnormal, and the models that explain it
chunks.text: Ch 1. What counts as abnormal, and the models that explain it No single criterion defines abnormality; psychology uses a convergence of indicators , the "4 Ds" . Deviance — the behaviour breaks the statistical or social norm (rare, or violates the rules a society lives by). Distress — it causes the person suffering (but not always: a person in a manic high feels great, so distress alone is neither necessary nor sufficient). Dysfunction — it interferes with daily functioning (work, relationships, self-care): this is the heaviest single criterion, and the one DSM/ICD both require. Danger — risk of harm to self or others (least common, often over-weighted by laypeople). A fifth qualifier rides on all of them: cultural and contextual relativity — the same act is healthy in one context and pathological in another (grief, trance, religious experience), so the clinician asks "is this deviant for this person's culture and situation? " The single best one-word criterion = dysfunction / impairment (harmful dysfunction, Wakefield). Distress is not required (mania, antisocial PD), and statistical rarity alone is not abnormality (genius is rare and not a disorder).

chunks.heading: The models of abnormality (each = a cause + a cure)
chunks.text: The models of abnormality (each = a cause + a cure) Model Cause of disorder Treatment it implies Biological / medical Genes, neurotransmitters, brain structure, endocrine Drugs, ECT, rTMS Psychodynamic (Freud) Unconscious conflict, early-childhood, defences Psychoanalysis, insight Behavioural Maladaptive learning (classical/operant conditioning) Behaviour therapy, exposure Cognitive (Beck, Ellis) Distorted thinking, irrational beliefs, schemas CBT, cognitive restructuring Humanistic-existential Blocked self-actualisation, incongruence, meaninglessness Person-centred, existential therapy Sociocultural / family-systems Social stress, labelling, family dynamics, culture Family/community therapy, social change Biopsychosocial All three layers interacting Integrated / multimodal care Diathesis-stress is the integrating idea. A diathesis (vulnerability: a gene, a temperament, a cognitive style) sits silent until a stressor activates it; the disorder is the product, not either alone. This is why identical-twin concordance for schizophrenia is ~50% not 100% (genes load the gun, environment pulls the trigger), and why it underlies nearly every "what causes X" answer in the modern syllabus. Recap Ch 1. Abnormality = 4 Ds (Deviance, Distress, Dysfunction, Danger) + cultural relativity; dysfunction is the core. Seven models, each pairing a cause with a cure; the biopsychosocial model run t

chunks.heading: Ch 2. Classification — the two systems, and the gap MCQs live in
chunks.text: Ch 2. Classification — the two systems, and the gap MCQs live in Two manuals classify mental disorders. DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual, 5th ed, Text Revision 2022 ) — published by the American Psychiatric Association (APA) , used mainly for research and in the US. ICD-11 (International Classification of Diseases, 11th rev) — published by the WHO , the global standard, came into effect 1 January 2022 ; its mental-disorders section is Chapter 06. India follows ICD officially, but exams test DSM criteria heavily, so you carry both. Feature DSM-5-TR (APA) ICD-11 (WHO) Scope Mental disorders only All diseases; mental disorders = Chapter 06 Approach Largely categorical, criteria-based, operationalised Prototype/description-based; more clinician judgment Axes Multiaxial system abandoned in DSM-5 (the old 5 axes are gone) Never used DSM-style axes Schizophrenia duration 6 months (incl. 1 month active) 1 month of active symptoms Schizophrenia subtypes Dropped (no more paranoid/catatonic/hebephrenic) Dropped too; uses symptom specifiers Personality disorders Kept the 10 categorical types (Section II); a dimensional model sits in Section III Fully dimensional — severity + 5 trait domains + a borderline pattern PTSD One PTSD (4 symptom clusters) Simplified PTSD + a separate Complex PTSD Bereavement Added Prolonged Grief Disorder (new in DSM-5-TR) Has Prolonged Grief Disorder t

chunks.heading: Ch 3. The Mental State Examination (how the disorder is observed)
chunks.text: Ch 3. The Mental State Examination (how the disorder is observed) Ahuja's MSE is the clinician's structured snapshot of the patient now . Learn the headings in order; vignette MCQs quote one cell and ask which heading it belongs to. Heading What's assessed · key terms 1. General appearance & behaviour Grooming, eye contact, rapport, psychomotor activity (retardation / agitation), mannerisms, catatonia 2. Speech Rate, volume, tone; pressure of speech (mania), poverty of speech (depression/negative) 3. Mood & affect Mood = sustained subjective ("how do you feel"); affect = observed, moment-to-moment (blunted, flat, labile, incongruent) 4. Thought Stream (flight of ideas, retardation), form (loosening of associations, tangentiality, circumstantiality, word salad, neologisms), content (delusions, obsessions, overvalued ideas) 5. Perception Hallucinations (modality), illusions, depersonalisation/derealisation 6. Cognition Consciousness, orientation (time/place/person), attention & concentration, memory (immediate/recent/remote), MMSE 7. Insight Awareness of being ill (graded I–VI); poor in psychosis/mania, retained in neurosis 8. Judgement Personal, social, test judgement Mood vs affect: mood is the climate (sustained, subjective), affect is the weather (immediate, observed). Form vs content of thought: form = how thoughts connect (loosening, tangentiality → schizophrenia); content

chunks.heading: Ch 4. Schizophrenia
chunks.text: Ch 4. Schizophrenia Core. A chronic psychotic disorder of disturbed thought, perception, affect and behaviour with relatively preserved consciousness and intellect. Lifetime risk ~1% , equal in both sexes (earlier onset in men, late teens–20s; women mid-20s–30s). The term is Eugen Bleuler's (1911, "splitting of psychic functions"); Emil Kraepelin earlier called it dementia praecox (early dementia, poor outcome). Clinical picture — three classic frameworks. Framework Content Bleuler's 4 A's (fundamental sx) A ffect (blunted/inappropriate), A ssociations (loosening), A mbivalence, A utism (withdrawal into inner world). Hallucinations/delusions are accessory , not fundamental. Schneider's First-Rank Symptoms Thought echo / insertion / withdrawal / broadcast ; delusional perception ; passivity (made acts, feelings, impulses, somatic passivity); third-person auditory hallucinations ( running commentary , voices arguing/discussing the patient). Highly suggestive but not pathognomonic. Positive vs negative (Crow's Type I/II) Positive (excess): delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech/behaviour — respond to drugs, dopamine-linked. Negative (deficit): 5 A's — Affective flattening, Alogia, Avolition, Anhedonia, Asociality (+ attention) — drug-resistant, worse prognosis. Diagnostic criteria. DSM-5: ≥2 of [delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, grossly disorganised/catatonic

chunks.heading: Ch 5. Other psychotic disorders
chunks.text: Ch 5. Other psychotic disorders Disorder Defining feature · duration Trap Delusional disorder ≥1 month of delusion(s) with otherwise intact functioning and no other psychotic features; classically non-bizarre (persecutory, jealous/Othello, grandiose, erotomanic/de Clérambault, somatic) Function preserved outside the delusion = NOT schizophrenia Brief psychotic disorder (DSM) Psychosis 1 day–1 month , full return to baseline; often post-stressor/postpartum <1 month + full recovery Acute & transient psychotic disorder (ICD) Abrupt onset (within 2 weeks), rapidly changing "polymorphic" picture; the ICD counterpart of brief psychosis ICD term, abrupt + fluctuating Schizophreniform (DSM) Full schizophrenia picture lasting 1–6 months The 1–6 month bridge Schizoaffective Schizophrenia + a mood episode concurrently , PLUS ≥2 weeks of delusions/hallucinations without prominent mood symptoms The 2-week psychosis-without-mood window separates it from psychotic mood disorder Shared psychotic disorder (folie à deux) A delusion transferred from a dominant ill person to a close, dependent partner "Induced" delusion in a healthy person Schizoaffective vs psychotic depression/mania. If psychotic symptoms occur only during mood episodes → it's a mood disorder with psychotic features . If there's a stretch of ≥2 weeks of psychosis with the mood normal → schizoaffective . Mood-congruent delusions

chunks.heading: Ch 6. Depressive disorders
chunks.text: Ch 6. Depressive disorders Core. Major Depressive Disorder (MDD): pervasive low mood and/or loss of interest with vegetative and cognitive symptoms. Lifetime prevalence ~15%, ~2× more common in women . Mean onset late 20s. DSM-5 criteria — ≥5 of 9 symptoms over the same 2 weeks, ≥1 being depressed mood or anhedonia. Mnemonic SIG E CAPS + mood: S leep (insomnia/hypersomnia), I nterest loss (anhedonia), G uilt/worthlessness, E nergy loss/fatigue, C oncentration impaired, A ppetite/weight change, P sychomotor agitation/retardation, S uicidality, + depressed mood . Causes distress/impairment; not due to substance/medical cause. ICD-11 groups by severity (mild/moderate/severe ± psychotic) and lists affective, cognitive and neurovegetative clusters. Specifiers / subtypes. Melancholic (anhedonia, early-morning waking, diurnal variation worse in AM, marked guilt, psychomotor change — the "biological" depression). Atypical (mood reactivity , hypersomnia, hyperphagia/weight gain, leaden paralysis, rejection sensitivity). Psychotic (mood-congruent delusions: guilt, nihilism/ Cotard , poverty). Seasonal (winter, light-responsive). Peripartum (within 4 weeks/pregnancy). Catatonic . Other depressive disorders. Persistent Depressive Disorder (PDD / dysthymia) — depressed mood most days for ≥2 years (1 year in children), milder but chronic. Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD) — luteal-phase

chunks.heading: Ch 7. Bipolar & related disorders
chunks.text: Ch 7. Bipolar & related disorders Mania = a distinct period of abnormally elevated, expansive or irritable mood + increased energy, lasting ≥1 week (or any duration if hospitalised), with ≥3 symptoms (4 if mood is only irritable). Mnemonic DIG FAST : D istractibility, I ndiscretion/impulsivity (risky pleasure: spending, sex), G randiosity, F light of ideas, A ctivity increase/goal-directed, S leep decreased (no need for sleep), T alkativeness (pressured speech). Marked impairment, may be psychotic. Hypomania = same symptoms but ≥4 days , no marked impairment, no psychosis, no hospitalisation. Disorder Defining requirement Bipolar I ≥1 manic episode (depression not even required for the diagnosis) Bipolar II ≥1 hypomanic + ≥1 major depressive episode, and never a full manic episode Cyclothymia ≥2 years of fluctuating subthreshold hypomanic and depressive symptoms (never meeting full episode criteria) Bipolar I vs II vs cyclothymia: one full mania = BP-I (forever, even if it never recurs). Hypomania + depression, no mania = BP-II. Chronic subthreshold ups-and-downs ≥2 years = cyclothymia (the bipolar analogue of dysthymia). A manic switch triggered by an antidepressant counts toward bipolarity. Etiology & treatment. Highly heritable (MZ concordance ~60–70%, the most genetic of the mood disorders). Lithium is the prototype mood stabiliser (also anti-suicidal; needs level monitorin

chunks.heading: Ch 8. Anxiety disorders
chunks.text: Ch 8. Anxiety disorders Anxiety disorders share excessive fear (response to real/perceived imminent threat) and anxiety (anticipation of future threat). DSM-5 split off OCD and PTSD into their own chapters, so the anxiety group now is: GAD, panic disorder, agoraphobia, specific phobia, social anxiety, separation anxiety, selective mutism. Disorder Core + the cut-off Trap Generalised anxiety (GAD) Excessive, hard-to-control worry about many things, ≥6 months , + ≥3 of [restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance] Free-floating, no single trigger; 6-month rule Panic disorder Recurrent unexpected panic attacks (peak in minutes: palpitations, choking, derealisation, fear of dying/going mad) + ≥1 month of worry about more attacks or behaviour change The attack ≠ the disorder; you need 1 month of anticipatory worry Agoraphobia Fear of ≥2 situations (crowds, transport, open/enclosed spaces, queues, being outside alone) where escape is hard Now a standalone diagnosis in DSM-5, not just a panic add-on Specific phobia Marked fear of a specific object/situation (animal, blood-injection-injury, situational, natural environment), ≥6 months Blood-injection-injury phobia uniquely causes a vasovagal faint (biphasic BP/HR) Social anxiety (social phobia) Fear of scrutiny/negative evaluation in social/performance settings, ≥6 months Fear of embarrass

chunks.heading: Ch 9. Obsessive-Compulsive & Related Disorders
chunks.text: Ch 9. Obsessive-Compulsive & Related Disorders DSM-5 carved OCD out of the anxiety chapter into its own "OCD and Related Disorders" grouping (so did ICD-11). OCD = obsessions (recurrent, intrusive, unwanted thoughts/images/urges causing anxiety — contamination, doubt, symmetry, taboo) and/or compulsions (repetitive behaviours or mental acts performed to neutralise the anxiety — washing, checking, counting, ordering), recognised (in adults) as excessive, time-consuming (>1 hr/day) or impairing. Insight is usually retained (ego-dystonic), unlike a delusion. Related disorder Core Body dysmorphic disorder Preoccupation with an imagined/slight physical defect + repetitive checking/mirror behaviours Hoarding disorder Persistent difficulty discarding possessions, distress at parting, clutter (new DSM-5 category) Trichotillomania Recurrent hair-pulling Excoriation Recurrent skin-picking Obsession vs compulsion vs OCPD vs psychotic insight. Obsession = the intrusive thought ; compulsion = the act that relieves it. OCD ≠ OCPD : OCD is ego-dystonic anxiety with true obsessions/compulsions (an Axis-I/clinical disorder); Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder (OCPD) is an ego-syntonic personality style (perfectionism, orderliness, control, no true obsessions). If the patient is distressed by the thoughts → OCD; if they think their rigidity is correct → OCPD. Etiology & treatment. Cortico

chunks.heading: Ch 10. Trauma- & Stressor-Related Disorders
chunks.text: Ch 10. Trauma- & Stressor-Related Disorders DSM-5 made trauma its own chapter (out of anxiety). All require an identifiable stressor. Disorder Core + duration PTSD After exposure to actual/threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence: 4 symptom clusters — intrusion (flashbacks, nightmares), avoidance , negative alterations in cognition/mood , arousal (hypervigilance, startle) — lasting >1 month Acute stress disorder Same symptom pool but 3 days–1 month after the trauma (the <1 month window before it becomes PTSD) Adjustment disorder Emotional/behavioural symptoms within 3 months of an ordinary stressor (job loss, breakup), out of proportion, resolving within 6 months of the stressor ending Reactive attachment / disinhibited social engagement Childhood disorders from grossly inadequate caregiving Prolonged grief disorder Persistent, disabling grief beyond ~12 months (new in DSM-5-TR; also in ICD-11) ICD-11 split PTSD in two. ICD-11 has a simplified PTSD (just three clusters: re-experiencing in the here and now , avoidance, persistent sense of current threat ) PLUS a separate Complex PTSD (CPTSD) for prolonged/repeated trauma (childhood abuse, captivity): PTSD plus " Disturbances in Self-Organisation " (DSO) — affect dysregulation, negative self-concept, relationship disturbances. DSM-5 has no Complex PTSD. This DSM-vs-ICD difference is a favourite stem. ASD vs PTSD vs adj

chunks.heading: Ch 11. Dissociative disorders
chunks.text: Ch 11. Dissociative disorders A disruption of the normally integrated functions of consciousness, memory, identity, perception — psychologically driven (often post-trauma), not organic. Disorder Core Dissociative amnesia Inability to recall important (usually traumatic) autobiographical information, too extensive for ordinary forgetting; dissociative fugue (sudden purposeful travel + amnesia for identity) is now a specifier of it in DSM-5 Dissociative Identity Disorder (DID) ≥2 distinct personality states ("alters") with recurrent gaps in recall; formerly "multiple personality disorder"; strongly linked to severe childhood trauma Depersonalisation / derealisation disorder Persistent detachment from one's self (depersonalisation) or surroundings feel unreal (derealisation), with intact reality testing Dissociative (psychogenic) amnesia vs organic amnesia: dissociative = selective, autobiographical, identity-linked, reversible, normal new learning; organic (e.g. Korsakoff, head injury) = anterograde failure to form new memories, gradient, with neurological cause. Depersonalisation ≠ psychosis : the person knows it feels unreal (insight intact). Recap Ch 11. Dissociation = split in consciousness/memory/identity, psychogenic. Amnesia (fugue = a specifier), DID (≥2 alters, childhood trauma), depersonalisation/derealisation (reality testing intact). Separate psychogenic from organic

chunks.heading: Ch 12. Somatic Symptom & Related Disorders
chunks.text: Ch 12. Somatic Symptom & Related Disorders Physical symptoms or health worries that dominate life, with no proportionate organic explanation. DSM-5 reorganised this whole group (the old "somatoform" cluster), shifting the emphasis from "medically unexplained" to the excessive thoughts/feelings/behaviours about the symptoms. Disorder Core · DSM-5 change Somatic symptom disorder ≥1 distressing somatic symptom + disproportionate thoughts/anxiety/time devoted to it (≥6 months). Merged the old somatisation, pain and undifferentiated somatoform disorders Illness anxiety disorder Preoccupation with having/getting a serious illness with minimal or no somatic symptoms — replaced "hypochondriasis" Conversion disorder (Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder) Neurological-type deficits (paralysis, blindness, non-epileptic seizures, aphonia) incompatible with known disease; classic "la belle indifférence" and primary/secondary gain Factitious disorder Deliberately feigning/inducing symptoms to assume the sick role (no external reward); "imposed on another" = Munchausen by proxy The three-way intent trap — conversion vs factitious vs malingering. Conversion = unconscious production (the patient is not faking; symptom relieves a conflict). Factitious = conscious production for the internal reward of being a patient (the sick role). Malingering = conscious production for an external reward (

chunks.heading: Ch 13. Feeding & Eating Disorders
chunks.text: Ch 13. Feeding & Eating Disorders Disorder Core features Anorexia nervosa Restriction of intake → significantly low body weight; intense fear of weight gain; disturbed body image . Two types: restricting and binge-eating/purging . DSM-5 dropped the amenorrhoea requirement . Highest mortality of any psychiatric disorder (starvation + suicide) Bulimia nervosa Recurrent binge eating + recurrent compensatory behaviour (self-induced vomiting, laxatives, fasting, exercise), ≥1×/week for 3 months; weight usually normal or above . Signs: Russell's sign (knuckle calluses), parotid swelling, dental erosion, hypokalaemia Binge-eating disorder Recurrent binges with loss of control, no compensatory behaviour → often overweight (new full diagnosis in DSM-5) Pica / Rumination / ARFID Eating non-food (pica); regurgitation (rumination); avoidant/restrictive intake without body-image disturbance (ARFID) Anorexia vs bulimia: the discriminator is weight and body image . Anorexia = underweight , denies the problem, distorted body image. Bulimia = normal/above weight, knows it's a problem, ego-dystonic. A binge-purger who is underweight is anorexia (binge-purge type), not bulimia. BED = binges with no purging. Recap Ch 13. chunks.heading: Ch 14. Substance Use & Addictive Disorders
chunks.text: Ch 14. Substance Use & Addictive Disorders Two systems classify differently. ICD-10/11 dependence syndrome (Edwards & Gross) = ≥3 of 6 over a year: (1) compulsion/craving , (2) impaired control , (3) withdrawal , (4) tolerance , (5) neglect of other interests / salience , (6) persistence despite harm. DSM-5 merged "abuse" and "dependence" into one "Substance Use Disorder" on a severity spectrum (≥2 of 11 criteria → mild 2–3 / moderate 4–5 / severe ≥6). DSM-5 also added Gambling disorder as a behavioural addiction; ICD-11 added Gaming disorder . Substance Intoxication / Withdrawal highlights Alcohol Withdrawal: tremor → seizures → delirium tremens (autonomic storm, confusion, hallucinations, can be fatal). Wernicke's encephalopathy (thiamine deficiency: confusion + ophthalmoplegia + ataxia) → Korsakoff's psychosis (anterograde amnesia + confabulation ). Screen with CAGE . Treat withdrawal with benzodiazepines + thiamine Opioids Intoxication: pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression (reverse with naloxone ); withdrawal: dysphoric but not life-threatening (lacrimation, piloerection, cramps). Maintenance: methadone/buprenorphine Stimulants (cocaine, amphetamine) Intoxication: euphoria, dilated pupils, paranoia, formication; withdrawal: "crash" — dysphoria, hypersomnia, craving Cannabis Intoxication: conjunctival injection, increased appetite, altered time, anxiety/paranoia Benzodiaz

chunks.heading: Ch 15. Personality Disorders
chunks.text: Ch 15. Personality Disorders An enduring, pervasive, inflexible pattern of inner experience and behaviour that deviates markedly from cultural expectation, is stable from adolescence/early adulthood, and causes distress or impairment. DSM-5 (Section II) keeps 10 categorical PDs in 3 clusters : Cluster Theme Disorders (one-line) A — "odd / eccentric" The "mad" cluster Paranoid (distrust, suspiciousness) · Schizoid (detached, no desire for relationships) · Schizotypal (odd beliefs, magical thinking, eccentric — on the schizophrenia spectrum) B — "dramatic / erratic" The "bad" cluster Antisocial (disregard for/violation of others' rights, since age 15; needs conduct disorder before 15) · Borderline (instability of affect, relationships, self-image; impulsivity, self-harm, fear of abandonment) · Histrionic (excessive emotionality + attention-seeking) · Narcissistic (grandiosity, need for admiration, lack of empathy) C — "anxious / fearful" The "sad/scared" cluster Avoidant (social inhibition, feelings of inadequacy, hypersensitive to rejection) · Dependent (excessive need to be cared for, clinging) · Obsessive-Compulsive PD (perfectionism, orderliness, control — ego-syntonic) ICD-11 scrapped the categories. ICD-11 abolished the 10 types and made personality disorder fully dimensional : first rate severity (mild / moderate / severe), then add up to 5 trait domain qualifiers — Negati

chunks.heading: Ch 16. Neurocognitive Disorders — delirium & dementia (organic)
chunks.text: Ch 16. Neurocognitive Disorders — delirium & dementia (organic) Delirium (acute confusional state) Dementia (major neurocognitive disorder) Onset Acute / abrupt (hours–days) Insidious , gradual (months–years) Course Fluctuating , worse at night (sundowning) Stable/progressive, steadily worse Consciousness Clouded / impaired (the key sign) Clear until late Attention Markedly impaired (the core deficit) Relatively preserved early Hallmark deficit Inattention, disorientation Memory (esp. recent), then other domains Reversibility Usually reversible (treat the cause) Usually irreversible /progressive Cause Medical: infection, drugs, metabolic, withdrawal Neurodegeneration Delirium vs dementia, the one-line discriminator: delirium = clouded consciousness + acute + fluctuating + reversible ; dementia = clear consciousness + insidious + progressive + memory-led . A demented patient who suddenly becomes confused and drowsy has a superimposed delirium — find the medical cause. Dementia type Signature Alzheimer's (most common, ~60%) Gradual memory loss first; amyloid plaques + neurofibrillary (tau) tangles ; hippocampal/temporo-parietal atrophy; acetylcholine deficit (→ cholinesterase inhibitors: donepezil) Vascular (2nd) Stepwise deterioration, focal signs, history of strokes/hypertension Lewy body Fluctuating cognition + visual hallucinations + spontaneous parkinsonism ; neuroleptic sen

chunks.heading: Ch 17. Neurodevelopmental Disorders
chunks.text: Ch 17. Neurodevelopmental Disorders Disorder Core Intellectual Disability (intellectual developmental disorder) Deficits in intellectual functioning (reasoning, ~IQ<70) AND adaptive functioning (conceptual/social/practical), onset in the developmental period . DSM-5 grades severity by adaptive function , not IQ alone Autism Spectrum Disorder Two domains: (1) persistent deficits in social communication/interaction ; (2) restricted, repetitive behaviours/interests (stereotypy, insistence on sameness, sensory issues). DSM-5 merged autism, Asperger's and PDD-NOS into one spectrum ADHD Inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity, ≥6 symptoms, several present before age 12 , in ≥2 settings. Three presentations: inattentive, hyperactive-impulsive, combined. Treat with stimulants (methylphenidate) + behavioural Specific Learning Disorder Dyslexia (reading), dyscalculia (maths), dysgraphia (writing) — unexpected for age/IQ Tic disorders / Tourette's Motor + vocal tics >1 year = Tourette's Communication disorders Language, speech-sound, childhood-onset fluency (stuttering), social (pragmatic) communication ASD vs social anxiety vs intellectual disability: ASD has the restricted/repetitive domain (not present in social anxiety or pure ID). DSM-5 abolished Asperger's as a separate label — it's "ASD without language/intellectual impairment." ADHD's gate is onset before age 12 (was 7 in DSM

chunks.heading: Ch 18. Sexual dysfunctions, gender & sleep (brief)
chunks.text: Ch 18. Sexual dysfunctions, gender & sleep (brief) Sexual dysfunctions — disturbance in the sexual response cycle (desire → arousal → orgasm → resolution; Masters & Johnson / Kaplan): erectile disorder, female sexual interest/arousal, orgasmic disorders, genito-pelvic pain, premature/delayed ejaculation. Paraphilic disorders — atypical sexual interest that causes distress or harm to others (exhibitionism, voyeurism, frotteurism, paedophilic, sexual sadism/masochism, fetishism): a paraphilia is only a disorder when it distresses the person or harms a non-consenting other. Gender dysphoria (DSM-5) = distress from incongruence between experienced and assigned gender; ICD-11 renamed it "gender incongruence" and moved it OUT of the mental-disorders chapter (into sexual-health conditions), de-pathologising it. Sleep-wake — insomnia (commonest), hypersomnolence , narcolepsy (sleep attacks + cataplexy + sleep paralysis + hypnagogic hallucinations; orexin/hypocretin loss), breathing-related (sleep apnoea), circadian-rhythm disorders, parasomnias (sleepwalking, night terrors in NREM; nightmares + REM-sleep behaviour disorder in REM). Gender incongruence: the headline DSM-vs-ICD difference is that ICD-11 removed it from mental disorders (DSM-5 still lists Gender Dysphoria, framed around the distress , not the identity). Night terror vs nightmare: terror = NREM, early night, no recall, chi

chunks.heading: Ch 19. Treatment map (drug class → what it treats)
chunks.text: Ch 19. Treatment map (drug class → what it treats) Class Examples Mechanism / use Typical antipsychotics Haloperidol, chlorpromazine D2 blockade; psychosis; EPS + tardive dyskinesia risk Atypical antipsychotics Risperidone, olanzapine, clozapine D2 + 5-HT2; fewer EPS; clozapine for resistant schizophrenia (agranulocytosis) SSRIs Fluoxetine, sertraline First-line for depression, anxiety, OCD, PTSD, bulimia SNRIs / TCAs / MAOIs Venlafaxine / imipramine, clomipramine / phenelzine Depression; clomipramine for OCD; MAOIs need tyramine-free diet Mood stabilisers Lithium , valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine Bipolar; lithium is anti-suicidal, narrow index Anxiolytics Benzodiazepines (diazepam), buspirone GABA agonists; short-term anxiety, dependence risk Stimulants Methylphenidate, amphetamine ADHD ECT — Severe/psychotic/suicidal/refractory depression, catatonia, severe mania Psychotherapies by indication (quick map): ERP → OCD; exposure / systematic desensitisation / flooding → phobias & PTSD; CBT → depression, anxiety, most disorders; DBT (Linehan) → borderline PD & self-harm; IPT → depression; family therapy / lowering EE → schizophrenia; CBT-E / family-based (Maudsley) → eating disorders; MI → addictions.

chunks.heading: Abnormal Psychology — the integrative approach, disorder by disorder (Barlow & Durand + DSM-5-TR + ICD-11)
chunks.text: Abnormal Psychology — the integrative approach, disorder by disorder (Barlow & Durand + DSM-5-TR + ICD-11) The Abnormal section built the way Barlow & Durand, Abnormal Psychology: An Integrative Approach teaches it: every disorder opens with a clinical case , then runs the book's four-beat frame — (1) clinical description · (2) statistics (prevalence, onset, sex ratio, course) · (3) causes , read through the multidimensional integrative model (biological × psychological × emotional × social × developmental) · (4) treatment . On top of the book, every disorder's classification is cross-checked against the current criteria so nothing is outdated: DSM-5-TR (APA, 2022) and ICD-11 (WHO, in force Jan 2022), shown side by side where they differ (the ICD-11 reclassifications are exactly what MET/NIMHANS/RCI fish for). Look-alike distinctions MCQs live on are in red trap boxes; where NIMHANS pushes past the book it's in purple . This is the companion to the Ahuja full-book page — same disorders, the integrative/case lens instead of the Indian-psychiatry lens. Built 2026-06-07. Abnormal (Barlow & Durand) Abnormal (Ahuja, full book) Abnormal cheatsheet ICD breakdown High-yield sheet Counselling (Sharf) Lookalikes What is "Barlow & Durand" and why a second abnormal page. The Ahuja page reads the field as Indian psychiatry: definitions, criteria, drugs, fast and exam-tight. Barlow & Durand

chunks.heading: Ch 1. What makes behaviour a disorder, and the three traditions
chunks.text: Ch 1. What makes behaviour a disorder, and the three traditions Barlow & Durand do not use a "4 Ds" list. Their working definition of a psychological disorder has three components , and all three usually travel together: (1) psychological dysfunction — a breakdown in cognitive, emotional or behavioural functioning; (2) distress or impairment — it hurts the person or wrecks their day-to-day functioning; (3) an atypical or culturally unexpected response — it deviates from what the culture expects (and is not merely a deviant act society dislikes). They lean on Wakefield's "harmful dysfunction" : a disorder is a failure of an internal mechanism to do what it evolved to do ( dysfunction ) and that failure is harmful to the person by their culture's standards. B&D's 3 vs Ahuja's 4 Ds. If a question cites " dysfunction + distress/impairment + atypical/culturally unexpected ," that's the Barlow & Durand definition (3 components). The "Deviance, Distress, Dysfunction, Danger" 4-D list is the more common Indian-text framing. Danger is NOT one of B&D's three. Both agree dysfunction/impairment is the indispensable core and distress alone is neither necessary nor sufficient (a person in mania feels great). Tradition Core claim · key names Treatment it implies Supernatural Possession, sin, the moon, witchcraft; Malleus Maleficarum (1487); the "mass hysteria"/St Vitus dances Exorcism, prayer

chunks.heading: Ch 2. The integrative (multidimensional) model — the signature of the book
chunks.text: Ch 2. The integrative (multidimensional) model — the signature of the book This is the chapter the rest of the book runs on, and the one most worth knowing cold. No disorder has one cause; B&D insist on a multidimensional integrative reading where several dimensions interact over time. Dimension What it contributes · the B&D concepts Genetic Genes rarely cause a disorder alone; they set vulnerability . Key B&D ideas: diathesis-stress (a gene/vulnerability lies dormant until stress triggers it), the reciprocal gene-environment model (your genetic make-up makes you seek environments that then express the gene), and epigenetics (experience switches gene expression on/off without changing DNA). Polygenic, not one "gene for" anything. Neuroscience Brain structure (limbic system, amygdala = fear; hippocampus; prefrontal cortex; basal ganglia; HPA axis) and neurotransmitters as currents, not switches: serotonin (regulation/restraint of behaviour), GABA (the brake — reduces anxiety; benzodiazepines act here), glutamate (the accelerator), norepinephrine (alarm/arousal), dopamine (reward, "switch" for other systems; implicated in schizophrenia & addiction). The HPA axis → cortisol is the body's stress engine. Behavioural & cognitive Classical & operant conditioning of maladaptive responses; learned helplessness (Seligman — uncontrollable aversive events → giving up → a model of depressio

chunks.heading: Ch 3. Clinical assessment & diagnosis
chunks.text: Ch 3. Clinical assessment & diagnosis Good assessment is reliable (consistent — same result across raters/time), valid (measures what it claims), and standardised (fixed procedure + norms). B&D's tools: the clinical interview + mental status exam (appearance/behaviour, thought process & content, mood & affect, intellectual functioning, sensorium); behavioural assessment (ABCs — antecedent, behaviour, consequence); psychological tests — projective (Rorschach, TAT — unstructured, weak psychometrics), objective/personality (MMPI), intelligence (WAIS/WISC), and neuropsychological (Halstead-Reitan, Luria-Nebraska); plus neuroimaging (CT/MRI structure; fMRI/PET function) and psychophysiology (EEG, heart rate, EDA). DSM-5-TR (APA, 2022) Mostly categorical (you have it or you don't) with criteria sets + thresholds. Multiaxial system abandoned in DSM-5 (the old Axes I–V are gone). Organised so related disorders sit together (anxiety / OCD / trauma split into 3 chapters). Adds dimensional severity ratings and cross-cutting measures alongside categories. ICD-11 (WHO, in force 2022) Global standard; mental disorders = Chapter 06 . India follows ICD officially. More prototype/description-based — leans on clinician judgement, fewer rigid counts. Built-in dimensionality (clearest in personality disorders). Never used DSM-style axes. Reliability ≠ validity. A test can be reliable (consistent)

chunks.heading: Ch 4. Anxiety disorders, and Barlow's triple vulnerability
chunks.text: Ch 4. Anxiety disorders, and Barlow's triple vulnerability B&D draw a sharp line between three states. Anxiety = a future-oriented mood state, apprehension about possible threat (cognitive/somatic tension). Fear = an immediate alarm reaction to present danger — the fight-flight response firing now. Panic attack = fear occurring when there is nothing to be afraid of — a false alarm. Cued (situational) vs uncued/unexpected panic attacks; only unexpected ones define panic disorder. The triple vulnerability theory (Barlow) — pure B&D, very testable. Anxiety disorders grow from three vulnerabilities stacking : (1) generalised biological vulnerability (a heritable tendency to be tense/neurotic); (2) generalised psychological vulnerability (a sense, from early experience, that the world is dangerous and uncontrollable); (3) specific psychological vulnerability (learning, from family/experience, what to focus the anxiety on — e.g. "physical symptoms are dangerous" → panic; "social evaluation is dangerous" → social anxiety). General vulnerabilities alone aren't enough; the specific one points the anxiety at its target.

chunks.heading: Generalised Anxiety Disorder (GAD)
chunks.text: Generalised Anxiety Disorder (GAD) Clinical snapshot A woman describes herself as a lifelong worrier: she frets about her kids, money, her health, being late, things that "might" go wrong, can't switch it off, feels keyed-up and tired, sleeps badly, neck always tense. There's no single feared object, just a roving, uncontrollable worry that has been there for years. Clinical description: excessive, uncontrollable worry about multiple everyday domains, with physical tension. The cognition (worry) is the engine; B&D note GAD patients show autonomic restriction (chronically tense, not spiking) — worry may be an avoidance of worse imagery. Statistics: ~3% (1-yr), insidious onset, often early; ~2:1 female. Causes: generalised biological + psychological vulnerability; worry as cognitive avoidance. Treatment: CBT (especially targeting the worry process), SSRIs/SNRIs, short-term benzodiazepines for acute relief only. DSM-5-TR — GAD Excessive anxiety/worry, more days than not, for ≥6 months , about several events. Worry is hard to control . ≥3 of 6 : restlessness, easily fatigued, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance. Distress/impairment; not substance/medical. ICD-11 — GAD Marked general apprehension or worry about multiple events, ≥ several months (most days). Plus additional symptoms: muscle tension, restlessness, autonomic overactivity, difficulty conc

chunks.heading: Ch 5. Panic disorder & agoraphobia
chunks.text: Ch 5. Panic disorder & agoraphobia Clinical snapshot A young man's heart suddenly races in a supermarket, he can't breathe, his hands tingle, he's sure he's having a heart attack and is going to die. ER tests are normal. Now he scans his body constantly and avoids supermarkets, then buses, then leaving home alone, in case "it" happens again where he can't get help. Clinical description: recurrent unexpected panic attacks (abrupt surge of fear peaking within minutes — palpitations, sweating, choking, chest pain, derealisation, fear of dying/going crazy) followed by persistent worry about more attacks or a maladaptive change in behaviour. Agoraphobia = fear/avoidance of situations where escape is hard or help unavailable if panic strikes (transport, open/enclosed spaces, crowds, queues, being out alone). Statistics: panic ~2–3%, onset adolescence–mid-30s, ~2:1 female; agoraphobia often follows panic. Causes (B&D's model): an initial false alarm (a panic attack out of the blue) becomes a learned alarm through interoceptive conditioning — the body's own sensations (racing heart) become conditioned cues for panic — layered on anxiety sensitivity (the belief that bodily sensations are dangerous). Treatment: CBT with interoceptive exposure (deliberately bring on the sensations and disconfirm catastrophe) + in-vivo exposure for agoraphobia; SSRIs/SNRIs; benzodiazepines only short-term.

chunks.heading: Ch 6. Specific phobia & social anxiety disorder
chunks.text: Ch 6. Specific phobia & social anxiety disorder Clinical snapshot (B&D's classic "Judy" case) A bright teenager faints whenever she sees blood, even a drop, even on TV in biology class — her blood pressure spikes then crashes (the vasovagal drop), she goes pale and passes out. She has reorganised her whole life to avoid the sight of blood or injury. Specific phobia = marked, persistent, unreasonable fear of a specific object/situation, ≥6 months, with avoidance. B&D's four subtypes: blood-injection-injury (BII) , situational (planes, lifts), natural environment (heights, water, storms), animal (+ "other"). BII is unique : a biphasic, diphasic vasovagal response — BP and HR briefly rise then sharply drop , causing fainting — and it runs strongly in families (the only phobia where you faint). Social anxiety disorder (social phobia) = marked fear of scrutiny/negative evaluation in social or performance situations. Causes: direct conditioning, vicarious learning (watching someone else's fear), information transmission, all on a base of prepared learning (Seligman) + the triple vulnerability. Treatment: exposure is first-line (graded exposure, systematic desensitisation, participant modelling); for BII add applied tension (tense muscles to keep BP up and prevent the faint); social anxiety adds cognitive restructuring + SSRIs. BII phobia is the one that makes you faint. Every other p

chunks.heading: Ch 7. Trauma- & stressor-related disorders (PTSD)
chunks.text: Ch 7. Trauma- & stressor-related disorders (PTSD) Clinical snapshot Months after a motorway pile-up, a driver still jolts awake from nightmares of the crash, can't drive past the spot, feels numb and detached from his family, can't remember part of the crash, and snaps at any sudden noise. It hasn't faded; it's running his life. PTSD follows exposure to actual/threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence (directly, witnessed, or learned-of for close others). DSM-5 moved PTSD out of the anxiety chapter into "Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders." Four symptom clusters: intrusion (flashbacks, nightmares), avoidance , negative alterations in cognition/mood , arousal/reactivity (hypervigilance, exaggerated startle), lasting >1 month . Acute Stress Disorder = the same picture lasting 3 days–1 month right after the trauma. Causes: the trauma is necessary but not sufficient — pre-trauma vulnerability (biological reactivity, prior trauma), peri-trauma severity, and post-trauma factors (lack of social support) decide who develops it; a conditioned-fear + failure-of-extinction model. Treatment: trauma-focused CBT, prolonged exposure , cognitive processing therapy, EMDR; SSRIs. DSM-5-TR — Trauma disorders One PTSD diagnosis, 4 clusters (intrusion, avoidance, negative cognition/mood, arousal), >1 month. Acute Stress Disorder for the 3-day–1-month window. A dissociative subtype of

chunks.heading: Ch 8. Obsessive-Compulsive & Related Disorders
chunks.text: Ch 8. Obsessive-Compulsive & Related Disorders Clinical snapshot A student washes his hands until they bleed because an intrusive image of "germs spreading death to my family" floods him with dread; the washing relieves it for minutes, then it returns. He knows it's irrational, hates it, and it now eats four hours a day. DSM-5 carved OCD out of anxiety into its own grouping (ICD-11 too). OCD = obsessions (recurrent, intrusive, unwanted thoughts/images/urges that cause anxiety — contamination, doubt, symmetry, taboo/aggressive) and/or compulsions (repetitive behaviours/mental acts done to neutralise the anxiety — washing, checking, counting, ordering, praying), time-consuming (>1 hr/day). Insight is usually retained ( ego-dystonic ). Related: Body Dysmorphic Disorder (preoccupation with an imagined/slight defect + mirror-checking), Hoarding disorder (new), Trichotillomania (hair-pulling), Excoriation (skin-picking). Causes: cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loop overactivity, serotonin; cognitively, thought-action fusion (treating a thought as morally equal to the act) and inflated responsibility maintain it; the compulsion is negatively reinforced by anxiety relief. Treatment: Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) is the treatment of choice (expose to the trigger, block the compulsion, let anxiety habituate) + SSRIs (often high-dose); clomipramine. OCD vs OCPD. OCD = ego-dyston

chunks.heading: Ch 9. Somatic symptom & related disorders
chunks.text: Ch 9. Somatic symptom & related disorders Clinical snapshot A man is convinced his stomach aches mean cancer. Test after test is clear, doctor after doctor reassures him, but within days the fear is back; he reads symptom websites for hours, books more scans, and his life narrows to monitoring his body. The body is the stage; the distress is psychological. DSM-5 collapsed the old "somatoform" list into fewer, clearer categories and dropped the requirement that symptoms be medically unexplained — what matters now is the excessive response to symptoms. Disorder Core Somatic Symptom Disorder One+ distressing somatic symptoms + excessive thoughts/feelings/behaviours about them (≥6 months). Symptom may even be medically real — it's the disproportionate response that's the disorder. Illness Anxiety Disorder Preoccupation with having/getting a serious illness with few or no somatic symptoms; high health anxiety, checking or avoidance. (The reworked "hypochondriasis.") Conversion Disorder (Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder) Neurological symptoms (paralysis, blindness, non-epileptic seizures, aphonia) incompatible with any medical disease; classic sign la belle indifférence (oddly calm about a dramatic deficit). Freud's original "hysteria." Factitious Disorder Deliberately faking/inducing symptoms to assume the sick role (no external reward). Imposed on another = factitious disor

chunks.heading: Ch 10. Dissociative disorders
chunks.text: Ch 10. Dissociative disorders A disruption of the normally integrated functions of consciousness, memory, identity and perception — usually trauma-linked. Disorder Core Dissociative Amnesia Inability to recall important (usually traumatic) autobiographical information, beyond ordinary forgetting. Dissociative fugue = amnesia + sudden purposeful travel /wandering, now a specifier of amnesia. Depersonalisation / Derealisation Disorder Persistent detachment from one's self (depersonalisation — "I'm watching myself," unreal body) or surroundings (derealisation — the world looks dreamlike/foggy), with intact reality testing . Dissociative Identity Disorder (DID) Two+ distinct personality states + recurrent gaps in memory. Strongly linked to severe, early, chronic trauma (the post-traumatic model). Formerly "multiple personality disorder." DID ≠ schizophrenia. "Split mind" (Bleuler's term for schizophrenia) = split among thought/emotion/behaviour, not split into multiple people. DID = multiple identity states. A common deliberate distractor. Also: depersonalisation keeps reality testing intact (you know it's not real), unlike psychosis. Recap Ch 10. Dissociation = breakdown of integrated consciousness/memory/identity. Amnesia (± fugue travel), depersonalisation/derealisation (detachment, reality intact), DID (≥2 identity states + amnesia, trauma-driven). DID is not schizophrenia. Par

chunks.heading: Ch 11. Mood (depressive & bipolar) disorders
chunks.text: Ch 11. Mood (depressive & bipolar) disorders Clinical snapshot For two months a woman has felt flat and hopeless, dropped the things she used to love, sleeps badly and wakes at 4am, can't concentrate at work, feels worthless and "a burden," and has started thinking everyone would be better off without her. B&D build the chapter from mood episodes (the building blocks) up to the disorders (defined by which episodes occur). Episode Definition Major depressive episode ≥5/9 over the same 2 weeks (≥1 = depressed mood or anhedonia): mood, anhedonia, weight/appetite, sleep, psychomotor change, fatigue, worthlessness/guilt, poor concentration, suicidality ( SIG E CAPS ). Manic episode Abnormally elevated/expansive/ irritable mood + increased energy, ≥1 week , ≥3 symptoms ( DIG FAST : distractibility, indiscretion, grandiosity, flight of ideas, activity↑, sleep need↓, talkativeness); marked impairment / may be psychotic. Hypomanic episode Same symptoms, ≥4 days , no marked impairment, no psychosis, no hospitalisation. Disorder Defining requirement Major Depressive Disorder ≥1 major depressive episode, no mania/hypomania ever. Persistent Depressive Disorder (dysthymia) Depressed mood most days ≥2 years (1 yr in youth); chronic but milder. "Double depression" = MDD on top of PDD. Bipolar I ≥1 full manic episode (depression not required). Bipolar II ≥1 hypomanic + ≥1 major depressive ; nev

chunks.heading: Ch 12. Suicide
chunks.text: Ch 12. Suicide B&D treat suicide in the mood chapter. Durkheim's sociological types: egoistic (low social integration, isolation), altruistic (over-integration, dying for the group), anomic (sudden disruption of norms — a crash, a job loss), fatalistic (over-regulation, no escape). Risk factors: prior attempt (the strongest predictor), a clear plan/means, hopelessness, male sex (men complete more; women attempt more), older age, substance use, recent loss, family history, access to lethal means. Terms: ideation → plan → attempt → completion ; parasuicide /non-suicidal self-injury (self-harm without intent to die). Prevention: means restriction, crisis lines, treating the underlying disorder; lithium specifically lowers suicide in bipolar. Men vs women. Women attempt suicide more often; men complete (die by) suicide more often, largely because of more lethal means. The single best predictor of a future attempt is a past attempt . Recap Ch 12. Durkheim: egoistic / altruistic / anomic / fatalistic. Strongest predictor = prior attempt; hopelessness + plan + means raise risk. Women attempt more, men complete more. Restrict means, treat the disorder. Part Five · Eating & sleep–wake disorders (B&D Ch 8)

chunks.heading: Ch 13. Eating disorders
chunks.text: Ch 13. Eating disorders Clinical snapshot A 17-year-old at 78% of expected weight insists she is "fat," skips meals, runs daily, weighs herself five times a day, and has stopped menstruating; her family is frightened but she cannot see a problem. Disorder Core Anorexia Nervosa Restriction → significantly low weight , intense fear of weight gain, distorted body image / denial of seriousness. Subtypes: restricting vs binge-eating/purging . (DSM-5 dropped the amenorrhoea requirement .) Highest mortality of any mental disorder. Bulimia Nervosa Recurrent binge + compensatory behaviour (vomiting, laxatives, fasting, over-exercise), self-evaluation over-tied to shape/weight; weight usually normal . Signs: Russell's sign (knuckle calluses), parotid swelling, eroded enamel. Binge-Eating Disorder Recurrent binges with no compensatory behaviour; distress; new full DSM-5 category . Most common eating disorder; linked to obesity. Statistics: ~90% female, onset adolescence, Western/industrialised & weight-focused subcultures over-represented. Causes (integrative): sociocultural thin-ideal internalisation + dieting + perfectionism + low self-esteem, on a genetic/temperamental base; serotonin involvement. Treatment: CBT is first-line for bulimia and binge-eating ; anorexia — weight restoration first, then family-based treatment (Maudsley) for adolescents; SSRIs help bulimia. DSM-5-TR — Eating

chunks.heading: Ch 14. Sleep–wake disorders
chunks.text: Ch 14. Sleep–wake disorders Group Key disorders Dyssomnias (amount/quality/timing) Insomnia disorder (trouble falling/staying asleep); Hypersomnolence ; Narcolepsy (sleep attacks + cataplexy + sleep-onset REM, low hypocretin/orexin); breathing-related ( sleep apnoea ); circadian-rhythm disorders. Parasomnias (abnormal events) NREM : sleepwalking & sleep terrors (deep slow-wave sleep, no dream recall, hard to wake). REM : nightmare disorder (vivid dreams, easily recalled) & REM sleep behaviour disorder. Sleep terror vs nightmare. Sleep terror = NREM (slow-wave), early night, child screams/agitated but unwakeable and amnesic for it. Nightmare = REM, later night, person wakes fully and remembers the dream. Narcolepsy's giveaway = cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone with emotion). Treatment: insomnia — CBT-I (stimulus control, sleep restriction, sleep hygiene) is first-line over hypnotics; narcolepsy — stimulants/modafinil + scheduled naps; apnoea — CPAP. Recap Ch 14. Dyssomnias (insomnia, narcolepsy+cataplexy, apnoea, circadian) vs parasomnias (NREM sleep terrors/sleepwalking — amnesic; REM nightmares — recalled). CBT-I first-line for insomnia. Part Six · Sexual / gender, substance & impulse (B&D Ch 10–11)

chunks.heading: Ch 15. Sexual dysfunctions, gender dysphoria & paraphilic disorders
chunks.text: Ch 15. Sexual dysfunctions, gender dysphoria & paraphilic disorders B&D split this into three very different things — don't blur them. Group Core Sexual dysfunctions Problems in the sexual response cycle: desire (low desire), arousal (erectile, female arousal), orgasm (premature/delayed/female orgasmic), pain (genito-pelvic pain/penetration). Persistent + distressing. Gender dysphoria Distress from a marked incongruence between experienced and assigned gender. The diagnosis is the distress, not the identity. Paraphilic disorders Intense atypical sexual interest (e.g. voyeuristic, exhibitionistic, frotteuristic, sexual sadism/masochism, pedophilic, fetishistic) that causes distress/impairment or harms others . A paraphilia is only a disorder when it harms or distresses. DSM-5-TR Keeps "Gender Dysphoria" as a diagnosis (distress-based) within mental disorders. Paraphilia vs paraphilic disorder distinction (interest vs harmful/distressing). ICD-11 Moved gender out of mental disorders : renamed "Gender incongruence," placed in a new chapter on sexual health — explicitly de-pathologised . Paraphilic = "Paraphilic disorders," focused on risk/non-consent. The MET/RCI favourite: ICD-11 removed gender incongruence from the mental-disorders chapter (it's now under sexual health), while DSM-5-TR still lists Gender Dysphoria. Also: a paraphilia (the interest) is not itself a disorder — it

chunks.heading: Ch 16. Substance-related, addictive & impulse-control disorders
chunks.text: Ch 16. Substance-related, addictive & impulse-control disorders DSM-5 merged abuse + dependence into a single Substance Use Disorder on a severity spectrum (mild/moderate/severe by symptom count across 4 groups: impaired control, social impairment, risky use, pharmacological = tolerance + withdrawal). Key terms: tolerance (need more for the same effect), withdrawal (a substance-specific syndrome on stopping), intoxication . Substance classes: depressants (alcohol, benzodiazepines, opioids — though opioids are often listed apart), stimulants (cocaine, amphetamines, nicotine, caffeine), opioids , hallucinogens , cannabis . Behavioural addiction: DSM-5 added Gambling Disorder (the first non-substance addiction, reflecting a shared reward-circuit/dopamine basis); ICD-11 added Gaming disorder too. Causes: dopamine reward pathway (nucleus accumbens, VTA), positive then negative reinforcement (use to feel good → use to stop feeling bad), genetic vulnerability, social learning, conditioning of cues. Treatment: motivational interviewing, CBT/relapse-prevention, contingency management, 12-step; agonist/antagonist meds (methadone/buprenorphine, naltrexone, disulfiram, nicotine replacement). Reclassifications to know: DSM-5 collapsed abuse + dependence into one Substance Use Disorder (severity-graded), and added Gambling Disorder as a behavioural addiction; ICD-11 added Gaming disorder . chunks.heading: Ch 17. Personality disorders
chunks.text: Ch 17. Personality disorders An enduring, pervasive, inflexible pattern of inner experience and behaviour deviating markedly from cultural expectation, stable from adolescence/early adulthood, causing distress/impairment — across cognition, affect, interpersonal functioning, impulse control. DSM-5 keeps 10 categorical types in three clusters . Cluster Theme Disorders (the one-line tell) A — "odd / eccentric" Withdrawn, mistrustful Paranoid (pervasive distrust); Schizoid (detached loner, no desire for relationships); Schizotypal (eccentric, magical thinking, odd perceptions — on the schizophrenia spectrum) B — "dramatic / erratic" Emotional, impulsive Antisocial (disregard for/violation of others' rights, deceit, no remorse; ≥18, conduct disorder before 15); Borderline (instability of relationships, self-image, affect + impulsivity, fear of abandonment, self-harm); Histrionic (attention-seeking, shallow dramatic emotion); Narcissistic (grandiosity, need for admiration, lack of empathy) C — "anxious / fearful" Tense, inhibited Avoidant (social inhibition, feels inadequate, hypersensitive to rejection); Dependent (clinging, can't decide alone, needs to be taken care of); Obsessive-Compulsive PD (perfectionism, orderliness, control — ego-syntonic) DSM-5-TR — PDs Kept the 10 categorical types in 3 clusters (Section II). An Alternative DSM-5 Model (dimensional: impairment + 5 trait d

chunks.heading: Ch 18. Schizophrenia & other psychotic disorders
chunks.text: Ch 18. Schizophrenia & other psychotic disorders Clinical snapshot A 21-year-old, withdrawn over the past year, now believes the TV is sending him coded messages, hears two voices commenting on everything he does, speaks in derailed half-sentences, and has stopped washing or going to class. Clinical description: a disturbance of thought, perception, affect and behaviour. Positive symptoms (excess of normal function): delusions (fixed false beliefs — persecutory, grandiose, referential, of control), hallucinations (usually auditory ), disorganised speech (derailment, tangentiality, word salad), grossly disorganised/catatonic behaviour. Negative symptoms (loss): avolition (apathy), alogia (poverty of speech), anhedonia , asociality , flat affect . Disorganised symptoms (speech + behaviour + inappropriate affect). Statistics: lifetime ~ 1% , equal sexes, earlier onset in men (late teens–20s) than women. Causes (integrative): strongest is genetic (MZ concordance ~48%, ~10% in a first-degree relative); the dopamine hypothesis (mesolimbic D2 overactivity → positive symptoms; all antipsychotics block D2) refined to include glutamate/NMDA; neurodevelopmental markers (enlarged ventricles, reduced grey matter, obstetric complications, winter birth, maternal infection); and the psychosocial expressed emotion (EE) finding — high family criticism/over-involvement predicts relapse . Treatmen

chunks.heading: Ch 19. Neurodevelopmental disorders
chunks.text: Ch 19. Neurodevelopmental disorders Onset in the developmental period (childhood), with deficits that impair personal/social/academic functioning. Disorder Core Intellectual Disability Deficits in intellectual (reasoning, IQ ~<70) and adaptive functioning, onset in development. Severity now graded by adaptive functioning , not IQ score alone. Autism Spectrum Disorder Two domains: (1) persistent deficits in social communication/interaction; (2) restricted, repetitive behaviours/interests + sensory sensitivities. DSM-5 merged autistic disorder, Asperger's and PDD-NOS into one spectrum with severity levels. ADHD Inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity , ≥6 symptoms, several before age 12 , in ≥2 settings. Presentations: inattentive, hyperactive-impulsive, combined. Treated with stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamines) + behavioural therapy. Specific Learning Disorder Difficulty in reading (dyslexia), writing or maths (dyscalculia) well below age, despite adequate instruction/IQ. Tic disorders Tourette's = multiple motor + ≥1 vocal tic, >1 year. ASD reclassification. DSM-5 abolished Asperger's as a separate diagnosis — it's folded into Autism Spectrum Disorder with severity levels. ADHD onset moved from "before 7" (DSM-IV) to "before age 12 " (DSM-5). High-yield change items. Recap Ch 19. ID (intellectual + adaptive, graded by adaptive function), ASD (social-communication +

chunks.heading: Ch 20. Neurocognitive disorders
chunks.text: Ch 20. Neurocognitive disorders Disorder Core · the delirium vs dementia split Delirium Acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention & awareness + cognition, over hours–days, from a medical cause (infection, drugs, metabolic). Reversible , clouded consciousness. A medical emergency. Major Neurocognitive Disorder (dementia) Gradual, progressive decline in ≥1 cognitive domain (memory, executive, language, etc.) that impairs independence, with clear consciousness . Subtypes: Alzheimer's (commonest — amyloid plaques + tau tangles, insidious memory-first), vascular, frontotemporal, Lewy body, Parkinson's, HIV. Mild NCD = decline without loss of independence. Delirium vs dementia — the exam's favourite pair. Delirium = acute onset, fluctuating , attention impaired, consciousness clouded , usually reversible . Dementia = gradual , progressive , memory -led, consciousness clear , usually irreversible. (DSM-5 renamed dementia " major neurocognitive disorder .") Recap Ch 20. Delirium = acute, fluctuating, attention/consciousness, reversible. Major NCD (dementia) = gradual, progressive, memory, clear consciousness; Alzheimer's = plaques + tangles, commonest. Don't swap the two. Part Ten · Exam armoury

chunks.heading: Self-test (cover the answers, active recall)
chunks.text: Self-test (cover the answers, active recall) What are Barlow & Durand's three components of a psychological disorder, and which "D" is missing vs the 4-D list? — dysfunction + distress/impairment + atypical/culturally unexpected; Danger is missing. Name the three vulnerabilities in Barlow's triple vulnerability theory. — generalised biological, generalised psychological, specific psychological. Equifinality vs multifinality? — many roads to one disorder vs one cause to many outcomes. Which neurotransmitter is the "brake" and which the "accelerator"? — GABA (brake), glutamate (accelerator). Panic disorder needs how long of anticipatory worry after the attacks? — ≥1 month. What is the B&D mechanism that turns a first panic attack into panic disorder? — interoceptive conditioning + anxiety sensitivity (false alarm → learned alarm). Which phobia makes you faint, and how is it treated? — blood-injection-injury (biphasic vasovagal); applied tension. Which manual has Complex PTSD? — ICD-11 (not DSM-5-TR). Conversion vs factitious vs malingering — split them. — unconscious / sick-role (internal) / external reward (and malingering isn't a disorder). DID vs schizophrenia — what does "split" actually mean in schizophrenia? — split among thought/emotion/behaviour (Bleuler), not multiple people. chunks.heading: Abnormal Psychology, Cheatsheet
chunks.text: Abnormal Psychology, Cheatsheet MET 2026 + NIMHANS · Built 2026-05-05 · The abnormal patch. How to use. Goes deeper than the high-yield revision sheet. Read once for coverage, then revise off tables + red TRAP boxes. Anything you blank on, mark it and re-read the matching section on the next pass.

chunks.heading: 1. Defining Abnormality (4 Ds)
chunks.text: 1. Defining Abnormality (4 Ds) Deviance — statistical or social norm violation. Distress — subjective suffering. Dysfunction — impairs daily life / role functioning. Danger — risk to self or others. TRAP: Deviance alone ≠ abnormal. A genius IQ is statistically deviant but not pathological. Always need at least distress or dysfunction with it. Some textbooks list a 5th D: Duration , especially for chronicity criteria (≥ 6 months, ≥ 2 years, etc.).

chunks.heading: 2. Historical Models
chunks.text: 2. Historical Models Era Model Key name(s) Prehistoric Supernatural (demons, possession) Trephination Greek / Roman Biological, four humors Hippocrates, Galen Middle Ages Demonological return, witch trials Malleus Maleficarum (1487) Renaissance Asylum reform begins Pinel (Bicêtre, "moral treatment"), Tuke (York Retreat) 19th c. Biological, classification Kraepelin ( dementia praecox ), Bleuler (renamed schizophrenia , 4 As) Early 20th c. Psychological Freud (psychoanalysis), Watson (behaviorism) Mid 20th c. Cognitive-behavioral Beck (depression), Ellis (REBT) 1980s+ Biopsychosocial integration Engel (1977) TRAP: Kraepelin coined dementia praecox . Bleuler renamed it schizophrenia ("split mind", referring to fragmented thought, not split personality). Don't confuse with DID.
