chunks.heading: Biopsychology — Carlson depth pass
chunks.text: Biopsychology — Carlson depth pass Source: Carlson & Birkett, Physiology of Behavior (the book Sihan named on 2026-05-28). This page is the delta on top of the Pinel chapter : it walks the systems Carlson goes deeper on than Pinel does, in Carlson's order, and locks the parts NIMHANS / MET love to test. Built 2026-05-28 — first section of the per-section depth pass rollout. Use this after reading the Pinel chapter ; together they cover the section in full. Why a Carlson pass on top of Pinel? The two books overlap on the basics (neurons, anatomy, vision/audition, sensorimotor, plasticity, lateralisation) but diverge on the mechanism-heavy systems. Carlson goes much deeper on (1) the mesolimbic reward circuit and drug-of-abuse mechanisms , (2) sleep neurochemistry and the flip-flop switch , (3) hunger as an arcuate-nucleus loop , (4) HPA axis + glucocorticoid feedback + hippocampal atrophy , (5) organising vs activating effects of gonadal hormones , (6) the molecular cascade for LTP , and (7) neurobiology of the major psychiatric disorders as a single mechanism-first chapter. That is what is unpacked below. Anything Pinel already nails (cranial nerves, visual receptive fields, split brain, Korsakoff) is not repeated here — read those on the Pinel page. Jump to: 1. How Carlson is organised 2. Neurotransmitter systems, by system 3. Reward circuit & mesolimbic DA 4. Drugs of abuse —

chunks.heading: 1. How Carlson is organised (and why that matters)
chunks.text: 1. How Carlson is organised (and why that matters) Carlson is a mechanism-first physiology book , not a "tour of the field" book. Pinel writes around case studies and divisions ; Carlson writes around systems : neurotransmitter system → behavior it produces → drug that hits that system → disorder when it fails. If a question asks "which transmitter / which circuit / which receptor / which drug", Carlson is the book it was written from. His chapters (in his order, condensed): structure of the nervous system → neurons & conduction → synaptic transmission → drugs & receptors → methods → vision → audition & somatosenses → control of movement → sleep → reproductive behavior → emotion → ingestive behavior → learning & memory → communication → neurological disorders → schizophrenia, mood disorders, anxiety → autism, ADHD, stress, addiction. Lock it: when an MCQ stem names a receptor subtype (D2, 5-HT2A, NMDA, GABA-A α1, μ-opioid), a circuit (mesolimbic, nigrostriatal, mesocortical, tuberoinfundibular, locus coeruleus, dorsal raphe), or a drug class with its mechanism (NSRI, MAO-B inhibitor, atypical antipsychotic), reach for Carlson, not Pinel.

chunks.heading: 2. Neurotransmitter systems, system by system
chunks.text: 2. Neurotransmitter systems, system by system Carlson's signature move: don't memorise transmitters in a list, learn each one as a system (cell-body cluster → projection pathway → receptors → behavior → drug). NIMHANS leans on these.

chunks.heading: Dopamine — three pathways, one transmitter
chunks.text: Dopamine — three pathways, one transmitter Pathway From → To Function What happens when it fails Nigrostriatal Substantia nigra (pars compacta) → dorsal striatum (caudate + putamen) Motor initiation, habit learning Loss = Parkinson's disease Mesolimbic Ventral tegmental area (VTA) → nucleus accumbens (NAc, ventral striatum), amygdala, hippocampus Reward, motivation, "wanting" Hyperactivity = positive symptoms of schizophrenia; addiction hijacks it Mesocortical VTA → prefrontal cortex Working memory, executive control, motivation Hypoactivity = negative symptoms of schizophrenia Tuberoinfundibular Arcuate nucleus (hypothalamus) → median eminence Inhibits prolactin release D2-blocking antipsychotics → hyperprolactinaemia → amenorrhoea, gynaecomastia Receptors: 5 subtypes, two families. D1-like (D1, D5) are G s -coupled → ↑ cAMP. D2-like (D2, D3, D4) are G i -coupled → ↓ cAMP. Classical antipsychotics block D2 . Atypicals add 5-HT2A blockade. TRAP — DA pathway naming. "Mesolimbic" and "mesocortical" share the VTA origin; the difference is the target. Mesolimbic → NAc (reward) ; mesocortical → PFC (cognition) . "Nigrostriatal" is a separate origin (substantia nigra, not VTA).

chunks.heading: Norepinephrine — one nucleus, the whole brain
chunks.text: Norepinephrine — one nucleus, the whole brain Cell bodies live in the locus coeruleus (pons). One small cluster projects diffusely across cortex, thalamus, hypothalamus, cerebellum, spinal cord. Function: arousal, vigilance, attention to novelty . NE firing rises during alertness, falls during sleep, peaks during stress. α1, α2, β1, β2, β3 receptors. β-blockers cross the blood-brain barrier (propranolol) → reduce somatic anxiety.

chunks.heading: Serotonin (5-HT) — raphe nuclei, fourteen receptors
chunks.text: Serotonin (5-HT) — raphe nuclei, fourteen receptors Cell bodies: raphe nuclei (midline brainstem). Dorsal raphe → forebrain, midbrain ; median raphe → limbic system; caudal raphe → spinal cord. ≥14 receptor subtypes; the exam-relevant ones: 5-HT1A — autoreceptor on raphe neurons; postsynaptic in hippocampus. Buspirone is a 5-HT1A partial agonist (anxiolytic). 5-HT2A — psychedelic site (LSD, psilocybin agonists); atypical antipsychotics antagonise it. 5-HT3 — the only ionotropic 5-HT receptor; ondansetron antagonist (antiemetic). SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram) raise synaptic 5-HT by blocking the reuptake transporter SERT.

chunks.heading: Acetylcholine — two systems
chunks.text: Acetylcholine — two systems Basal forebrain (nucleus basalis of Meynert + medial septum) → cortex + hippocampus. Drives attention & learning. Lost first in Alzheimer's — basis for donepezil / rivastigmine / galantamine. Pontine cholinergic (PPT + LDT) → thalamus + basal forebrain. Drives cortical arousal in waking and REM sleep . Receptors: nicotinic (ionotropic, fast, at NMJ + brain) and muscarinic M1–M5 (metabotropic). Anticholinergic drugs (atropine, benztropine, scopolamine) cause confusion + memory loss + dry mouth + mydriasis — classic in old-age psychiatry.

chunks.heading: GABA & glutamate — the workhorses
chunks.text: GABA & glutamate — the workhorses Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter (≈ 80% of cortical synapses). Receptors: AMPA — fast Na+ ionotropic; "the everyday excitation". NMDA — Na+/Ca2+ ionotropic, voltage-and-glutamate-gated, blocked at rest by Mg2+. Carrier of LTP. Blocked by ketamine, PCP, MK-801 → schizophrenia-like state. mGluR — metabotropic, modulatory. GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter. GABA-A is an ionotropic Cl⁻ channel; benzodiazepines + barbiturates + alcohol + neurosteroids all bind allosterically to it. GABA-B is metabotropic (G i ) → K⁺ efflux; baclofen agonist. TRAP — benzo vs barbiturate site. Both are GABA-A positive allosteric modulators but at different sites . Benzos increase the frequency of Cl⁻ channel opening; barbiturates increase the duration . That is why barbiturates kill at overdose (open the channel all the way) and benzos do not, on their own.

chunks.heading: Neuropeptides — the slow channel
chunks.text: Neuropeptides — the slow channel Peptides act on G-protein receptors with slow, modulatory effects. The exam-rated set: endorphin / enkephalin / dynorphin (opioids — μ, δ, κ receptors), substance P (pain), oxytocin / vasopressin (bonding, fluid balance), NPY / AgRP (hunger), orexin / hypocretin (wakefulness; loss = narcolepsy). Recap §2. Each NT system has a cell-body cluster, a projection, a receptor family, a behavior, and a drug. Lock the table: DA = VTA/SN, NE = locus coeruleus, 5-HT = raphe, ACh = basal forebrain + pontine, Glu/GABA = everywhere. Pathway naming + receptor subtypes are the MCQ engine.

chunks.heading: 3. Reward circuit & mesolimbic dopamine
chunks.text: 3. Reward circuit & mesolimbic dopamine This is Carlson's signature chapter. Pinel covers it; Carlson lives in it.

chunks.heading: The core circuit, end-to-end
chunks.text: The core circuit, end-to-end VTA (ventral tegmental area, midbrain) is the origin of mesolimbic DA neurons. They project up the medial forebrain bundle (MFB) — the very bundle Olds & Milner (1954) stuck electrodes into and got self-stimulation. The main target is the nucleus accumbens (NAc) in the ventral striatum. From NAc, output goes to the ventral pallidum , then back via mediodorsal thalamus → prefrontal cortex . PFC sends glutamatergic feedback to NAc + VTA; amygdala & hippocampus also feed NAc with affective + contextual signal.

chunks.heading: What dopamine actually signals
chunks.text: What dopamine actually signals Not "pleasure" — Carlson is firm on this. Dopamine signals reward prediction error (Schultz's work, after Wolfram Schultz): when an outcome is better than expected , DA fires; when expected, DA doesn't change; when worse than expected, DA dips below baseline. This is the substrate Carlson uses to explain learning, craving and addiction. Why it matters. "Wanting" (incentive salience, mesolimbic DA) is dissociable from "liking" (the hedonic hotspot, opioid + cannabinoid signalling in NAc shell + ventral pallidum). Addiction is mostly wanting without liking — the addict still craves long after the drug stops being fun. Berridge & Robinson's incentive-sensitisation theory is the model Carlson hangs the chapter on.

chunks.heading: Self-stimulation, place preference, self-administration — the three behavioural assays
chunks.text: Self-stimulation, place preference, self-administration — the three behavioural assays Assay What it shows Key result Intracranial self-stimulation (Olds & Milner, 1954) Brain sites where electrical stimulation is rewarding MFB & VTA give the highest rates of lever-pressing Conditioned place preference Drug-paired environment becomes attractive Cocaine, opiates, food all produce CPP via NAc DA Drug self-administration Animal will work to inject a drug Lesion NAc DA → self-admin of cocaine drops; lesion DA terminals selectively in NAc > in dorsal striatum Lock it: reward = VTA → MFB → NAc; Olds & Milner = the experiment that founded the field; DA codes reward prediction error , not pleasure; "wanting" ≠ "liking".

chunks.heading: 4. Drugs of abuse — mechanism by class
chunks.text: 4. Drugs of abuse — mechanism by class The unifying claim Carlson makes: every drug of abuse, by some route, raises dopamine in NAc . Different drugs do it at different points in the circuit; that is what makes their effects (and treatments) differ. Class Example Primary molecular action How it raises NAc DA Antagonist / treatment Psychostimulants Cocaine Blocks DAT (dopamine reuptake) DA released by VTA is not cleared from NAc synapse Cognitive-behavioural; no good pharm Amphetamine / methamphetamine Reverses DAT — pumps DA out of terminal; also empties vesicles via VMAT2 Floods NAc with cytoplasmic DA Same — behavioural Opioids Morphine, heroin, fentanyl μ-opioid receptor agonist on GABA interneurons in VTA Disinhibits VTA DA neurons → ↑ NAc DA. Direct μ action in NAc shell + ventral pallidum = "liking" Naloxone (acute), naltrexone (relapse prevention), methadone / buprenorphine (substitution) Nicotine Tobacco Nicotinic ACh receptor agonist (α4β2) on VTA DA neurons Direct excitation of VTA DA cells Varenicline (partial agonist), bupropion, NRT Alcohol Ethanol Positive allosteric modulator at GABA-A; NMDA antagonist; releases endogenous opioids Endogenous opioids → disinhibit VTA DA Naltrexone (anti-craving), acamprosate (NMDA-glutamate stabiliser), disulfiram (aversive — blocks ALDH) Cannabinoids THC CB1 partial agonist (Gi-coupled) CB1 on GABA interneurons in VTA → disinhibi

chunks.heading: 5. Sleep neurochemistry & the flip-flop switch
chunks.text: 5. Sleep neurochemistry & the flip-flop switch Pinel walks through the stages and the EEG. Carlson explains the switch : how the brain stays in one state and not another.

chunks.heading: The wake-promoting system
chunks.text: The wake-promoting system Pontine cholinergic neurons (PPT, LDT) → thalamus → cortical desynchronisation. Locus coeruleus (NE) → cortex. Dorsal raphe (5-HT) → cortex. Tuberomammillary nucleus (histamine) → cortex. (This is why old-generation H1 antihistamines sedate.) Lateral hypothalamus orexin/hypocretin neurons → all the above. Orexin is the "supervisor" that holds the wake system on. Lose it → narcolepsy with cataplexy .

chunks.heading: The sleep-promoting system
chunks.text: The sleep-promoting system Ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO) of the anterior hypothalamus → GABA + galanin → inhibits every wake-promoter above.

chunks.heading: The flip-flop switch
chunks.text: The flip-flop switch VLPO inhibits the wake nuclei; the wake nuclei inhibit VLPO. Mutual inhibition makes the system bistable : one side wins fast, transitions are sharp, intermediate states are unstable. Orexin from the lateral hypothalamus biases the switch toward "wake" by exciting the wake nuclei. Lose orexin → switch flips erratically → sleep attacks in daytime, fragmented sleep at night = narcolepsy.

chunks.heading: REM atonia
chunks.text: REM atonia During REM, descending glycine + GABA inhibition from the sublaterodorsal nucleus (subLDT) → medulla (gigantocellular nucleus) → spinal motor neurons paralyses skeletal muscle (sparing diaphragm + eye muscles). Lesion this in cats (Jouvet's classic experiment) → "REM without atonia" → cats act out their dreams. The human analogue is REM sleep behaviour disorder , which strongly predicts Parkinson's / Lewy body dementia within 10–15 years. Lock it: sleep = VLPO; wake = ARAS (cholinergic + NE + 5-HT + histamine) supervised by orexin; REM atonia = subLDT → medulla → spinal cord. Loss of orexin = narcolepsy. REM-without-atonia in humans = REM sleep behaviour disorder = prodromal Parkinson's. TRAP — "which transmitter is highest in REM?" ACh. NE + 5-HT both drop in REM (the "aminergic-cholinergic" model — REM is when ACh wins). Histamine drops too. NIMHANS angle. "Cataplexy on emotional triggers + sleep paralysis + hypnagogic hallucinations + sleep attacks" = narcolepsy type 1 (with cataplexy) = loss of orexin neurons. CSF orexin low. HLA-DQB1*06:02 association.

chunks.heading: 6. Hunger — arcuate POMC/AgRP loop
chunks.text: 6. Hunger — arcuate POMC/AgRP loop Pinel teaches the old dual-centre hypothesis (LH = hunger, VMH = satiety). Carlson teaches the modern arcuate-nucleus model , which the syllabus increasingly tests.

chunks.heading: The two arcuate populations
chunks.text: The two arcuate populations Neurons Co-release What they do POMC / CART neurons α-MSH (a POMC product) + CART Promote satiety — project to paraventricular nucleus, activate MC4R receptor → ↓ food intake NPY / AgRP neurons NPY + AgRP + GABA Promote hunger — same target, AgRP blocks MC4R, NPY excites feeding directly. Inhibits POMC neurons too.

chunks.heading: The peripheral signals that drive the loop
chunks.text: The peripheral signals that drive the loop Leptin — from adipose tissue, proportional to fat stores. Excites POMC, inhibits NPY/AgRP → satiety. Leptin deficiency or receptor mutation → obesity. Most obese humans have high leptin = leptin resistance. Insulin — from pancreas (β-cells) post-meal. Same direction as leptin (satiety). Ghrelin — from empty stomach (X/A cells). Excites NPY/AgRP → hunger. Rises before meals, falls after. PYY 3-36 — from gut L-cells, post-meal. Inhibits NPY → satiety. CCK — from gut I-cells, fat/protein meal. Acts via vagus → NTS → satiety, meal termination.

chunks.heading: The downstream integrator
chunks.text: The downstream integrator Arcuate POMC + NPY/AgRP project to the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) of the hypothalamus, and the lateral hypothalamus (LH) . LH neurons fire orexin → both promotes feeding and arousal (an animal must wake up to eat). This is why orexin sits at the centre of both chapters. Lock it: leptin from fat + insulin from pancreas + PYY/CCK from gut = satiety (act on POMC). Ghrelin from stomach = hunger (acts on NPY/AgRP). LH orexin links hunger to arousal. MC4R mutations are the commonest monogenic cause of obesity in humans. TRAP — leptin and obesity. Leptin levels are high in obese people, not low. The pathology is leptin resistance , not leptin deficiency (rare congenital exception aside).

chunks.heading: 7. HPA axis, glucocorticoids & the hippocampus
chunks.text: 7. HPA axis, glucocorticoids & the hippocampus This is where Carlson, Sapolsky and clinical neuropsychology converge. The depth pass here is the receptor-level feedback story, because every MCQ on cortisol & the hippocampus rides on it.

chunks.heading: The axis, end-to-end
chunks.text: The axis, end-to-end Stressor sensed by amygdala (threat) + prefrontal/hippocampus (contextual appraisal). Paraventricular nucleus (PVN) of the hypothalamus releases CRH + vasopressin into the hypophyseal portal vein. Anterior pituitary corticotropes release ACTH into systemic blood. Adrenal cortex (zona fasciculata) releases cortisol . Cortisol acts everywhere (gluconeogenesis, immunosuppression, sodium retention) and feeds back to shut off CRH + ACTH.

chunks.heading: Two receptors, two feedback loops
chunks.text: Two receptors, two feedback loops Receptor Affinity Where Role MR (mineralocorticoid) High Hippocampus & some PVN Tonic, basal cortisol regulation; saturated at low cortisol levels GR (glucocorticoid) Low Hippocampus, PFC, amygdala, hypothalamus, pituitary, everywhere Stress-level feedback shutoff; recruited when cortisol is high The hippocampus is the brain's main inhibitor of the HPA axis via GR. That is the load-bearing fact.

chunks.heading: What chronic stress does to the hippocampus
chunks.text: What chronic stress does to the hippocampus Sustained high cortisol → hippocampal neurons in CA3 + dentate gyrus suffer dendritic atrophy , suppression of neurogenesis in the dentate , eventual volume loss . Less hippocampus → less feedback shutoff → more cortisol → more damage. This is the loop Sapolsky describes; it appears in PTSD, major depression, Cushing's disease. Lock it: PVN → CRH → ACTH → cortisol → MR (low) + GR (high) → hippocampus shuts the axis off. Chronic stress shrinks hippocampus → feedback fails → cortisol stays high. NIMHANS angle. Smaller hippocampal volume on MRI is reported in PTSD, MDD with melancholia, Cushing's, and chronic schizophrenia. Dexamethasone suppression test (a synthetic GR agonist) → non-suppression of morning cortisol = an old biological marker for melancholic depression; sensitivity is low but it is the marker NIMHANS still asks about.

chunks.heading: 8. Sex hormones — organising vs activating
chunks.text: 8. Sex hormones — organising vs activating The cleanest two-word concept in the book, and a perennial MCQ. Organising effects — during a critical period (perinatal in humans, in utero in rodents), gonadal hormones permanently build sexually dimorphic brain circuits. Effects are permanent and structural . Example: prenatal testosterone in males masculinises the sexually dimorphic nucleus (SDN) of the medial preoptic area (mPOA) . Activating effects — after puberty, the same hormones switch on the behavior in the already-built circuit. Effects are reversible . Castrate an adult male rat → mounting drops; replace testosterone → it comes back.

chunks.heading: The circuits, by sex
chunks.text: The circuits, by sex Behavior Critical region Hormone Male sexual behavior (mounting, intromission) Medial preoptic area (mPOA) Testosterone → aromatised to estradiol → ERα binding (the "aromatisation hypothesis") Female sexual behavior (lordosis in rodents) Ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) Estradiol → priming → progesterone receptor expression Maternal behavior mPOA + bed nucleus of stria terminalis Estradiol + prolactin + oxytocin Pair-bonding (prairie vole work) Ventral pallidum, NAc Vasopressin (males), oxytocin (females) TRAP — the aromatisation hypothesis. In rodents, testosterone masculinises the male brain by being converted to estradiol within the brain (aromatase enzyme). The same chemical (estradiol) masculinises male brains and feminises female brains, depending on when and where it acts. Female fetuses are protected from circulating maternal estradiol by alpha-fetoprotein. Lock it: organising = perinatal, permanent, structural. Activating = adult, reversible, behavioural. Male = mPOA (testosterone → aromatised). Female = VMH (estradiol → progesterone). Maternal behavior + pair bonds = oxytocin/vasopressin.

chunks.heading: 9. LTP — the molecular cascade
chunks.text: 9. LTP — the molecular cascade If the exam asks "molecular basis of learning", they want this story. Baseline: glutamate is released onto the postsynaptic dendritic spine. AMPA receptors open → Na+ in → depolarises the spine. NMDA receptors are also bound by glutamate, but at resting potential Mg2+ plugs the channel . Nothing flows. Strong / paired stimulation: the postsynaptic membrane depolarises enough that the Mg2+ plug is electrostatically expelled. NMDA channel is now open with glutamate and voltage. Ca2+ flows in. Ca2+ activates CaMKII (calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase II). CaMKII phosphorylates AMPA receptors (more conductance) and inserts new AMPA receptors into the spine membrane. Same spine, next glutamate release → bigger AMPA response. The synapse is potentiated . With sustained activity, gene transcription (CREB) + protein synthesis (Arc, BDNF) makes the change last hours to days → late-phase LTP . Why it matters. NMDA = the coincidence detector (needs glutamate AND depolarisation simultaneously). That is Hebb's "cells that fire together wire together" in molecules. Block NMDA (APV, ketamine) → no LTP → no spatial learning (Morris water maze, Morris & Frey). Lock it: NMDA = coincidence detector (Mg2+ block, voltage-and-ligand-gated). LTP carrier = Ca2+ → CaMKII → AMPA insertion. Late phase = CREB → protein synthesis. APV / ketamine block LTP.

chunks.heading: 10. Neurobiology of the major psychiatric disorders
chunks.text: 10. Neurobiology of the major psychiatric disorders Carlson collapses these into one chapter. The MCQ trick is to map each disorder to a one-line neurobiological hypothesis + its drug logic.

chunks.heading: Schizophrenia
chunks.text: Schizophrenia Dopamine hypothesis (original): too much DA. Evidence: D2-blocking drugs work; amphetamine (raises DA) produces a paranoid psychosis indistinguishable from schizophrenia. Updated: mesolimbic hyperdopaminergia → positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions); mesocortical hypodopaminergia → negative symptoms (avolition, flat affect) + cognitive symptoms. Glutamate hypothesis: NMDA hypofunction. Evidence: PCP / ketamine produce the full spectrum (positive + negative + cognitive), classical DA-only drugs produce only positive symptoms. Structural: ventricular enlargement, reduced cortical grey matter (esp. PFC + temporal), reduced hippocampal volume. Drug logic: typicals (haloperidol, chlorpromazine) = pure D2 blockade → EPS. Atypicals (clozapine, risperidone, olanzapine) = D2 + 5-HT2A blockade → fewer EPS, more metabolic side effects. Clozapine = only one shown to help treatment-resistant + reduce suicide; needs WBC monitoring (agranulocytosis).

chunks.heading: Depression
chunks.text: Depression Monoamine hypothesis: deficit of 5-HT & NE. Evidence: tricyclics raise both; SSRIs raise 5-HT; MAOIs raise everything. But: monoamine rises in hours, antidepressant effect takes weeks — so the simple deficit story is incomplete. Neuroplasticity / BDNF hypothesis: depression involves loss of hippocampal volume, low BDNF. Effective antidepressants raise BDNF + promote hippocampal neurogenesis over weeks — fits the time course. HPA hypothesis: hypercortisolism + DST non-suppression in melancholic depression (see §7). Drug logic: SSRI (first line), SNRI, atypical (bupropion = NDRI; mirtazapine = α2 + 5-HT2/3 antagonist), TCA, MAOI. Ketamine (NMDA antagonist) → rapid antidepressant effect — re-frames the whole field as glutamate-dependent.

chunks.heading: Bipolar
chunks.text: Bipolar Strong genetic loading, polygenic. Lithium = mood stabiliser of choice; mechanism partly via inositol monophosphatase + GSK-3β inhibition; also reduces suicide in bipolar specifically. Antidepressant monotherapy can flip a bipolar patient into mania — classic exam trap.

chunks.heading: Anxiety
chunks.text: Anxiety Amygdala-centred fear circuit (see §12). Increased reactivity, weaker prefrontal regulation. GABA-A modulation (benzos) → fast relief. 5-HT (SSRI / SNRI) → first-line maintenance for panic, GAD, OCD, PTSD, social anxiety. OCD specifically responds to high-dose SSRI + cortico-striatal-thalamic loop involvement (caudate hyperactivity on PET, normalises with treatment).

chunks.heading: Addiction
chunks.text: Addiction Hijack of mesolimbic DA (see §3–4). Repeated drug exposure → tolerance (receptor downregulation) + sensitisation (incentive-salience strengthening) + withdrawal (opponent process: NAc DA below baseline, amygdala stress system activated). Long-term cue-induced craving driven by amygdala + PFC + hippocampus, not VTA-NAc alone. Recap §10. Schiz = DA imbalance + NMDA hypofunction. Depression = monoamines + plasticity + cortisol. Bipolar = mood stabilisers, watch the antidepressant switch. Anxiety = amygdala + GABA + 5-HT. Addiction = mesolimbic hijack + opponent withdrawal.

chunks.heading: 11. Sensorimotor — what Carlson adds over Pinel
chunks.text: 11. Sensorimotor — what Carlson adds over Pinel The basics (motor cortex map, basal ganglia, cerebellum) are on the Pinel page. Carlson's two extra emphases: Direct vs indirect basal ganglia loops. The direct pathway (cortex → striatum → GPi/SNr → thalamus → cortex) facilitates movement; the indirect pathway (striatum → GPe → STN → GPi) inhibits movement. D1 receptors on direct-pathway neurons (go), D2 receptors on indirect-pathway neurons (no-go). DA from substantia nigra biases the system toward "go" — lose it and you get Parkinson's bradykinesia. Mirror neurons (di Pellegrino, Rizzolatti, area F5 of macaque premotor cortex) — neurons that fire both when the monkey executes a goal-directed action and when it watches another do it. Hypothesised role in imitation, action understanding, theory of mind; human homologues in inferior frontal gyrus + inferior parietal lobule. TRAP — direct vs indirect pathway receptor. Direct = D1 (facilitating). Indirect = D2 (inhibiting). DA excites direct and inhibits indirect, so it pushes both ways toward "more movement". L-DOPA in Parkinson's restores both.

chunks.heading: 12. Emotion — amygdala in detail
chunks.text: 12. Emotion — amygdala in detail The Papez circuit / James-Lange / Cannon-Bard story is on the Pinel page. Carlson focuses on the amygdala as the emotion hub .

chunks.heading: Amygdala nuclei
chunks.text: Amygdala nuclei Lateral nucleus — sensory input from thalamus + cortex. The "input gate". Basal + accessory basal nuclei — integrate input with cortical (PFC, hippocampus) context. Central nucleus (CeA) — output to hypothalamus (autonomic), PAG (freezing, analgesia), brainstem (startle), basal forebrain (vigilance). The "output gate" of fear.

chunks.heading: Fear conditioning circuit (LeDoux)
chunks.text: Fear conditioning circuit (LeDoux) Two roads to the amygdala: the low road = thalamus → lateral amygdala, fast & crude (the snake-shaped stick); the high road = thalamus → cortex → lateral amygdala, slower & precise (it's a stick). Lateral amygdala stores the CS-US association via LTP at its glutamate synapses. CeA drives the output (freeze + autonomic burst).

chunks.heading: Klüver-Bucy
chunks.text: Klüver-Bucy Bilateral anterior temporal lobectomy (originally in monkeys, then in humans with HSV encephalitis or post-surgical) → hypersexuality, hyperorality (mouthing objects), placidity, visual agnosia, hypermetamorphosis . Damage to amygdala + adjacent temporal cortex. Lock it: amygdala = fear / threat detection. Lateral = input, central = output. LeDoux's two roads = thalamus-amygdala (low) and thalamus-cortex-amygdala (high). Klüver-Bucy = bilateral temporal damage.

chunks.heading: 13. NIMHANS-tilt — clinical hooks from this page
chunks.text: 13. NIMHANS-tilt — clinical hooks from this page Carlson's chapters that NIMHANS clinical neuropsychology leans on most heavily, and the exact stem you might see: Clinical scenario Underlying Carlson chapter The answer Resting tremor + rigidity + bradykinesia, responds to L-DOPA Nigrostriatal DA loss Parkinson's disease — substantia nigra pars compacta Memory loss, basal forebrain cholinergic loss Basal forebrain ACh; AD Alzheimer's; treat with donepezil / rivastigmine / galantamine + memantine (NMDA partial antagonist) in moderate-severe REM-without-atonia in a 60-yr-old man, acting out dreams SubLDT lesion analogue REM sleep behaviour disorder → prodromal Parkinson's / DLB Daytime sleep attacks + cataplexy on laughter Lateral hypothalamus orexin loss Narcolepsy type 1; CSF orexin low; HLA-DQB1*06:02 Disinhibition + hyperorality + hypersexuality + visual agnosia after HSV encephalitis Bilateral temporal / amygdala Klüver-Bucy syndrome Chronic alcohol + ataxia + confabulation + anterograde amnesia Thiamine deficiency → mammillary body + dorsomedial thalamus Wernicke-Korsakoff (Carlson covers in addiction chapter) Treatment-resistant schizophrenia 5-HT2A + D2 atypical Clozapine (monitor WBC for agranulocytosis) Major depression with cortisol non-suppression on DST HPA + GR dysregulation Melancholic depression Caudate hyperactivity on PET, normalises with SSRI / CBT Cortico-stria

chunks.heading: 14. Carlson vs Pinel — every divergence worth knowing
chunks.text: 14. Carlson vs Pinel — every divergence worth knowing Topic Pinel's framing Carlson's framing (what to take from here) Reward Olds & Milner + Berridge wanting/liking Full mesolimbic circuit, DA = reward-prediction-error (Schultz) Addiction Behavioural — tolerance, sensitisation, withdrawal Per-drug receptor mechanism + treatment drug Sleep Stages, REM-NREM cycle VLPO ↔ ARAS flip-flop, orexin supervisor, subLDT → REM atonia Hunger LH = hunger, VMH = satiety, leptin briefly Arcuate POMC vs NPY/AgRP, MC4R, leptin/insulin/ghrelin/PYY/CCK Stress Selye GAS, HPA outlined MR vs GR feedback, hippocampal atrophy loop Sex Hormones & behaviour, briefly Organising vs activating, aromatisation hypothesis, mPOA vs VMH Memory Amnesia patients (HM), systems NMDA coincidence detector, Ca2+ → CaMKII → AMPA insertion → late phase via CREB Schizophrenia DA hypothesis + drugs Mesolimbic-hyper + mesocortical-hypo + NMDA hypofunction Depression Monoamines Monoamines + BDNF/neuroplasticity + HPA + ketamine/glutamate Movement Cortex, BG, cerebellum Direct (D1) vs indirect (D2) basal ganglia loops; mirror neurons

chunks.heading: 15. MCQ traps Carlson sets that Pinel does not
chunks.text: 15. MCQ traps Carlson sets that Pinel does not Cocaine = DAT blocker. Amphetamine = DAT reverser + VMAT2 emptier. Not the same. Benzos = ↑ GABA-A frequency. Barbiturates = ↑ GABA-A duration. (Same channel, different sites.) Direct pathway = D1 = go. Indirect pathway = D2 = no-go. (DA pushes both toward "go".) Mesolimbic = positive symptoms (hyper). Mesocortical = negative + cognitive symptoms (hypo). Antipsychotics work on the first; they make the second worse. NMDA receptor is voltage-AND-ligand-gated; Mg2+ is the voltage-dependent block. AMPA is ligand-only. Leptin is elevated in human obesity (leptin resistance), not deficient. Ghrelin = stomach, pre-meal, hunger. Don't confuse with ghrelin/leptin direction. MR (mineralocorticoid) is the high-affinity cortisol receptor; GR is the low-affinity one recruited in stress. Hippocampus has both. Aromatisation : testosterone is converted to estradiol in the male brain, which is what masculinises it. Orexin loss → narcolepsy type 1 (with cataplexy). Orexin neurons live in the lateral hypothalamus . Clozapine is the only antipsychotic shown to lower suicide in schizophrenia. Side effect: agranulocytosis. Lithium reduces suicide in bipolar. Mechanism: GSK-3β + inositol monophosphatase inhibition. Acamprosate stabilises NMDA glutamate signalling in alcohol use disorder. Disulfiram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase. Varenicline is a partial

chunks.heading: 16. Self-test — Carlson topics only
chunks.text: 16. Self-test — Carlson topics only Name the four DA pathways with origin and target. What is the "wanting vs liking" distinction and which transmitter system carries each? Walk Olds & Milner's intracranial self-stimulation experiment in three sentences. For each: cocaine, amphetamine, heroin, alcohol, nicotine, cannabis — state the primary receptor / transporter action. What does the VLPO inhibit, and what supervises the switch? Why does orexin loss produce both daytime sleep attacks and cataplexy? Where is REM atonia generated, and what is the human disorder of its failure? Which two arcuate populations regulate feeding, what do they release, and on what target? Why is leptin high in obesity? Distinguish MR and GR by affinity, location, and role. What is the chronic-stress feedback loop that involves the hippocampus? State the organising vs activating distinction with one rodent example each. What is the aromatisation hypothesis? Walk the NMDA → Ca2+ → CaMKII → AMPA-insertion cascade. For schizophrenia, give one piece of evidence each for the DA hypothesis and the NMDA hypothesis. Why is the time-course problem the killer of the simple monoamine hypothesis of depression? Direct vs indirect basal ganglia pathway — receptor + behaviour. Klüver-Bucy: lesion site + four features. Name LeDoux's "two roads" to the amygdala. One-line clinical pearls (any five from §13). Page built 2

chunks.heading: Biopsychology — the full chapter, from scratch
chunks.text: Biopsychology — the full chapter, from scratch Read this like a textbook, not a cheatsheet. Every system explained from first principles, then the names, numbers and traps. Anchored to your Pinel & Barnes, Biopsychology (11th ed.) , walked through chapter by chapter in book order, prioritised for NIMHANS clinical neuropsychology. Divisions of biopsychology · evolution & genetics · neuroanatomy · neural conduction & synapses · research methods · vision · audition & other senses · sensorimotor · development · brain damage & plasticity · memory & amnesia · hunger · hormones & sex · sleep · addiction & reward · lateralisation & language · emotion & stress · psychiatric disorders · Built 2026-05-05 · Rewritten as a full teaching chapter 2026-05-24 · Expanded to full depth 2026-05-24 (added the landmark experiments walked through step by step, an extended concept bank covering every remaining Pinel term per chapter, an A–Z glossary, and a by-chapter self-test) How to use this page. It is built to learn from , not just revise. Each system has: (1) the problem it solves / what it is for, (2) the core mechanism in plain language with an everyday example, (3) the parts unpacked one by one, then the tables, and (4) a coloured box recapping the exam-testable fact and the trap. Amber boxes = the intuition / why it matters. Green = the line to lock. Red = the MCQ trap. Purple = NIMHANS-speci

chunks.heading: 1. Biopsychology as a neuroscience (Pinel ch. 1)
chunks.text: 1. Biopsychology as a neuroscience (Pinel ch. 1) The one idea behind the whole book. Biopsychology is the scientific study of the biology of behaviour : it asks how the nervous system produces what we think, feel and do. It is one branch of neuroscience (the larger study of the nervous system), the branch that keeps behaviour at the centre. Pinel's recurring lesson is that mind and brain are not two things: every thought is a physical event in tissue.

chunks.heading: The six divisions of biopsychology
chunks.text: The six divisions of biopsychology Pinel splits the field by what you study and how . Learn each by its defining method, because the paper tests "which division does X?". Division What it studies Typical method Physiological psychology Neural mechanisms of behaviour Direct manipulation of the brain in controlled experiments (lesions, stimulation), usually in lab animals Psychopharmacology Effects of drugs on behaviour and the brain Manipulate behaviour with drugs; develop therapeutic drugs Neuropsychology Psychological effects of brain damage in human patients Case studies + standardised tests; the most applied division (NIMHANS leans here) Psychophysiology Relation between physiology and behaviour using non-invasive body measures in healthy humans EEG, heart rate, skin conductance (GSR), pupil size Cognitive neuroscience Neural bases of cognition (thought, memory, attention) Mainly functional brain imaging (fMRI, PET) in humans Comparative psychology Behaviour across species, evolution, genetics, ethology Cross-species comparison, naturalistic + lab study TRAP — psychophysiology vs physiological psychology. Both have "physiolog" in the name. Physiological psychology = invasive manipulation of the brain, usually in animals . Psychophysiology = non-invasive recording from the surface of healthy humans . And neuropsychology = the study of human brain-damaged patients.

chunks.heading: Kinds of research, kinds of inference
chunks.text: Kinds of research, kinds of inference Pure vs applied. Pure = curiosity-driven knowledge; applied = solving a practical problem. Most real work is a blend. Experiments vs non-experiments. Only a true experiment (the researcher manipulates an independent variable and randomly assigns) can support a causal claim. Quasi-experiments and case studies cannot fully rule out confounds. Converging operations. Because every single method is flawed, biopsychology trusts a conclusion only when several different methods point the same way . This is Pinel's signature methodological value. The Morgan's Canon / law of parsimony spirit: prefer the simplest explanation that fits, and do not attribute a higher mental process when a lower one will do. Lock it: human brain-damaged patients = neuropsychology ; drugs = psychopharmacology ; non-invasive measures in healthy humans = psychophysiology ; imaging of cognition = cognitive neuroscience ; animal brain manipulation = physiological psychology ; across species = comparative . Recap §1. Biopsychology = biology of behaviour, six divisions sorted by method. Causation needs a true experiment. Converging operations: trust the conclusion many methods agree on.

chunks.heading: 2. Evolution, genetics & experience (Pinel ch. 2)
chunks.text: 2. Evolution, genetics & experience (Pinel ch. 2) The problem this chapter fixes. The old "nature versus nurture" question is a false dichotomy. Pinel's "nature-nurture done right" is that genes and experience are not rival causes adding up to 100%; they interact continuously. A trait is the product of a genetic program read out in an environment. You cannot say a behaviour is "60% genetic" for an individual, only how much variation in a population is associated with genetic variation (heritability).

chunks.heading: Evolution of the brain
chunks.text: Evolution of the brain Natural selection (Darwin): heritable traits that improve fitness (reproductive success) spread. Behaviour evolves too. Larger brains are not automatically "better"; what matters is brain size relative to body size and the expansion of specific regions, especially the cerebral cortex in primates. Convergent evolution = similar traits arise independently (analogous structures). Homologous structures share a common ancestor. Do not read similarity as shared ancestry. Spandrels & exaptations: not every trait is a direct adaptation; some are by-products later co-opted for new uses.

chunks.heading: Mendelian genetics & the molecular layer
chunks.text: Mendelian genetics & the molecular layer Gene = a stretch of DNA on a chromosome. We have 23 pairs; the 23rd is the sex pair (XX female, XY male). Dominant vs recessive alleles; homozygous vs heterozygous ; genotype (the genes) vs phenotype (the expressed trait). Dizygotic (fraternal) twins share ~50% of genes (like ordinary siblings); monozygotic (identical) twins share ~100%. Comparing them is the classic heritability tool. Central dogma: DNA → (transcription) → mRNA → (translation) → protein.

chunks.heading: Epigenetics: experience changes which genes are read
chunks.text: Epigenetics: experience changes which genes are read Why this matters. Epigenetics is the mechanism that finally dissolves nature-vs-nurture. The DNA sequence does not change, but experience can switch genes on or off via chemical tags, especially DNA methylation (silences genes) and histone modification . These marks can persist and even be inherited. So early experience literally edits gene expression: that is how environment becomes biology.

chunks.heading: Ontogeny vs phylogeny
chunks.text: Ontogeny vs phylogeny Term Meaning Everyday handle Ontogeny Development of the individual across its own lifespan One person growing up Phylogeny Evolutionary history of the species/lineage The family tree of life TRAP: Ontogeny = individual development; phylogeny = species evolution. The mnemonic "ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny" (Haeckel) is largely discredited, but examiners still test which word means which. Also: heritability is a population statistic, not a personal percentage. Recap §2. Genes × experience interact (epigenetics is the bridge: methylation silences genes). Natural selection acts on fitness. Ontogeny = the individual; phylogeny = the species. MZ twins ~100%, DZ ~50%.

chunks.heading: 3. Anatomy of the nervous system (Pinel ch. 3)
chunks.text: 3. Anatomy of the nervous system (Pinel ch. 3) Before any function makes sense you need the map and the cells that build it. We start with the cells, then the divisions, then the protective wrappings, the directions, and finally the brain regions.

chunks.heading: The neuron, part by part
chunks.text: The neuron, part by part External features of a neuron. Pinel & Barnes, 11th ed. · Fig 3.5 Internal features of a neuron. Pinel & Barnes, 11th ed. · Fig 3.6 Unipolar, bipolar & multipolar neurons and an interneuron. Pinel & Barnes, 11th ed. · Fig 3.8 Dendrites receive input; surface area is multiplied by spines . Soma (cell body) integrates input; holds nucleus, ribosomes, mitochondria. Axon hillock is the trigger zone; it decides whether threshold is reached. Axon conducts the action potential; may be myelinated. Axon terminals (buttons) release neurotransmitter at the synapse.

chunks.heading: Neuron types by function
chunks.text: Neuron types by function Sensory (afferent) — periphery → CNS. Often pseudounipolar. Motor (efferent) — CNS → muscles/glands. Multipolar. Interneurons — local processing inside the CNS; the most numerous.

chunks.heading: Glia — the six you must know
chunks.text: Glia — the six you must know Myelination: an oligodendrocyte (CNS) vs a Schwann cell (PNS). Pinel & Barnes, 11th ed. · Fig 3.9 Cell Location Function Oligodendrocyte CNS Myelinates many axons (one cell, many segments) Schwann cell PNS Myelinates one axon segment per cell; aids PNS regeneration Astrocyte CNS Blood-brain barrier, K⁺ buffering, NT recycling, structural support Microglia CNS Immune defence, phagocytosis Ependymal cell Ventricles Produces and circulates CSF Satellite cell PNS ganglia Supports cell bodies in the PNS TRAP: CNS myelination = oligodendrocyte ; PNS myelination = Schwann cell . And Schwann cells, not oligodendrocytes, support axonal regeneration (see §10).

chunks.heading: The divisions: CNS and PNS
chunks.text: The divisions: CNS and PNS The major divisions of the nervous system. Pinel & Barnes, 11th ed. · Fig 3.2 Nervous System ├── CNS (brain + spinal cord) └── PNS ├── Somatic NS (voluntary, skeletal muscle; afferent + efferent) └── Autonomic NS ├── Sympathetic ("fight/flight") — thoracolumbar, NE ├── Parasympathetic ("rest/digest") — craniosacral, ACh └── Enteric ("gut brain")

chunks.heading: Autonomic contrasts
chunks.text: Autonomic contrasts Sympathetic Parasympathetic Origin T1–L2 (thoracolumbar) CN III, VII, IX, X + S2–S4 (craniosacral) Pre/post-ganglionic NT ACh / NE ACh / ACh Heart ↑ rate ↓ rate (vagus) Pupil Dilate Constrict GI motility ↓ ↑ Sweat glands ACh (exception) —

chunks.heading: Meninges, CSF and ventricles
chunks.text: Meninges, CSF and ventricles The CNS is protected by three membranes, the meninges , from outside in: dura mater (tough outer), arachnoid mater (web-like middle), pia mater (delicate, hugs the brain). Between arachnoid and pia is the subarachnoid space , filled with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) . CSF cushions the brain, removes waste, and lets it float (reducing effective weight). It is produced by the choroid plexus in the ventricles. Ventricles: two lateral → third → cerebral aqueduct → fourth → central canal / subarachnoid space. Blockage causes hydrocephalus .

chunks.heading: Directional terms (orient yourself before lesions)
chunks.text: Directional terms (orient yourself before lesions) Horizontal, frontal (coronal) and sagittal planes. Pinel & Barnes, 11th ed. · Fig 3.16 Term Means Anterior / rostral Toward the front (nose) Posterior / caudal Toward the back (tail) Dorsal Toward the back/top (in the brain, top) Ventral Toward the belly/bottom Medial / lateral Toward / away from the midline Ipsilateral / contralateral Same side / opposite side

chunks.heading: Forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain
chunks.text: Forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain The five divisions of the adult human brain. Pinel & Barnes, 11th ed. · Fig 3.19 Region Structures Function Forebrain (prosencephalon) Cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, limbic system, thalamus, hypothalamus Higher cognition, emotion, motor planning, autonomic control Midbrain (mesencephalon) Tectum (superior + inferior colliculi), tegmentum, substantia nigra, red nucleus, PAG Visual/auditory reflexes, motor control, pain modulation Hindbrain (rhombencephalon) Pons, medulla, cerebellum Vital functions (breathing, heart rate), balance, fine motor coordination Quick handle for the colliculi: S uperior colliculus = S ight (visual reflexes/orienting); I nferior colliculus = " I hear" (auditory). The brainstem = midbrain + pons + medulla, the part keeping you alive.

chunks.heading: Cortex — the four lobes
chunks.text: Cortex — the four lobes The lobes of the cerebral hemisphere. Pinel & Barnes, 11th ed. · Fig 3.25 Lobe Key areas Lesion produces Frontal Motor cortex (precentral gyrus), prefrontal, Broca's (L) Paralysis, executive deficits, Broca's aphasia, personality change (Phineas Gage) Parietal Somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus), association cortex Hemispatial neglect if right, Gerstmann's syndrome if left, agnosia Temporal Primary auditory, Wernicke's (L), hippocampus, amygdala Wernicke's aphasia, anterograde amnesia, Klüver-Bucy Occipital Primary visual (V1), visual association Cortical blindness, visual agnosia, prosopagnosia (fusiform) The cortex is mostly six-layered neocortex . The deep grey matter and limbic structures sit below it.

chunks.heading: Subcortical structures
chunks.text: Subcortical structures The limbic system. Pinel & Barnes, 11th ed. · Fig 3.27 The basal ganglia. Pinel & Barnes, 11th ed. · Fig 3.28 Thalamus — sensory relay for all senses except smell . LGN (vision), MGN (hearing), VPL (body touch), VPM (face). Hypothalamus — homeostasis, hormones, the "4 Fs" (feeding, fighting, fleeing, mating). VMH lesion = hyperphagia + obesity; LH lesion = aphagia; suprachiasmatic nucleus = circadian clock; supraoptic → ADH; paraventricular → oxytocin + CRH. Basal ganglia — caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra. Red nucleus is NOT basal ganglia (it is midbrain tegmentum). Function: motor initiation/selection. Lesions: Parkinson's (SN), Huntington's (caudate/putamen), hemiballismus (subthalamic). Limbic system — hippocampus (memory), amygdala (fear), cingulate (emotion/attention), fornix, mammillary bodies, septum. Cerebellum — coordination, timing, motor learning. Lesions: ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor.

chunks.heading: Hemisphere specialisation (overview; full treatment in §16)
chunks.text: Hemisphere specialisation (overview; full treatment in §16) Left: language (Broca, Wernicke), logic, sequential processing, calculation. Right: spatial, music, faces, holistic, emotional prosody. Corpus callosum — the major commissure; severance produces the split-brain (Sperry, Gazzaniga).

chunks.heading: The 12 cranial nerves
chunks.text: The 12 cranial nerves # Name Type Function I Olfactory S Smell. Only CN that does NOT relay through the thalamus. II Optic S Vision. Decussates at the optic chiasm . III Oculomotor M Most extraocular muscles, levator palpebrae, pupillary constriction. IV Trochlear M Superior oblique only. Smallest CN. V Trigeminal B Face sensation, mastication. VI Abducens M Lateral rectus only. VII Facial B Facial expression, taste (anterior 2/3 tongue), salivation, lacrimation. VIII Vestibulocochlear S Hearing + balance. IX Glossopharyngeal B Taste (posterior 1/3), pharynx, parotid. X Vagus B Parasympathetic to thorax/abdomen, larynx, pharynx. XI Spinal accessory M SCM and trapezius. XII Hypoglossal M Tongue movement. Mnemonic: "Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter Most" → S = sensory, M = motor, B = both, in order I–XII. Recap §3. CNS + PNS (somatic + autonomic). Meninges DAP (dura-arachnoid-pia), CSF from choroid plexus through ventricles. Forebrain/midbrain/hindbrain. Thalamus relays all but smell; hypothalamus runs homeostasis. Glia: oligo (CNS) vs Schwann (PNS).

chunks.heading: 4. Neural conduction & synaptic transmission (Pinel ch. 4)
chunks.text: 4. Neural conduction & synaptic transmission (Pinel ch. 4) Full primer: action potential page . Here is the teaching version.

chunks.heading: The resting potential: why a neuron sits charged
chunks.text: The resting potential: why a neuron sits charged An unstimulated neuron holds its inside about −70 mV negative to the outside. Three forces set this up: the Na⁺/K⁺ pump (pushes 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in, using ATP), leaky K⁺ channels (K⁺ drifts out down its gradient), and large negative proteins trapped inside. The membrane is a charged battery waiting to discharge.

chunks.heading: The action potential, step by step
chunks.text: The action potential, step by step Na⁺ and K⁺ channels across the three phases of the action potential. Pinel & Barnes, 11th ed. · Fig 4.5 Threshold ~ −55 mV must be reached at the axon hillock. Depolarisation: voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open → Na⁺ rushes in → spike to ~ +30 mV. Repolarisation: Na⁺ channels inactivate; voltage-gated K⁺ channels open → K⁺ flows out. Hyperpolarisation (undershoot): K⁺ channels close slowly → dips below −70 mV briefly. All-or-none law: once threshold is reached the AP fires at constant amplitude . Stimulus intensity is coded by frequency of firing, never by spike size.

chunks.heading: Refractory periods
chunks.text: Refractory periods Absolute refractory period — Na⁺ channels inactivated; no stimulus, however strong, can fire another AP. This sets the maximum firing rate and forces the AP to travel one way. Relative refractory period — membrane is hyperpolarised; a stronger-than-usual stimulus can fire one.

chunks.heading: Saltatory conduction
chunks.text: Saltatory conduction In myelinated axons the AP regenerates only at the Nodes of Ranvier and "jumps" between them. This is faster and far more energy-efficient than continuous conduction. Demyelination (as in MS ) destroys this and slows or blocks conduction.

chunks.heading: The synapse: step by step
chunks.text: The synapse: step by step Anatomy of a typical synapse. Pinel & Barnes, 11th ed. · Fig 4.7 AP arrives at the terminal. Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open; Ca²⁺ enters. Vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane (SNARE proteins) and release NT. NT crosses the cleft and binds postsynaptic receptors. EPSP (depolarising) or IPSP (hyperpolarising); spatial + temporal summation at the axon hillock decides if a new AP fires. NT is cleared by reuptake , enzymatic breakdown , or diffusion . Receptors come in two styles: ionotropic (ligand-gated ion channels, fast, e.g. nicotinic ACh, GABA-A, AMPA/NMDA) and metabotropic (G-protein-coupled, slower, longer-lasting, e.g. muscarinic ACh, most dopamine receptors). Autoreceptors on the presynaptic terminal sense the cell's own NT and provide feedback.

chunks.heading: The seven neurotransmitter families (high-yield)
chunks.text: The seven neurotransmitter families (high-yield) The classes of neurotransmitters. Pinel & Barnes, 11th ed. · Fig 4.16 NT Class Made from Cleared by Clinical link Acetylcholine (ACh) Quaternary amine Choline + acetyl-CoA Acetylcholinesterase Alzheimer's (low ACh), myasthenia gravis (anti-AChR), NMJ Dopamine Catecholamine Tyrosine → DOPA → DA Reuptake, MAO, COMT ↑ mesolimbic = +ve schizophrenia. Low nigrostriatal = Parkinson's. Reward / addiction. Norepinephrine Catecholamine DA + β-hydroxylase Reuptake, MAO Arousal, sympathetic. Locus coeruleus. Low in depression. Serotonin (5-HT) Indolamine Tryptophan Reuptake (SERT), MAO Mood, sleep, appetite. Low → depression, OCD. Raphe nuclei. Glutamate Amino acid Glutamine Reuptake by astrocytes Main excitatory NT. NMDA, AMPA, kainate. LTP, learning. Excess = excitotoxicity. GABA Amino acid Glutamate (via GAD) Reuptake Main inhibitory NT. GABA-A = ionotropic, target of benzos, alcohol, barbiturates. Endorphins Peptide POMC Peptidases Pain modulation, runner's high. μ, κ, δ receptors. TRAP: LTP in hippocampus depends on NMDA receptors. NMDA = a coincidence detector : it needs glutamate AND postsynaptic depolarisation to displace its Mg²⁺ block. Ca²⁺ entry through NMDA triggers LTP; AMPA carries the fast EPSP. Dopamine is built from tyrosine , serotonin from tryptophan , do not swap the precursors. Recap §4. Rest −70 mV (Na/K pump + leaky K

chunks.heading: 5. Research methods of biopsychology (Pinel ch. 5)
chunks.text: 5. Research methods of biopsychology (Pinel ch. 5) Every claim about brain and behaviour rests on a method, and every method answers a different question. Pinel groups them into lesion, recording, imaging, and stimulation.

chunks.heading: Lesion / ablation methods
chunks.text: Lesion / ablation methods Ablation / lesion: remove or destroy tissue and observe the behavioural deficit (the oldest approach). Aspiration (suction), radio-frequency / electrolytic lesions, knife cuts , and chemical excitotoxic lesions (kainic acid spares fibres of passage, killing only cell bodies). Reversible lesions: cooling or local anaesthetic (lidocaine) temporarily knock out a region, then it recovers, a cleaner causal test. Stereotaxic surgery: the stereotaxic atlas + instrument lets you reach a deep target by 3-D coordinates from the bregma landmark on the skull. This is how electrodes and cannulae are placed.

chunks.heading: Recording methods
chunks.text: Recording methods Method What it records Strength Single-unit recording Firing of one neuron via a microelectrode Best spatial + temporal resolution (one cell) EEG Summed cortical electrical activity from scalp electrodes Excellent temporal resolution; poor spatial. Used for sleep stages, seizures, ERPs Event-related potential (ERP) EEG time-locked and averaged to a stimulus Tracks the timing of cognitive processing (e.g. P300, N400)

chunks.heading: Imaging methods
chunks.text: Imaging methods Method What it shows Note CT (CAT) X-ray structural image Fast, good for bleeds/fractures; uses radiation MRI Structural image from magnetic fields Higher resolution than CT, no radiation fMRI Function: the BOLD signal (blood oxygenation) Good spatial resolution, slower temporal; the workhorse of cognitive neuroscience PET Function: metabolism/blood flow via radioactive tracer (e.g. 2-DG, or ligands for receptors) Can map neurotransmitter receptors; uses radiation DTI White-matter tracts (diffusion of water) Maps connectivity TRAP — structure vs function and resolution. CT/MRI = structure ; fMRI/PET = function . EEG = great timing, poor location; fMRI = great location, poorer timing. Examiners pair these opposites. BOLD is the fMRI signal.

chunks.heading: Stimulation methods
chunks.text: Stimulation methods Electrical brain stimulation (ESB): drive a region and see the evoked behaviour (Penfield's cortical mapping; Olds & Milner's reward stimulation). Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS): a magnetic pulse non-invasively excites or transiently disrupts a cortical area, a "virtual lesion" in healthy humans, and a treatment for depression. Optogenetics (newer): light switches genetically modified neurons on/off with millisecond precision.

chunks.heading: Psychophysiological measures (non-invasive, on the body)
chunks.text: Psychophysiological measures (non-invasive, on the body) Skin conductance (SCR/GSR) — sympathetic arousal via sweat; used in lie detection and emotion research. ECG / heart rate , EMG (muscle), EOG (eye movement), pupillometry . Lock the pairings: deep target by coordinates = stereotaxic ; one neuron = single-unit ; timing of cognition = ERP/EEG ; non-invasive virtual lesion = TMS ; receptor mapping = PET ; structure = CT/MRI; function = fMRI/PET. Recap §5. Lesion (incl. reversible) + stereotaxic placement; recording (single-unit, EEG, ERP); imaging (CT/MRI structure, fMRI/PET function); stimulation (ESB, TMS, optogenetics); psychophysiology (SCR, HR, EMG, EOG).

chunks.heading: 6. The visual system (Pinel ch. 6)
chunks.text: 6. The visual system (Pinel ch. 6) Vision is the model sensory system in Pinel because we know its wiring best. The job: turn patterns of light into a neural representation of the world.

chunks.heading: The retina: where light becomes neural signal
chunks.text: The retina: where light becomes neural signal The cellular structure of the retina. Pinel & Barnes, 11th ed. · Fig 6.5 Light passes through the retina's layers to reach the photoreceptors at the back, so the retina is "inside out". Rods — peripheral, very light-sensitive, no colour, low acuity (night/scotopic vision). Cones — concentrated at the fovea , colour, high acuity (day/photopic vision). Cones are densest at the fovea centralis. The optic disc (where the optic nerve leaves) has no photoreceptors = the blind spot . Signal flow within the retina: photoreceptors → bipolar cells → retinal ganglion cells (whose axons form the optic nerve), with horizontal and amacrine cells doing lateral interaction. Lateral inhibition sharpens edges (Mach bands).

chunks.heading: The retina-geniculate-striate pathway
chunks.text: The retina-geniculate-striate pathway The retina-geniculate-striate pathway. Pinel & Barnes, 11th ed. · Fig 6.13 Retina → optic nerve → optic chiasm (nasal fibres cross, so the left visual field of both eyes goes right) → optic tract → LGN of the thalamus → optic radiations → primary visual cortex (V1 / striate cortex) in the occipital lobe. The map is retinotopic (neighbouring retina → neighbouring cortex). Hubel & Wiesel found V1 cells are feature detectors (simple, complex, hypercomplex cells tuned to edges and orientation).

chunks.heading: Two cortical streams: what vs where
chunks.text: Two cortical streams: what vs where Stream Route Job Lesion Ventral ("what") V1 → temporal lobe Object and face recognition Visual agnosia, prosopagnosia Dorsal ("where / how") V1 → parietal lobe Spatial location, visually guided action Optic ataxia, neglect

chunks.heading: Theories of colour vision (these are complementary, not rivals)
chunks.text: Theories of colour vision (these are complementary, not rivals) Trichromatic (Young-Helmholtz) — three cone types (S/M/L, "blue/green/red"); colour = ratio of their activity. Operates at the receptor (retinal) level . Opponent-process (Hering) — colour coded in opposing pairs: red-green, blue-yellow, black-white. Operates after the retina (ganglion cells, LGN). Explains negative afterimages and why we never see "reddish-green". TRAP: the two colour theories are both right at different stages : trichromatic at the cones, opponent-process downstream. Negative afterimages = opponent-process evidence. Rods do not code colour. Dorsal = where/how (parietal), Ventral = what (temporal): "dorsal is up and points to where". Recap §6. Rods (dim, no colour) vs cones (fovea, colour). Pathway: retina → chiasm → LGN → V1. Dorsal = where (parietal), ventral = what (temporal). Colour = trichromatic at cones + opponent-process after.

chunks.heading: 7. Mechanisms of perception: audition & the other senses (Pinel ch. 7)
chunks.text: 7. Mechanisms of perception: audition & the other senses (Pinel ch. 7)

chunks.heading: Audition
chunks.text: Audition Anatomy of the ear. Pinel & Barnes, 11th ed. · Fig 7.4 Path: outer ear → middle ear ossicles ( malleus, incus, stapes ) → inner ear cochlea . Hair cells on the basilar membrane → CN VIII → cochlear nuclei → superior olive → inferior colliculus → MGN of thalamus → primary auditory cortex ( Heschl's gyrus , temporal lobe).

chunks.heading: How is pitch coded? Three theories
chunks.text: How is pitch coded? Three theories Theory Mechanism Best for Place theory (von Békésy) Different frequencies peak at different places on the basilar membrane: high at the base , low at the apex High frequencies Frequency (temporal) theory The whole membrane fires at the rate of the sound's frequency Low frequencies (< ~500 Hz) Volley principle Groups of neurons fire in rotating "volleys" to track frequencies above any single neuron's limit Mid-range (bridges the two) TRAP: Place = high frequency (base of cochlea), frequency theory = low , volley = middle . Loudness is coded by firing rate + number of hair cells, not by place.

chunks.heading: Somatosensation: two ascending highways
chunks.text: Somatosensation: two ascending highways The dorsal-column medial-lemniscus system. Pinel & Barnes, 11th ed. · Fig 7.10 The anterolateral system. Pinel & Barnes, 11th ed. · Fig 7.11 Dorsal column–medial lemniscus (DCML) Anterolateral / spinothalamic Carries Fine touch, vibration, proprioception Pain, temperature, crude touch Decussates In the medulla (high up) At the spinal level of entry (immediately) Speed/fibres Fast, large myelinated Slower, small fibres Why the decussation level matters clinically. Because the two systems cross at different levels, a one-sided spinal cord lesion ( Brown-Séquard ) loses fine touch/proprioception on the same side (DCML crosses later, up in the medulla) but pain/temperature on the opposite side (spinothalamic crossed immediately). That dissociation is a favourite exam item. Pain & gate control (Melzack & Wall): non-painful input (rubbing) can "close a gate" in the dorsal horn and reduce pain; descending signals from the PAG (periaqueductal grey), via endorphins, also dampen pain.

chunks.heading: Chemical senses
chunks.text: Chemical senses Taste (gustation): five basics, sweet, salty, sour, bitter, umami. CN VII (anterior 2/3 tongue), IX (posterior 1/3), X (epiglottis). Insula = primary gustatory cortex. Smell (olfaction): olfactory epithelium → olfactory bulb → piriform cortex , with no thalamic relay (the exception). Direct limbic ties explain odour-evoked emotional memory.

chunks.heading: Attention
chunks.text: Attention Perception is selective. Cocktail-party effect : you track one voice in a crowd, yet your own name still breaks through (so unattended channels are partly processed). The posterior parietal cortex and frontal eye fields shift spatial attention; damage to the right parietal causes hemispatial neglect (§19). Pinel distinguishes endogenous (goal-driven, top-down) from exogenous (stimulus-driven, bottom-up) attention. Recap §7. Audition: ossicles → cochlea → basilar membrane → MGN → Heschl's gyrus; place=high, frequency=low, volley=mid. Touch: DCML (fine touch, crosses in medulla) vs spinothalamic (pain/temp, crosses at entry). Smell skips the thalamus. Attention: endogenous vs exogenous.

chunks.heading: 8. The sensorimotor system (Pinel ch. 8)
chunks.text: 8. The sensorimotor system (Pinel ch. 8) The sensorimotor system as a hierarchy. Pinel & Barnes, 11th ed. · Fig 8.1 The organising idea: a hierarchy. Movement is planned top-down and executed bottom-up. High levels set goals; low levels handle the muscle detail; sensory feedback flows back up. The chain runs: association cortex (intention) → secondary motor cortex (SMA + premotor, the plan) → primary motor cortex M1 (the command) → brainstem & spinal circuits → muscle , with the basal ganglia and cerebellum tuning it from the side.

chunks.heading: Pyramidal tract (corticospinal)
chunks.text: Pyramidal tract (corticospinal) Origin: primary motor cortex (M1, Brodmann area 4) and premotor. Path: internal capsule → cerebral peduncle → pons → medullary pyramids. Decussates at the pyramids of the medulla (~85–90%) → lateral corticospinal tract (fine, distal, voluntary movement). The remaining 10–15% form the anterior corticospinal tract and decussate at the spinal segment.

chunks.heading: Extrapyramidal pathways
chunks.text: Extrapyramidal pathways Rubrospinal — from the red nucleus; flexor bias. Vestibulospinal — postural extensors, balance. Reticulospinal — locomotion, posture, gross movements. Tectospinal — head/neck orienting to stimuli.

chunks.heading: Who does what in the hierarchy (NIMHANS swap-traps)
chunks.text: Who does what in the hierarchy (NIMHANS swap-traps) The motor homunculus. Pinel & Barnes, 11th ed. · Fig 8.6 Structure Job Lock the trap Posterior parietal association cortex Integrates body position + external space to form the intention to move and guide reaching. Lesion → apraxia, neglect. Premotor cortex Plans externally / sensory-cued movement: you see something and reach for it. Preps posture and muscle groups before M1 fires. Premotor = external / cue-driven . SMA (supplementary motor area) Plans internally generated, self-initiated movement; sequencing complex moves from memory + bimanual coordination. SMA = internal / from within . (premotor vs SMA = external vs internal, that one distinction is half the question) Primary motor cortex (M1) Issues the movement command; somatotopically organised (the motor homunculus ). Lesion → contralateral weakness/paralysis. Basal ganglia Initiate / select movement and gate it (move or not). Set the vigour : scale force and amplitude . Bradykinesia in Parkinson's is this failing. "Scales force / amplitude / vigour" → basal ganglia . Lesions go two ways: Parkinson's (hypokinetic, resting tremor) and Huntington's / chorea (hyperkinetic). Cerebellum Coordination, timing, balance, error correction, motor learning. Compares intended vs actual and smooths speed/accuracy while the movement is happening . "Timing / smoothing / coordination"

chunks.heading: Upper vs lower motor neuron signs
chunks.text: Upper vs lower motor neuron signs UMN lesion LMN lesion Tone Spasticity (↑) Flaccidity (↓) Reflexes Hyperreflexia, clonus, + Babinski Hyporeflexia / areflexia Atrophy Mild, late (disuse) Severe, early Fasciculations Absent Present Lock it: UMN = spastic, hyperreflexic, Babinski up, no fasciculations. LMN = flaccid, areflexic, atrophy + fasciculations. (ALS strikes both.) Recap §8. Hierarchy: association cortex → SMA (internal) / premotor (external) → M1 → brainstem/spinal → muscle. Pyramidal crosses at the medullary pyramids. Basal ganglia = force/gating (resting tremor); cerebellum = timing/coordination (intention tremor). UMN spastic vs LMN flaccid.

chunks.heading: 9. Development of the nervous system (Pinel ch. 9)
chunks.text: 9. Development of the nervous system (Pinel ch. 9) The question: how does a single fertilised cell become a brain with ~86 billion neurons wired into the right circuits? Pinel walks five phases, then myelination and pruning. Neural tube formation (neurulation): the ectoderm folds into the neural tube (~week 3–4); its hollow centre becomes the ventricles, the anterior end becomes the brain. Failure = spina bifida / anencephaly (folic acid protects). Proliferation: cells in the ventricular zone divide to produce neurons and glia. Migration: new neurons travel to their destinations, many guided along radial glia ; the cortex is built inside-out (deep layers first). Differentiation & axon growth: neurons take on their type; the growth cone navigates by chemical cues (chemoaffinity, Sperry). Synaptogenesis: synapses form, in huge excess at first. Then two sculpting processes refine the over-built brain: Neural death (apoptosis) & synaptic pruning: ~50% of neurons die, and unused synapses are eliminated. Neurotrophins (e.g. NGF) keep useful connections alive: "use it or lose it". Myelination: continues for years after birth (the prefrontal cortex finishes myelinating in the early–mid 20s, which is why mature judgement comes late). Critical / sensitive periods. Some circuits must get the right experience within a time window or they wire abnormally for life. Hubel & Wiesel's monocular

chunks.heading: 10. Brain damage & neuroplasticity (Pinel ch. 10)
chunks.text: 10. Brain damage & neuroplasticity (Pinel ch. 10)

chunks.heading: Causes of brain damage
chunks.text: Causes of brain damage Cause Key facts Tumours (neoplasms) Encapsulated/benign (meningioma) vs infiltrating/malignant (glioma); metastatic from elsewhere. Cerebrovascular (stroke) Ischaemic (clot: thrombosis/embolism) vs haemorrhagic (bleed). Penumbra = salvageable tissue. Excitotoxic glutamate cascade kills neurons. Traumatic brain injury (TBI) Closed-head: contusions, contrecoup injury, concussion. Repeated TBI → chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) . Infections Encephalitis, meningitis, abscess; neurosyphilis. Neurotoxins Heavy metals (lead, mercury), MPTP (causes Parkinsonism), alcohol. Genetic / programmed See the genetic-disorders table below and the dementias.

chunks.heading: Degeneration & regeneration
chunks.text: Degeneration & regeneration Anterograde degeneration = the cut axon segment away from the cell body dies. Retrograde = the segment toward the cell body (and sometimes the cell) degenerates. Regeneration is much better in the PNS than the CNS, largely because Schwann cells (PNS) guide and support regrowth, whereas CNS oligodendrocytes /glial scarring inhibit it.

chunks.heading: Plasticity & recovery of function
chunks.text: Plasticity & recovery of function The brain rewires. "Plasticity" means the brain changes its structure and connections with experience and after injury. Mechanisms of recovery: cortical reorganisation (neighbouring areas take over), collateral sprouting , redundant circuits, and behaviourally driven relearning (the basis of rehabilitation). Adult neurogenesis occurs in the hippocampal dentate gyrus and the olfactory bulb/SVZ, but is limited.

chunks.heading: The major neurological disorders & dementias (NIMHANS-weighted)
chunks.text: The major neurological disorders & dementias (NIMHANS-weighted) Disorder Pathology Hallmark Alzheimer's disease Amyloid-β plaques + tau neurofibrillary tangles ; loss of cholinergic neurons (nucleus basalis of Meynert) Progressive anterograde memory loss first; treated with cholinesterase inhibitors + memantine (NMDA) Parkinson's disease Loss of dopamine neurons in substantia nigra (pars compacta) ; Lewy bodies (α-synuclein) Resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability; L-DOPA Huntington's disease Caudate/putamen atrophy; CAG expansion (HTT, chr 4), autosomal dominant Chorea + cognitive decline + psychiatric change; anticipation across generations Multiple sclerosis (MS) Autoimmune demyelination of CNS white matter Relapsing-remitting deficits; slowed conduction (loss of saltatory conduction) Epilepsy Hypersynchronous neuronal discharge Generalised (e.g. tonic-clonic, absence) vs focal/partial; aura, ictal, post-ictal

chunks.heading: Genetic disorders (retained, high-yield)
chunks.text: Genetic disorders (retained, high-yield) Disorder Genetics Notes Huntington's disease Autosomal dominant; CAG trinucleotide expansion on chromosome 4 (HTT gene) Anticipation across generations. Caudate atrophy, chorea, dementia, onset age 30–50. Down syndrome Trisomy 21 Intellectual disability, characteristic features, ↑ Alzheimer's risk. Fragile X X-linked CGG expansion (FMR1) Most common inherited cause of intellectual disability. PKU Autosomal recessive Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency. Diet treatable; untreated → intellectual disability. Klinefelter XXY Male, hypogonadism, mild learning issues. Turner XO Female, short stature, gonadal dysgenesis. TRAP: Alzheimer's = plaques (amyloid) + tangles (tau) , memory-first. Parkinson's = substantia nigra dopamine loss + Lewy bodies , movement-first. Huntington's = caudate, CAG, dominant . Adult neurogenesis happens mainly in the hippocampal dentate gyrus . PNS (Schwann) regenerates better than CNS. Recap §10. Damage from tumour/stroke (ischaemic vs haemorrhagic)/TBI/infection/toxin. PNS regenerates better (Schwann). Plasticity drives recovery; neurogenesis in dentate gyrus. Dementias: Alzheimer's (plaques+tangles), Parkinson's (SN/Lewy), Huntington's (caudate/CAG), MS (demyelination).

chunks.heading: 11. Learning, memory & amnesia (Pinel ch. 11)
chunks.text: 11. Learning, memory & amnesia (Pinel ch. 11) The landmark case that built the field. Patient H.M. had both medial temporal lobes (including the hippocampus) removed in 1953 to stop seizures. He could no longer form new long-term explicit memories (severe anterograde amnesia ) yet kept old memories, normal IQ, and could still learn new motor skills (mirror drawing) without remembering having practised. This single dissociation proved (1) the hippocampus is needed to form new declarative memories but is not the storehouse, and (2) declarative and procedural memory are separate systems.

chunks.heading: The taxonomy of memory
chunks.text: The taxonomy of memory Type Subtype Brain region Declarative (explicit) Episodic (events) Hippocampus + medial temporal lobe Semantic (facts) Temporal neocortex Non-declarative (implicit) Procedural (skills, habits) Striatum / basal ganglia Classical conditioning (motor) Cerebellum Emotional conditioning Amygdala Patient K.C. lost episodic memory (could not re-experience events) but kept semantic knowledge, dissociating the two. Amygdala = emotional memory and fear conditioning; cerebellum = conditioned motor responses (eyeblink); striatum = habit/procedural learning.

chunks.heading: Long-term potentiation (LTP): the synaptic mechanism
chunks.text: Long-term potentiation (LTP): the synaptic mechanism The major components of the hippocampus. Pinel & Barnes, 11th ed. · Fig 11.4 LTP = a long-lasting strengthening of a synapse after high-frequency stimulation, the leading cellular model of learning, first shown in the hippocampus. It depends on the NMDA receptor , a coincidence detector: it opens only when glutamate binds and the postsynaptic cell is already depolarised (relieving its Mg²⁺ block). Ca²⁺ then floods in and drives AMPA receptor insertion , making the synapse stronger. This is the molecular face of Hebb's rule: "neurons that fire together wire together." LTD (long-term depression) is the opposite, weakening unused synapses; both enable plasticity.

chunks.heading: Amnesias
chunks.text: Amnesias Retrograde vs anterograde amnesia after a closed-head TBI. Pinel & Barnes, 11th ed. · Fig 11.5 Anterograde = cannot form new memories after the event (H.M.). Retrograde = lost memories from before the event. Ribot's law: recent memories are more vulnerable than remote ones. Korsakoff's syndrome = thiamine (B1) deficiency , usually from chronic alcoholism; damages the mammillary bodies + dorsomedial thalamus . Hallmark: dense anterograde amnesia + confabulation . The acute precursor is Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia), together Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (see §19). The engram = the physical memory trace; Lashley searched for it (mass action / equipotentiality), Richard Semon coined the term, and modern work locates engram cells in the hippocampus. TRAP: H.M. = bilateral medial temporal/hippocampus → anterograde amnesia, intact procedural learning. Korsakoff = thiamine , mammillary bodies + thalamus, confabulation . Hippocampus forms declarative memory but is not the permanent store. LTP needs NMDA ; AMPA carries the fast current. Recap §11. H.M. → hippocampus forms new declarative memory; procedural is separate (striatum/cerebellum/amygdala). LTP via NMDA + Ca²⁺ → AMPA insertion = Hebbian learning. Korsakoff = thiamine + mammillary bodies + confabulation.

chunks.heading: 12. Hunger, eating & health (Pinel ch. 12)
chunks.text: 12. Hunger, eating & health (Pinel ch. 12) The classic theory and its limits. The old dual-centre hypothalamic hypothesis said the lateral hypothalamus (LH) is the "hunger/go" centre and the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) is the "satiety/stop" centre. Lesion evidence: VMH lesion → hyperphagia + obesity (the rat overeats); LH lesion → aphagia (the rat stops eating). True but oversimplified, eating is regulated by a network and many peptides, not two switches.

chunks.heading: The hormonal signals
chunks.text: The hormonal signals Signal Source Effect on appetite Leptin Adipose (fat) tissue ↓ appetite (long-term adiposity signal); acts via the arcuate nucleus Ghrelin Stomach (empty) ↑ appetite (the "hunger hormone") Insulin Pancreas ↑ satiety; glucose uptake CCK Duodenum ↑ short-term satiety (meal termination) PYY Intestine ↓ appetite after eating

chunks.heading: Two competing frameworks for regulation
chunks.text: Two competing frameworks for regulation Set-point theory: the body defends a fixed weight/energy level like a thermostat; you eat to correct a deficit. Explains homeostasis but not why we eat when full or why obesity is rising. Positive-incentive theory (Pinel favours this): we eat largely because of the anticipated pleasure of food (its incentive value), shaped by taste, learning, and availability, not just internal depletion. Explains overeating in a food-rich world.

chunks.heading: Disorders of eating
chunks.text: Disorders of eating Obesity: mismatch between an evolved drive to store energy and an environment of cheap palatable food; leptin resistance in many cases. Anorexia nervosa (restriction, low weight, body-image disturbance) and bulimia nervosa (binge-purge); high mortality for anorexia. TRAP: VMH = satiety (lesion → obese); LH = feeding (lesion → aphagia). Leptin from fat lowers appetite; ghrelin from the stomach raises it (do not swap). Pinel argues positive-incentive beats pure set-point. Recap §12. VMH satiety / LH hunger. Leptin (fat) ↓ appetite via arcuate; ghrelin (stomach) ↑; insulin/CCK/PYY ↑ satiety. Set-point vs positive-incentive (Pinel prefers incentive).

chunks.heading: 13. Hormones & sex (Pinel ch. 13)
chunks.text: 13. Hormones & sex (Pinel ch. 13) The endocrine system is the body's slow, broadcast signalling system: glands release hormones into the blood to act on distant targets. The brain commands it through the hypothalamus → pituitary link.

chunks.heading: The endocrine map
chunks.text: The endocrine map Gland Hormone Action Hypothalamus CRH, TRH, GHRH, GnRH, somatostatin, dopamine Releasing/inhibiting factors to the anterior pituitary Anterior pituitary ACTH, TSH, GH, FSH/LH, prolactin Trophic hormones Posterior pituitary ADH (vasopressin), oxytocin Made in hypothalamus, stored/released by posterior pituitary. ADH → water reabsorption. Oxytocin → labour, milk ejection, bonding.
