chunks.heading: Blatt & Spitz — Anaclitic vs Introjective Depression
chunks.text: Blatt & Spitz — Anaclitic vs Introjective Depression Abnormal · Mood disorders · Exam-grade · Built 2026-06-07 Why this page exists: Both Blatt and Spitz showed up on the NIMHANS paper . That makes them high-yield, not edge cases. This is the focused one-pager; the same content folds into the Abnormal book's mood-disorders chapter. The single biggest trap is below: there are two different "anaclitic depressions" (one infant, one adult) and they get conflated constantly. THE TRAP, up front: "Anaclitic depression" means two different things depending on who said it. Spitz's anaclitic depression = an infant syndrome caused by separation from the mother (clinical/developmental observation, 1946). Blatt's anaclitic depression = an adult depression subtype / personality configuration centred on dependency (theory of depression, 1974). Both come from the same root word "anaclitic" = leaning on / depending on (Greek anaklinein , to lean upon). Same word, different age group, different theorist. If a stem mentions infants/separation → Spitz. If it mentions an adult dependency-vs-self-criticism split → Blatt.

chunks.heading: 1. The Word: "Anaclitic"
chunks.text: 1. The Word: "Anaclitic" Anaclitic = leaning on / dependent on another for support. From Greek anaklinein ("to lean upon"). Freudian root: anaclitic object-choice = choosing a love object on the model of the person who fed/protected you (mother), i.e. love based on dependency, vs narcissistic object-choice (loving someone like yourself). So "anaclitic depression" in both Spitz and Blatt = a depression organised around dependency and loss of the caregiving/loved other .

chunks.heading: 2. Blatt — Two-Polarities (Two-Configurations) Model
chunks.text: 2. Blatt — Two-Polarities (Two-Configurations) Model Sidney J. Blatt (Yale) argued that personality develops along two fundamental, lifelong coordinates / developmental lines : Line Also called What it is about Anaclitic Relatedness (interpersonal) Establishing and maintaining close, satisfying relationships — intimacy, trust, mutuality. Introjective Self-definition (identity) Establishing a stable, coherent, realistic, positive sense of self — autonomy, identity, self-worth. Core claim: Normal personality development is a dialectic — the two lines develop in reciprocal, synergistic interaction. You need relatedness to define a self, and a self to relate. Maturity = a balance of both. Blatt, 1974 (and refined through 1992, 2004/2008 Polarities of Experience ). Psychopathology = a one-sided, exaggerated over-development of one line at the expense of the other. You compensate on one axis because the other is distorted. Two corresponding configurations of depression fall out of this (next section).

chunks.heading: 3. Blatt's Two Types of Depression
chunks.text: 3. Blatt's Two Types of Depression Anaclitic depression (dependent) Introjective depression (self-critical) Polarity Relatedness disturbed Self-definition disturbed Core theme Loss of the other / fear of abandonment Loss of self-worth / failure to meet standards Felt experience Helplessness, weakness, loneliness, emptiness, depletion; longing to be loved, cared for, fed, protected Guilt, worthlessness, inferiority, failure, self-criticism; feeling one has not lived up to expectations Central fear Being abandoned / unloved Loss of approval / recognition , disapproval of a harsh conscience Superego / conscience Not the main driver Harsh, punitive superego ; perfectionism Developmental tie Oral, early dependency; disrupted attachment Later, autonomy/achievement; self-evaluation What they seek Closeness, reassurance, being taken care of Achievement, control, perfection, approval TRAP: Don't map "anaclitic = sad" and "introjective = guilty" too crudely. The cleaner split: anaclitic depression is about the relationship (losing the other) ; introjective depression is about the self (failing the self/standards) . Dependency vs self-criticism.

chunks.heading: 3.1 How Blatt's split lines up with other two-factor depression models
chunks.text: 3.1 How Blatt's split lines up with other two-factor depression models Examiners love asking which models are "the same idea under different names." Blatt's anaclitic/introjective parallels: Author Dependency / relatedness pole Self-criticism / self-definition pole Blatt Anaclitic Introjective Beck Sociotropy Autonomy Arieti & Bemporad Dominant other Dominant goal Bakan Communion Agency Freud (work/love) Love (Lieben) Work (Arbeiten) One-liner: Blatt = Beck's sociotropy/autonomy from a psychoanalytic angle. Anaclitic ≈ sociotropic; introjective ≈ autonomous.

chunks.heading: 3.2 The measure
chunks.text: 3.2 The measure Depressive Experiences Questionnaire (DEQ) — Blatt, D'Afflitti & Quinlan (1976). Yields the factors Dependency (anaclitic) and Self-Criticism (introjective) — plus an Efficacy factor. If a question names the DEQ → it's Blatt's anaclitic/introjective framework.

chunks.heading: 4. Spitz — Anaclitic Depression (the infant syndrome)
chunks.text: 4. Spitz — Anaclitic Depression (the infant syndrome) René Spitz (1887–1974), Austrian-American psychoanalyst, studied infants in institutions and foundling homes. Anaclitic depression (Spitz, 1946): a syndrome in infants roughly 6–18 months old who, after forming a good, normal attachment to the mother , are separated from her for a prolonged period (about 3 months) with no adequate substitute caregiver . Course: at first the infant protests/cries and clings; then withdraws, becomes weepy, apprehensive, sad, refuses contact ; loses appetite and weight, develops insomnia ; motor/cognitive development slows and regresses; becomes susceptible to infection; a frozen, dejected expression. Reversibility: if the mother (or an adequate substitute) is returned within ~3–5 months , the infant typically recovers . The key is that the infant had a good relationship and then lost it — it is a depression of loss , not of never-having-had. "Anaclitic" because the depression follows the loss of the love object on whom the infant was anaclitically (dependently) leaning . Spitz anaclitic depression in one line: good attachment → prolonged separation (~3 months) in mid-infancy → withdrawal, weight loss, developmental arrest → reversible if the mother comes back in time .

chunks.heading: 5. Spitz — Hospitalism (the severe, often irreversible deprivation)
chunks.text: 5. Spitz — Hospitalism (the severe, often irreversible deprivation) Hospitalism (Spitz, 1945): the extreme, prolonged deterioration — physical, cognitive, emotional — of infants raised in institutions (foundling homes) under severe emotional / maternal deprivation , even when physical and nutritional needs are met and hygiene is good. Spitz's classic comparison: Foundling Home — infants cared for by overworked nurses (about one nurse to seven infants), almost no individual mothering. Despite clean, hygienic, well-fed conditions, infants showed catastrophic decline : severe developmental delay, marasmus (wasting), high susceptibility to infection, and a very high mortality rate . Nursery (a women's prison) — infants cared for by their own mothers . These infants thrived and developed normally. Conclusion: it is maternal/emotional contact , not just food and hygiene, that infants need. Emotional deprivation alone produces devastating, often irreversible harm. Linked downstream to marasmus (failure to thrive / wasting) and to Bowlby's maternal deprivation work and Harlow's monkeys.

chunks.heading: 6. Spitz: Anaclitic Depression vs Hospitalism
chunks.text: 6. Spitz: Anaclitic Depression vs Hospitalism Anaclitic depression Hospitalism Year 1946 1945 Deprivation Partial — lost a mother it had Total / prolonged emotional deprivation, often never had mothering Precondition A prior good attachment , then separation Institutional rearing with no individual mother figure Reversibility Reversible if mother returns within ~3–5 months Often irreversible ; marasmus, high mortality Severity Serious but recoverable Most severe; can be fatal TRAP: Both are Spitz, both are infants, both are emotional deprivation. The dividing line is partial & reversible (anaclitic depression) vs total & often irreversible (hospitalism) . Hospitalism is the worse, institutional one with the high death rate.

chunks.heading: 7. The Master Comparison (Blatt vs Spitz on "anaclitic")
chunks.text: 7. The Master Comparison (Blatt vs Spitz on "anaclitic") Spitz — anaclitic depression Blatt — anaclitic depression Who Infants (~6–18 months) Adults What kind of construct A clinical syndrome from real separation A personality configuration / subtype of adult depression Cause Actual loss of the mother Over-development of the relatedness line; dependency vulnerability Paired with Hospitalism (the severe form) Introjective (self-critical) depression Year / work 1946 1974, DEQ 1976 Memory hook: Spitz = small (infants) , anaclitic vs hospitalism . Blatt = big (adults) , anaclitic vs introjective . Same word "anaclitic," different theorist, different age.

chunks.heading: 8. High-Yield MCQ Lines
chunks.text: 8. High-Yield MCQ Lines Anaclitic = leaning on / dependent (Greek, to lean upon). Spitz, 1946: anaclitic depression = infant separated from an attached mother for ~3 months → withdrawal, weight loss, developmental arrest; reversible if she returns in time . Spitz, 1945: hospitalism = institution-reared infants, severe emotional deprivation despite good physical care → marasmus, high mortality, often irreversible . Spitz's foundling-home vs nursery study showed emotional/maternal contact matters more than food & hygiene. Blatt's two-polarities model: personality develops along relatedness (anaclitic) and self-definition (introjective) lines, in a dialectic. Blatt's anaclitic depression = dependency, helplessness, fear of abandonment, longing to be cared for. Blatt's introjective depression = self-criticism, guilt, worthlessness, harsh superego, failure to meet standards. Blatt ≈ Beck: anaclitic ≈ sociotropy, introjective ≈ autonomy. Also Arieti's dominant-other vs dominant-goal; Bakan's communion vs agency. Measure of Blatt's types = Depressive Experiences Questionnaire (DEQ) (1976): Dependency, Self-Criticism, Efficacy. Do not confuse Spitz's infant anaclitic depression with Blatt's adult anaclitic depression subtype.

chunks.heading: 9. 30-Second Recall Script
chunks.text: 9. 30-Second Recall Script "Anaclitic" = leaning/dependent. Two theorists, two age groups. Spitz (infants): anaclitic depression (1946) is an infant who had a good mother, lost her ~3 months in mid-infancy, withdrew, lost weight, stopped developing — reversible if she comes back; hospitalism (1945) is institution-reared infants with total emotional deprivation despite food & hygiene — marasmus, high death rate, often irreversible (foundling home vs prison nursery study). Blatt (adults): personality grows along two lines — relatedness (anaclitic) and self-definition (introjective) — in a dialectic; pathology = lopsided over-development of one. Anaclitic depression = dependency, abandonment fear, wanting care; introjective depression = self-criticism, guilt, harsh superego, failing one's standards. Maps onto Beck's sociotropy/autonomy. Measured by the DEQ . Built 2026-06-07 — focused one-pager off the NIMHANS-tested Blatt + Spitz questions. Folds into the Abnormal book's mood-disorders chapter. Pair with the Barlow & Durand and Ahuja abnormal pages. Sihan MET 2026 + NIMHANS Prep

chunks.heading: Bronfenbrenner, Ecological Systems Theory
chunks.text: Bronfenbrenner, Ecological Systems Theory Developmental Psychology · Exam-grade · Built 2026-05-05

chunks.heading: 1. Core Idea
chunks.text: 1. Core Idea Urie Bronfenbrenner (1917-2005), Russian-born American developmental psychologist. Development is shaped by ongoing interaction between the person and a set of nested environmental systems . Originally Ecological Systems Theory , "The Ecology of Human Development" (1979). Later renamed Bioecological Model (1994, refined 2005) to give biology more weight and add the PPCT mechanism. Co-founded the Head Start program (1965) in the US, applied use of the theory. One-line answer: Development = person × proximal processes × nested context × time.

chunks.heading: 2. The 5 Systems (innermost to outermost)
chunks.text: 2. The 5 Systems (innermost to outermost)

chunks.heading: 2.1 Microsystem
chunks.text: 2.1 Microsystem Immediate settings with direct face-to-face contact . Examples: family, school, peer group, neighbourhood, daycare, workplace (for adults). Influence is bidirectional : child shapes the environment, environment shapes the child. Most direct effect on development.

chunks.heading: 2.2 Mesosystem
chunks.text: 2.2 Mesosystem Interactions between two or more microsystems . Not a setting itself, a system of microsystems . Examples: parent-teacher communication, family-peer overlap, home-daycare links. Strong, supportive mesosystem links = better developmental outcomes.

chunks.heading: 2.3 Exosystem
chunks.text: 2.3 Exosystem Settings the child does not directly participate in , but which still affect them via the microsystem. Examples: parent's workplace, school board decisions, mass media, parent's social network, local government policy. TRAP: Exosystem ≠ no influence. Child isn't in it, but it shapes them through their microsystem (e.g. dad loses job → stress at home → child's development affected).

chunks.heading: 2.4 Macrosystem
chunks.text: 2.4 Macrosystem The overarching cultural blueprint , the "cultural envelope" around all the other systems. Examples: ideologies, customs, laws, religion, SES, cultural values, economic system, war/peace. Doesn't refer to a specific setting, refers to the cultural patterning that shapes all settings.

chunks.heading: 2.5 Chronosystem
chunks.text: 2.5 Chronosystem The time dimension . Added later (after the original 4 systems). Three flavours of "time" effects: Life transitions , normative (school entry, puberty) and non-normative (parents' divorce, death of parent). Historical events the person lives through (pandemic, war, recession). Sociohistorical conditions of the cohort (cohort effects). TRAP: Chronosystem was added later . Older textbooks list only 4 systems. If a question says "Bronfenbrenner originally proposed 5 systems" — false. Originally 4, chronosystem added later.

chunks.heading: 3. Quick-Reference Table
chunks.text: 3. Quick-Reference Table System What it is Examples Microsystem Direct, face-to-face settings Family, school, peers, daycare Mesosystem Interactions between microsystems Parent-teacher meetings, home-school link Exosystem Indirect settings, child not in them Parent's workplace, school board, media Macrosystem Cultural blueprint Ideology, laws, religion, SES, customs Chronosystem Time dimension Divorce, pandemic, historical era

chunks.heading: 4. PPCT Model (1994 refinement, often asked)
chunks.text: 4. PPCT Model (1994 refinement, often asked) Bronfenbrenner refined the theory into the Bioecological Model using the PPCT mechanism. This is the engine of the modern version.

chunks.heading: 4.1 Process — proximal processes
chunks.text: 4.1 Process — proximal processes The engine of development . Most important driver. Regular, reciprocal interactions over extended time between the person and people/objects/symbols in the immediate environment. Examples: parent-child play, reading together, sustained peer activity, learning a skill from a mentor. Must be regular and over long stretches of time to count as proximal processes (not one-off events).

chunks.heading: 4.2 Person — individual traits
chunks.text: 4.2 Person — individual traits Three sub-types: Sub-type Definition Examples Demand characteristics Visible traits that pull responses from others Age, gender, skin colour, physical appearance Resource characteristics Skills, abilities, experiences Intelligence, prior knowledge, social skills Force characteristics Temperament, motivation, persistence Curiosity, drive, distractibility, regulation

chunks.heading: 4.3 Context — the 5 nested systems
chunks.text: 4.3 Context — the 5 nested systems Micro / Meso / Exo / Macro / Chrono. Already covered above.

chunks.heading: 4.4 Time
chunks.text: 4.4 Time Micro-time : continuity vs interruption within an activity (e.g. uninterrupted reading session). Meso-time : consistency of activities across days and weeks. Macro-time : chronosystem level, sociohistorical change across the lifespan.

chunks.heading: 5. High-Yield Exam Pointers
chunks.text: 5. High-Yield Exam Pointers Originally 4 systems , chronosystem added later. Bidirectionality is a key examiner trigger word, especially in microsystem questions. Theory has two phases: Ecological Systems Theory (1979) → Bioecological Model (1994) with PPCT. Proximal processes are the engine , not the context. Context modifies how proximal processes operate. Mesosystem is not a setting , it's a system of relationships between settings .

chunks.heading: 6. Compare and Contrast (very high-yield)
chunks.text: 6. Compare and Contrast (very high-yield) Theorist Focus Mechanism Piaget Cognitive stages, internal Schemas, assimilation, accommodation Vygotsky Sociocultural ZPD, scaffolding (Bruner), more knowledgeable other Bronfenbrenner Ecological / multi-layered context Person × Process × Context × Time Erikson Psychosocial stages 8 crises across lifespan Bandura Social learning Observation, modeling, self-efficacy Rule of thumb: If the question stem mentions nested environments , cultural context , parent's workplace affecting child , or indirect influence → answer is Bronfenbrenner.

chunks.heading: 7. Applications
chunks.text: 7. Applications Child welfare policy — interventions at multiple system levels (family + school + community). Inclusive education — coordinating microsystems (home, school, peers). Public health — tobacco control, vaccination uptake (macro + exo levels). Family therapy — recognising that family microsystem sits inside larger systems. Head Start program (Bronfenbrenner co-founded) — early childhood intervention targeting micro + meso systems.

chunks.heading: 8. Critique
chunks.text: 8. Critique Hard to operationalise and test empirically — too many simultaneous variables. Originally underplayed biology (fixed in the bioecological revision via "Person" component). Criticised for being descriptive more than predictive , doesn't say which system dominates when. Cultural specificity is unclear — macrosystem treats "culture" as a single bucket.

chunks.heading: 9. One-line MCQ Traps
chunks.text: 9. One-line MCQ Traps Exosystem ≠ no influence. Child isn't in it, but it still affects them via the microsystem (e.g. parent loses job). Mesosystem is not a setting , it's the link between two settings the child is in. Chronosystem was added later , originally 4 systems. Bidirectionality is a microsystem feature (child also shapes parent), not a one-way arrow. Proximal processes are the engine of development, not the context. Context only shapes their effect. PPCT belongs to the Bioecological Model (1994) , not the original 1979 theory. Mass media affecting a child = exosystem , not macrosystem (media is a setting, not a cultural blueprint). "Culture, religion, ideology, SES" = macrosystem . Parent's workplace = classic exosystem example. Sibling fight at home = microsystem . Parent-teacher meeting = mesosystem .

chunks.heading: 10. 30-Second Recall Script
chunks.text: 10. 30-Second Recall Script Bronfenbrenner. Five nested systems, innermost out: Micro (direct, family/school, bidirectional), Meso (links between micros), Exo (indirect, parent's workplace), Macro (culture, laws, ideology), Chrono (time, life transitions, history, added later). 1979 Ecological Systems Theory → 1994 Bioecological Model with PPCT : P roximal P rocesses are the engine, C ontext = the 5 systems, T ime = micro/meso/macro time. Person split into demand, resource, force characteristics. Built 2026-05-05 from MET-grade Bronfenbrenner request. Pair with the dev psych cheatsheet for the wider section context. Sihan MET 2026 + NIMHANS Prep
