chunks.heading: High-Yield Concept Pack
chunks.text: High-Yield Concept Pack A batch of the exact concepts that keep showing up and keep costing you: Lewin's whole toolkit , the motivation theories (Herzberg, McClelland), attachment (Bowlby, Ainsworth, the four styles), the Johari window , proactive vs retroactive interference , and the full Indian psychology load (trigunas, pancha kosha, purusha/prakriti, the four avasthas, antahkarana, RCI 1986 vs 1993). Each one is widened out the same way as the rest of the site: the core idea, the why so it actually sticks, and the precise trap they use to catch you. Read top to bottom once, then re-pass the trap boxes before the exam. 1 Lewin (the big one) 2 Herzberg & McClelland 3 Johari window 4 Attachment 5 Interference 6 Indian psychology Self-test

chunks.heading: 1. Kurt Lewin: the one name behind half the social/org questions
chunks.text: 1. Kurt Lewin: the one name behind half the social/org questions Lewin is the founder of social psychology, group dynamics, and organisational change . If a question is about change in groups, leadership climate, or "behaviour comes from the present situation," it is almost certainly tracing back to Lewin. Five of his ideas are tested again and again: field theory (B = f(P,E)) , action research , force field analysis , unfreeze / change / refreeze , and the three leadership styles .

chunks.heading: Field theory: B = f(P, E)
chunks.text: Field theory: B = f(P, E) Behaviour is a function of the Person and the Environment acting together. P and E are not separate causes you add up; they form one interdependent whole that Lewin called the life space (the totality of everything influencing the person at that moment). Behaviour is driven by the present field of forces, not by buried childhood drives or fixed traits. Why it matters. This is Lewin's break from both psychoanalysis (which looks to the past) and trait theory (which looks to stable dispositions). For Lewin the explanation of why you act is "here and now": what forces are pushing on you in this situation right now. Change the field, change the behaviour. That is the bridge to his change models below. The trap: B = f(P,E) is pure Lewin. Do not read P and E as "nature vs nurture", and do not attribute the formula to anyone else. P (person) and E (environment) are interdependent parts of one present life space, not two historical causes.

chunks.heading: Action research
chunks.text: Action research Lewin coined action research : a cyclical, participatory method where you solve a real social problem and build knowledge at the same time, working with the people in the situation rather than studying them from outside. The cycle spirals: plan → act → observe → reflect , then re-plan and go again. His line for it: "No action without research, no research without action." And the much-quoted "Nothing is as practical as a good theory" is also Lewin. The trap: action research is applied, cyclical, and participatory , the opposite of detached basic/lab research. If a stem describes practitioners studying and fixing their own setting in repeating cycles, that is action research, and the name to pick is Lewin.

chunks.heading: Force field analysis
chunks.text: Force field analysis Any stable situation is a quasi-stationary equilibrium : it sits still because two sets of forces balance out. Driving forces push toward change; restraining forces push back and hold the status quo. To produce change you can either add driving forces or weaken restraining forces. The key finding: it is more effective to reduce the restraining forces than to pile on more driving forces. Adding driving force raises tension and provokes resistance; removing a restraint lets change happen with less conflict. The trap: the "best way to create change" answer is weaken/reduce the restraining forces , not "increase the driving forces." That second option is the distractor.

chunks.heading: Unfreeze → change (move) → refreeze
chunks.text: Unfreeze → change (move) → refreeze Lewin's three-stage model of planned change, and it maps straight onto force field analysis. Stage What happens Force-field link Unfreeze Create the motivation to change; destabilise the old equilibrium; build awareness that the current state is not working. Tip the balance by reducing restraining forces. Change / Move The transition itself: new behaviours, attitudes, and ways of working are adopted; cognitive restructuring. The system moves to a new position. Refreeze Stabilise and lock in the new state so it does not slide back; embed it in norms, habits, and structures. A new equilibrium is established and held. The trap: order and meaning. Refreeze = making the change permanent , not "going back." Unfreeze is first and is about loosening the status quo, not implementing the change yet. Stems love to scramble the three.

chunks.heading: The three leadership / group-climate styles (Lewin, Lippitt & White, 1939)
chunks.text: The three leadership / group-climate styles (Lewin, Lippitt & White, 1939) Style How the leader acts What happens in the group Autocratic (authoritarian) Leader decides alone, dictates tasks, stays apart. High output only while watched ; more hostility/aggression or apathy; work stops when the leader leaves; dependent members. Democratic Decisions shared, leader guides and explains, members participate. Best quality work, highest satisfaction and cohesion; output continues even when the leader is away. Generally the most effective. Laissez-faire Hands-off, little guidance or feedback, leaves the group to it. Lowest productivity , low satisfaction, members directionless and frustrated. The trap: "most effective" is democratic (best quality + morale + self-sustaining), but watch the nuance: autocratic can give high quantity in the short term while supervised. Laissez-faire is the least productive , not democratic. Do not mix laissez-faire ("hands-off") with democratic ("shared"). NIMHANS depth (other Lewin items worth knowing): he founded group dynamics and sensitivity training / T-groups . The Zeigarnik effect (unfinished tasks remembered better) came out of his circle, named for his student Bluma Zeigarnik. He also gave the three conflict types : approach-approach (two goods), avoidance-avoidance (two bads, "between a rock and a hard place"), and approach-avoidance (one goal wi

chunks.heading: 2. Motivation at work: Herzberg and McClelland
chunks.text: 2. Motivation at work: Herzberg and McClelland

chunks.heading: Herzberg's two-factor (motivation-hygiene) theory
chunks.text: Herzberg's two-factor (motivation-hygiene) theory Herzberg's big claim: satisfaction and dissatisfaction are not two ends of one scale, they are two separate scales driven by two different sets of factors. Fixing what makes people unhappy does not make them motivated; it only makes them "not unhappy." Factor type Examples What it controls Hygiene factors (extrinsic, "maintenance", dissatisfiers) Salary/pay, company policy, supervision, working conditions, interpersonal relations, job security, status. Their absence causes dissatisfaction . Their presence only removes dissatisfaction; it does not motivate. Motivators (intrinsic, satisfiers) Achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement, growth. Their presence produces real satisfaction and motivation ; their absence leaves people neutral, not dissatisfied. Why the two-scale idea is the whole point. The opposite of "dissatisfied" is not "satisfied", it is "not dissatisfied." So you can have a well-paid, comfortable job (good hygiene) and still feel zero drive, because none of the motivators are present. You raise motivation through job enrichment (building in more responsibility, achievement, and growth), not through better pay. The trap: salary is a HYGIENE factor, not a motivator. This is the single most common Herzberg question. Also do not confuse job enrichment (adding motivators, vertical) with job

chunks.heading: McClelland's acquired-needs theory and nAch
chunks.text: McClelland's acquired-needs theory and nAch McClelland said motivation runs on three learned needs, present in different strengths in everyone, and measured projectively with the TAT (Thematic Apperception Test) . Need What the person wants nAch (achievement) To accomplish, master, meet a standard of excellence; driven by the success itself. nPow (power) To influence, control, have impact on others. nAff (affiliation) To be liked, belong, maintain warm relationships. The high nAch profile is the one they test: prefers tasks of moderate difficulty / calculated risk , wants personal responsibility for outcomes, and wants immediate, concrete feedback on performance. Driven by the achievement, not by the money or praise. McClelland linked high national nAch to economic development in The Achieving Society . The trap: high nAch prefers moderate risk, not high risk (too random, no credit for skill) and not low risk (no real achievement). Also: the need is measured by the TAT , a projective test. And the best managers tend to be high in socialised nPow , not necessarily highest in nAch.

chunks.heading: 3. The Johari window
chunks.text: 3. The Johari window A model of self-awareness and interpersonal disclosure by Joseph Luft and Harrington Ingham ("Joe" + "Hari" = Johari). A 2 × 2 grid: what is known/unknown to self crossed with what is known/unknown to others . Known to self Unknown to self Known to others Open / Arena : shared, public self. Blind spot : others see it, you don't. Unknown to others Hidden / Façade : you know it, you conceal it. Unknown : neither you nor others know (latent). How the quadrants move: feedback from others shrinks the Blind area; self-disclosure shrinks the Hidden area. Both enlarge the Open quadrant, which is the goal of healthy communication and good teamwork. The trap: do not flip Blind and Hidden. Blind = others know, you don't (reduced by feedback). Hidden/Façade = you know, others don't (reduced by self-disclosure). The "Unknown" quadrant is known to neither.

chunks.heading: 4. Attachment: Bowlby, Ainsworth, and the four styles
chunks.text: 4. Attachment: Bowlby, Ainsworth, and the four styles

chunks.heading: Bowlby: the theory
chunks.text: Bowlby: the theory John Bowlby is the father of attachment theory. Drawing on ethology and evolution , he argued attachment is an innate survival system : infants are biologically driven to keep proximity to a caregiver because it protects them. Key Bowlby concepts: Concept Meaning Monotropy One primary attachment figure sits at the top of a hierarchy of figures. Internal working model A mental template of relationships, built from early care, that shapes later relationships. Critical / sensitive period Roughly 6 months to ~2.5 years for forming the primary bond. Maternal deprivation Prolonged disruption of the bond can cause lasting harm (his "44 thieves" study linked it to affectionless psychopathy). Separation response Three stages on separation: protest → despair → detachment . The trap: Bowlby = the theory; Ainsworth = the measurement (the Strange Situation). Do not credit the Strange Situation to Bowlby. Monotropy means one main figure, not "many equal figures."

chunks.heading: Ainsworth: the Strange Situation
chunks.text: Ainsworth: the Strange Situation Mary Ainsworth (Bowlby's collaborator) built the empirical test. The Strange Situation is a structured lab procedure for infants around 12 to 18 months , run as eight short episodes involving separations from and reunions with the caregiver, plus a stranger. It scores: use of the caregiver as a secure base for exploration, stranger anxiety , separation anxiety , and most importantly the infant's reunion behaviour . The classifier: it is the reunion behaviour (how the baby responds when the caregiver comes back) that mainly decides the attachment style, not the crying at separation.

chunks.heading: The four attachment styles
chunks.text: The four attachment styles Style Behaviour in the Strange Situation Caregiving linked to it Secure (Type B) ~60-65% Explores using caregiver as a base, distressed at separation, easily comforted at reunion. Sensitive, responsive. Insecure-Avoidant (Type A) ~20% Little distress at separation, avoids/ignores caregiver at reunion, treats stranger much the same. Unresponsive, rejecting. Insecure-Resistant / Ambivalent (Type C) ~10-15% Intense distress, clingy AND resistant at reunion: seeks contact then pushes it away, hard to soothe. Inconsistent. Disorganised (Type D) Confused, contradictory, freezing, fearful, no coherent strategy. Frightening / abusive (often added later by Main & Solomon). The trap: Type A = avoidant, Type C = resistant/ambivalent. The "ambivalent / clingy-but-rejecting" one is C, not A. Disorganised (Type D) was added by Main & Solomon , not part of Ainsworth's original three. And classification rests on reunion behaviour. NIMHANS depth: the adult parallels (Hazan & Shaver, and the secure / dismissing / preoccupied / fearful four-category adult model) extend the same logic to romantic relationships. Avoidant infants minimise attachment needs; resistant infants maximise them.

chunks.heading: 5. Proactive vs retroactive interference
chunks.text: 5. Proactive vs retroactive interference Interference theory says we forget not because the trace fades but because other learning gets in the way . The only thing to get right is the direction : which set of information is doing the interfering, old or new. Type Direction What you cannot recall Everyday example Proactive interference Old → new (forward). Previously learned material blocks new learning. You struggle to recall the NEW info. Your old phone number keeps coming out instead of the new one. Retroactive interference New → old (backward). Recently learned material blocks older memories. You struggle to recall the OLD info. A new password makes you forget the old one. The mnemonic that fixes it for good: PRO active = the PR ior (past) learning reaches forward. RETRO active = the recent learning reaches back ("retro" = backward). Or simply: P roactive = P ast interferes; R etroactive = R ecent interferes. The trap: the direction gets flipped under time pressure. Always ask two things: (1) which info is being recalled , and (2) which info is doing the interfering . In proactive you fail to recall the new (old intrudes); in retroactive you fail to recall the old (new intrudes).

chunks.heading: 6. Indian psychology: the cluster MET over-weights
chunks.text: 6. Indian psychology: the cluster MET over-weights MET leans on Indian psychology harder than NIMHANS does, often a whole cluster in one paper. Over-prepare this section, do not just touch it.

chunks.heading: Trigunas: the three gunas
chunks.text: Trigunas: the three gunas From Samkhya philosophy (and the Bhagavad Gita), the three fundamental qualities of prakriti (nature, and therefore of the mind and personality). Everyone has all three; your makeup is their proportion . Guna Quality Sattva Purity, clarity, harmony, knowledge, calm, balance, light. Rajas Activity, passion, restlessness, desire, drive, movement. Tamas Inertia, dullness, darkness, ignorance, lethargy. The trap: map each one exactly. Sattva = clarity/balance, Rajas = activity/passion, Tamas = inertia/ignorance. The yogic goal is to cultivate sattva and ultimately go beyond all three ( gunatita ).

chunks.heading: Pancha kosha: the five sheaths
chunks.text: Pancha kosha: the five sheaths From the Taittiriya Upanishad : five layers or "coverings" wrapped around the true Self (Atman), running from the grossest (outer, physical) to the subtlest (inner, bliss) . # Kosha Layer 1 Annamaya Food / physical body (outermost). 2 Pranamaya Vital energy, breath (prana). 3 Manomaya Mind, emotions (manas). 4 Vijnanamaya Intellect, wisdom, discernment (buddhi). 5 Anandamaya Bliss (innermost). The trap: do not confuse Anna maya (food/body, outermost) with Ananda maya (bliss, innermost). They sound alike and sit at opposite ends. Order is physical → bliss, gross → subtle.

chunks.heading: Purusha and Prakriti: the Samkhya dualism
chunks.text: Purusha and Prakriti: the Samkhya dualism Samkhya (attributed to the sage Kapila ) is a dualistic system built on two ultimate realities. Purusha Prakriti What it is Pure consciousness, the Self, the witness. Primordial matter/nature, the source of everything material and mental. Nature Passive, eternal, unchanging, plural, just observes. Active, unconscious, ever-changing; made of the three gunas. Contains Nothing; it is the silent observer. Even mind, intellect, and ego evolve out of Prakriti. Liberation (kaivalya) comes from viveka : discriminating Purusha (consciousness) from Prakriti (matter), realising the Self is the witness, not the changing mind. The trap: Purusha = consciousness (inactive witness); Prakriti = matter/nature (active, carries the gunas). The mind, intellect, and ego are part of Prakriti , not Purusha. And Samkhya is dualistic , in contrast to Advaita Vedanta's monism.

chunks.heading: The four avasthas: states of consciousness
chunks.text: The four avasthas: states of consciousness From the Mandukya Upanishad , the four states of the Self. # Avastha State 1 Jagrat Waking: outward awareness of gross objects. 2 Swapna (taijasa) Dream: inward awareness of subtle impressions. 3 Sushupti Deep dreamless sleep: no desires, undifferentiated, blissful. 4 Turiya The "fourth": pure transcendental consciousness, the witness underlying the other three. The trap: Turiya is the fourth, transcendent state, not deep sleep. Deep dreamless sleep is Sushupti . Keep the order jagrat → swapna → sushupti → turiya.

chunks.heading: Antahkarana: the "inner instrument"
chunks.text: Antahkarana: the "inner instrument" Antahkarana ("antah" = inner, "karana" = instrument) is the inner mental apparatus in Vedanta, classically fourfold. Faculty Function Manas Mind: takes in the senses, doubts, deliberates (the lower, indecisive mind). Buddhi Intellect: discriminates, decides, judges, the seat of wisdom. Ahamkara Ego, the "I-maker": the sense of a separate self/identity. Chitta Memory store: the reservoir of impressions (samskaras), "mind-stuff." The trap: Buddhi decides/discriminates; Manas doubts and handles the senses; Ahamkara is the ego/I-sense; Chitta is the memory storehouse. Note that in Patanjali's Yoga , "chitta" means the whole mind-field (as in yogah chitta-vritti-nirodhah , yoga is the stilling of the modifications of the mind), whereas Vedanta lists chitta as just one of the four.

chunks.heading: RCI: 1986 vs 1993
chunks.text: RCI: 1986 vs 1993 The Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) regulates the training and registration of rehabilitation professionals, including clinical and rehabilitation psychologists . The "1986 vs 1993" point is about its change in legal status. Year What happened 1986 RCI is first set up as a registered society (voluntary, non-statutory body). 1992 / 1993 The RCI Act, 1992 is passed by Parliament and comes into force on 1 July 1993 , making RCI a statutory regulatory body with legal teeth. 2000 Act amended to add promotion of research in rehabilitation and special education. So: 1986 = a society (no legal authority); 1992 Act / 1993 in force = a statutory council that maintains the Central Rehabilitation Register . Practising as a rehab professional without RCI registration is an offence. The trap: the Act is dated 1992 (passed) but came into force in 1993 , and the council itself predates the Act (1986, as a society) . Do not confuse RCI with the MCI/NMC (doctors), the RPwD Act 2016 , the older PWD Act 1995 , or the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 . RCI is specifically about training and registering rehabilitation personnel .

chunks.heading: Self-test: answer before opening
chunks.text: Self-test: answer before opening What does B = f(P,E) mean and whose is it? Lewin's field theory: behaviour is a function of the Person and the Environment together (the life space), driven by the present field of forces, not the past. To create change, is it better to add driving forces or reduce restraining forces? Reduce the restraining forces. Adding driving force raises tension and resistance. (Force field analysis.) Put Lewin's change stages in order and say what "refreeze" means. Unfreeze → change/move → refreeze. Refreeze = locking in the new state so it becomes permanent, not reverting. Which leadership style gives the best quality and morale, and which is least productive? Democratic gives best quality + morale (and continues without the leader). Laissez-faire is least productive. Is salary a motivator or a hygiene factor (Herzberg)? Hygiene factor. Its absence causes dissatisfaction; its presence does not motivate. Motivators are achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, growth. What level of risk does a high-nAch person prefer, and how is the need measured? Moderate / calculated risk (not high, not low). Measured by the TAT. McClelland's three needs: achievement, power, affiliation. In the Johari window, which quadrant is reduced by feedback, and which by self-disclosure? Feedback shrinks the Blind area (others know, you don't). Self-disclosure shri

chunks.heading: Counselling & Psychotherapy Theories — the full book, chapter by chapter (Sharf)
chunks.text: Counselling & Psychotherapy Theories — the full book, chapter by chapter (Sharf) Not a summary. This is Richard S. Sharf, Theories of Psychotherapy and Counseling: Concepts and Cases walked through in the book's own order, one chapter per theory, with the book's signature recurring frame kept intact for each: (1) background / originator · (2) theory of personality / view of human nature (how problems develop) · (3) goals of therapy · (4) techniques / how therapy is done · (5) the therapeutic relationship · (6) what it's used for / evidence · (7) criticisms . The "this-vs-that" distinctions MCQs live on are flagged in red trap boxes; where NIMHANS pushes past Sharf it's flagged in purple . Built 2026-05-29. Effects Phenomena Theories Theorists Social Psych Cognitive Personality Counselling (Sharf) Lookalikes How counselling theory is tested. (1) Name the theory from its claim ("we dispute irrational beliefs" = REBT). (2) Pin the theory to its founder (choice theory = Glasser). (3) Pin the named technique to its theory ("miracle question" = solution-focused / de Shazer; "empty chair" = Gestalt / Perls). (4) Tell rival theories apart, that's where the distractor lives: REBT vs Beck's CT, Wolpe's desensitisation vs flooding, Bowen vs Minuchin vs Haley. Learn each technique in its contrast pair , and learn each theory's place on the master axes below. The frame that organises the wh

chunks.heading: Ch 1. Theory, and the role of theory in counselling
chunks.text: Ch 1. Theory, and the role of theory in counselling Sharf opens by asking what a theory of psychotherapy is and why a counsellor needs one. A theory is a coherent set of assumptions that explains how problems arise and how change happens; without one, a counsellor is improvising. A theory gives the clinician three things: a map of personality (what a person is made of and how distress develops), a set of goals , and a set of techniques that follow logically from the goals. A good theory , Sharf says, is precise / clear , comprehensive (covers a wide range of behaviour), parsimonious (no needless complexity), useful / applicable (generates testable predictions and practical methods), and verifiable / testable by research. He also sets up the recurring chapter frame used throughout the book: history of the originator , theory of personality , theory of psychotherapy (goals, the therapeutic relationship, assessment, techniques), application to a brief case , treatment of specific disorders, brief / short-term versions, current trends , use with diverse populations and gender issues , group counselling applications, a summary , and research / critique . Brief history. Counselling grew from several roots: Freud's psychoanalysis (the depth tradition), the vocational-guidance movement (Frank Parsons, early 1900s), psychometrics and the testing movement, and later the humanistic reacti

chunks.heading: Ch 2. Psychoanalysis — Sigmund Freud
chunks.text: Ch 2. Psychoanalysis — Sigmund Freud Originator. Sigmund Freud (1856–1939), Viennese neurologist, founder of psychoanalysis. Working with hysteria (and Breuer's patient Anna O., source of the "talking cure"), he concluded symptoms have hidden mental causes in the unconscious. The first systematic theory of psychotherapy; the tradition every later theory reacts to. Theory of personality / how problems develop. Behaviour is driven by instincts (life/Eros with its energy libido , and death/Thanatos), and by an unconscious we cannot access directly. The mind has a topographic layout (conscious / preconscious / unconscious) and a structural one: the id (pleasure principle), ego (reality principle, mediator), and superego (internalised morality). Personality forms through five psychosexual stages (oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital); over- or under-gratification produces fixation . Problems arise from unconscious conflict and unresolved early-childhood experience; the ego manages anxiety with defence mechanisms (repression the master defence, plus projection, displacement, reaction formation, sublimation, denial, regression, rationalisation, etc., catalogued by Anna Freud). Goals of therapy. Make the unconscious conscious; bring repressed material into awareness so the ego can deal with it; strengthen the ego; resolve childhood conflicts that are re-enacted in the present. Insight

chunks.heading: Ch 3. Jungian analysis — analytical psychology
chunks.text: Ch 3. Jungian analysis — analytical psychology Originator. Carl Gustav Jung (1875–1961), Swiss psychiatrist, Freud's "crown prince" until their 1913 break over the sexual nature of libido. Founded analytical psychology . Theory of personality. Jung kept the unconscious but enlarged it and de-sexualised libido into general psychic energy. The psyche = ego (consciousness) + personal unconscious (your own forgotten/repressed material, organised into emotionally charged complexes ) + collective unconscious (an inherited layer shared by all humanity, containing the archetypes : persona , shadow , anima/animus , the self ). Jung coined introversion / extraversion and added four functions (thinking, feeling, sensing, intuiting) → psychological types . Problems often reflect a one-sided development and a failure of individuation , especially at midlife. Goals. Individuation : integrate the conscious and unconscious, the persona and shadow, into a balanced self . Restore the dialogue with the unconscious. Techniques. Dream analysis read in series, with amplification (linking dream symbols to myth and culture) rather than Freud's free association; active imagination (dialoguing with inner images); the word-association test (reveals complexes); analysis of symbol and myth. Therapy has four stages (confession, elucidation, education, transformation). Relationship. A collaborative, mutual e

chunks.heading: Ch 4. Adlerian therapy — individual psychology
chunks.text: Ch 4. Adlerian therapy — individual psychology Originator. Alfred Adler (1870–1937), Viennese, broke from Freud in 1911 over the sexual emphasis, founding individual psychology . A major forerunner of humanistic and cognitive therapy. Theory of personality. The one dynamic force is striving for superiority (really, striving for competence and completion). Everyone starts small and feels inferiority ; healthy growth means compensating for it, while derailment yields an inferiority complex or an over-compensating superiority complex . Each person builds a unique style of life by about age 5; we are pulled by future fictional goals ( fictional finalism ), we are not passive (the creative power of the self ), and the mark of mental health is social interest ( Gemeinschaftsgefühl ) — a feeling of kinship with humanity. Birth order shapes the style of life. Problems = a mistaken style of life and discouragement / low social interest. Goals. Foster social interest , correct the mistaken style of life and faulty basic mistakes , replace discouragement with encouragement , and move the client toward useful goals. Techniques. Lifestyle assessment , early recollections (the earliest memory reveals the style of life), birth-order analysis, exploring family constellation , encouragement , "the question" ("how would your life be different if you were well?"), acting as if , catching oneself

chunks.heading: Ch 5. Existential therapy — May, Yalom, Frankl
chunks.text: Ch 5. Existential therapy — May, Yalom, Frankl Originators. Not one founder but a movement: Rollo May (brought existentialism to US psychology), Irvin Yalom (the four ultimate concerns), and Viktor Frankl (logotherapy, forged in the concentration camps). Philosophical roots in Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Heidegger, Sartre, Binswanger, Boss. Theory of personality / human nature. There is no fixed human nature; we are free and responsible, and we create ourselves through choices (existence precedes essence). Distress comes not mainly from the past but from facing, or fleeing, the ultimate concerns / givens of existence . Yalom's four givens : death (and its anxiety), freedom (and the responsibility / groundlessness it brings), isolation (existential aloneness), and meaninglessness . Avoiding these through inauthenticity / "bad faith" produces existential anxiety and guilt. The three modes of being-in-the-world: Umwelt (physical), Mitwelt (social), Eigenwelt (self). Goals. Help the client live authentically , accept freedom and responsibility, confront the givens, and find or create meaning . Not symptom removal but a fuller, more honest way of living. Techniques. Existential therapy is deliberately light on technique; the relationship is the method. Frankl's logotherapy is the main exception, with named methods: paradoxical intention (deliberately wish for the feared thing, to break

chunks.heading: Ch 6. Person-centred therapy — Carl Rogers
chunks.text: Ch 6. Person-centred therapy — Carl Rogers Originator. Carl Rogers (1902–1987), American; created the humanistic "client-centred" (later "person-centred") approach and pioneered recorded-session psychotherapy research. Theory of personality / human nature. Deeply optimistic : every organism has an innate actualising tendency toward growth. The self develops from experience; trouble starts when the child, needing love, takes on conditions of worth ("I'm valued only if…") and so distorts or denies experience that doesn't fit the self-concept. The gap between the organism's experience and the self-concept is incongruence , the source of anxiety and maladjustment. Goals. Reduce incongruence; help the client drop conditions of worth, reconnect with their own organismic valuing, and move toward becoming a fully functioning person (open to experience, present-living, self-trusting, free, creative). Techniques / how therapy is done. Famously non-directive : no diagnosis, no advice, no technique in the usual sense. Change is produced by the relationship itself . Rogers specified six necessary and sufficient conditions for change; the three the therapist provides are the core triad : congruence / genuineness (the therapist is real, not a façade), unconditional positive regard (UPR, non-possessive warmth and acceptance), and empathic understanding (accurately sensing the client's inner wo

chunks.heading: Ch 7. Gestalt therapy — Fritz Perls
chunks.text: Ch 7. Gestalt therapy — Fritz Perls Originator. Fritz (Frederick) Perls (1893–1970), with Laura Perls and Paul Goodman. Roots in Gestalt perceptual psychology (figure/ground), psychoanalysis, and existentialism. Theory of personality / human nature. A person is a whole in constant contact with the environment, organising experience into figure (what's salient now) and ground . Health = staying aware in the here-and-now and completing the cycle of need → contact → satisfaction → withdrawal. Trouble = unfinished business (unexpressed feelings from the past intruding on the present) and breaks in awareness produced by contact-boundary disturbances : introjection (swallowing others' values whole), projection , retroflection (turning back on the self what you'd do to others), confluence (no boundary), and deflection . Perls described five layers of neurosis (phony, phobic, impasse, implosive, explosive). Goals. Restore awareness in the present; help the client re-own disowned parts and feelings; finish unfinished business; move from environmental support to self-support . Techniques / experiments. All aimed at present awareness: the empty-chair technique (dialogue with an absent person or a part of the self), the two-chair / top-dog vs under-dog dialogue (the "shoulds" tyrant vs the resisting victim within), staying with feeling, exaggeration, the " I take responsibility " exercise,

chunks.heading: Ch 8. Behaviour therapy
chunks.text: Ch 8. Behaviour therapy Originators. No single founder. Roots in classical conditioning ( Pavlov ; Watson & Rayner 's Little Albert), operant conditioning ( Skinner ), and the clinical pioneers Joseph Wolpe (systematic desensitisation), Hans Eysenck , and Arnold Lazarus (later, multimodal therapy). Theory of personality / how problems develop. No deep "personality" structure; behaviour (including symptoms) is learned and maintained by its antecedents and consequences. Problems are maladaptive learned responses : a phobia is a conditioned fear, a habit is a reinforced operant. Change the learning, change the behaviour. Strong focus on observable behaviour , the present, and measurement. Goals. Concrete, specific, measurable behavioural change agreed with the client; remove maladaptive behaviour and build adaptive behaviour. Techniques. Built on the conditioning principles: systematic desensitisation (Wolpe — pair a graded fear hierarchy with relaxation, using reciprocal inhibition , so relaxation displaces anxiety); exposure therapies including flooding (intense, prolonged exposure to the feared stimulus with no graded hierarchy and no relaxation, until anxiety extinguishes) and in-vivo / imaginal exposure; token economy (operant — earn tokens for target behaviour, exchange for reinforcers, classically on wards); aversion therapy (pair the unwanted behaviour with an unpleasant s

chunks.heading: Ch 9. Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy (REBT) — Albert Ellis
chunks.text: Ch 9. Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy (REBT) — Albert Ellis Originator. Albert Ellis (1913–2007), American; created REBT in the mid-1950s, the first of the cognitive-behavioural therapies (predates Beck). Theory of personality / how problems develop. It is not events that disturb us but our beliefs about them. Humans have an innate tendency to think both rationally and irrationally ; emotional disturbance comes from irrational beliefs — rigid, absolutist demands expressed as musts, shoulds, oughts ( musturbation ), and their derivatives: awfulising / catastrophising , low frustration tolerance ("I-can't-stand-it-itis") , and global self/other-rating / damnation . Goals. Identify and dispute irrational beliefs and replace them with rational, flexible preferences; reach a deep philosophical change and unconditional self-acceptance . The model — A-B-C-D-E. A = activating event; B = belief about it (rational or irrational); C = emotional/behavioural consequence. The insight: it's B , not A , that causes C . Therapy adds D = disputing the irrational belief (logical, empirical, pragmatic disputation), leading to E = a new effective philosophy / emotion. (Sometimes written A-B-C-D-E-F, F = new feeling.) Techniques. Active-directive disputing , cognitive (challenging beliefs, cost-benefit analysis), emotive (rational-emotive imagery, shame-attacking exercises , humour, forceful self-

chunks.heading: Ch 10. Cognitive therapy — Aaron Beck
chunks.text: Ch 10. Cognitive therapy — Aaron Beck Originator. Aaron T. Beck (1921–2021), American psychiatrist; developed cognitive therapy in the 1960s out of his research on depression . (Daughter Judith Beck carried it forward.) Theory of personality / how problems develop. Emotion and behaviour are shaped by how we interpret events. Early experience lays down schemas (core beliefs); these generate, in the moment, automatic thoughts (rapid, plausible-feeling appraisals just below awareness). When schemas are dysfunctional, perception is filtered through cognitive distortions — systematic errors such as all-or-nothing / dichotomous thinking , overgeneralisation , magnification / minimisation (catastrophising), selective abstraction / mental filter , arbitrary inference , personalisation , labelling , "should" statements , mind-reading / fortune-telling . Depression is marked by the cognitive triad : negative view of the self , the world , and the future . Goals. Identify, test and correct distorted thinking; change dysfunctional automatic thoughts and, deeper, the underlying schemas; teach the client to become their own therapist. Techniques — cognitive restructuring. Socratic questioning / guided discovery , identifying and testing automatic thoughts (thought records, the dysfunctional-thought log), collaborative empiricism (client + therapist treat beliefs as hypotheses and gather evid

chunks.heading: Ch 11. Reality therapy / Choice theory — William Glasser
chunks.text: Ch 11. Reality therapy / Choice theory — William Glasser Originator. William Glasser (1925–2013), American psychiatrist; developed reality therapy in the 1960s, later grounding it in choice theory (originally "control theory"). Theory of personality / how problems develop. Behaviour is our best attempt to meet five innate basic needs : survival , love/belonging , power/achievement , freedom , and fun . We act to close the gap between what we want (our "quality world") and what we perceive we're getting. Choice theory : we choose nearly all our behaviour, and we are responsible for it. Total behavior has four inseparable components — acting, thinking, feeling, physiology — and we have the most direct control over acting and thinking (Glasser often uses verbs: "depressing," "anxietying," to stress that even these are chosen). Problems = irresponsible choices and unsatisfying relationships, not "mental illness." Goals. Help the client make more effective, responsible choices to meet their needs and rebuild relationships; take ownership rather than blaming the past or others. Techniques — the WDEP system (Robert Wubbolding's formalisation): W = explore Wants (and needs / quality world); D = examine Doing / current behaviour and direction; E = Evaluation (the client self-evaluates: "is what you're doing getting you what you want?"); P = make a Plan (specific, achievable, committed-t

chunks.heading: Ch 12. Solution-Focused Brief Therapy & Narrative therapy
chunks.text: Ch 12. Solution-Focused Brief Therapy & Narrative therapy These constructivist / postmodern approaches share a premise: reality is socially constructed through language and story, so therapy works on meaning, not on a fixed underlying pathology. They are brief, collaborative, and resolutely non-pathologising ; the client is the expert on their own life.

chunks.heading: Solution-Focused Brief Therapy (SFBT)
chunks.text: Solution-Focused Brief Therapy (SFBT) Originators. Steve de Shazer and Insoo Kim Berg at the Brief Family Therapy Center, Milwaukee (building on the MRI brief-therapy tradition and Milton Erickson). Core idea. Don't analyse the problem, build the solution . Focus on what the client wants and on times the problem is already absent. The future is created and negotiable. Goals. Co-construct a clear, concrete preferred future and amplify what already works; small change leads to bigger change. Signature techniques. The miracle question ("Suppose tonight while you sleep a miracle happens and the problem is solved — what would you notice tomorrow that tells you?"), exception questions ("when is the problem not happening, or less?"), scaling questions ("on 0–10, where are you, and what would +1 look like?"), the formula first-session task , coping questions , and compliments . Rule of thumb: if it works do more of it; if it doesn't, do something different. Relationship. Collaborative, respectful, client-as-expert; therapist asks, doesn't prescribe. Used for / evidence. Brief, broad applicability; growing evidence; popular in schools and agencies. Criticisms. May be too quick, can gloss over real pathology and emotion, may not suit complex/chronic cases.

chunks.heading: Narrative therapy
chunks.text: Narrative therapy Originators. Michael White (Australia) and David Epston (New Zealand). Core idea. We live by stories we tell about ourselves; a problem-saturated "dominant story" can trap a person. The problem is the problem; the person is not the problem. Goals. Separate the person from the problem and help them re-author a richer, preferred story rooted in their own values and competence. Signature techniques. Externalising the problem (talk about "the Anger" or "the Depression" as a separate entity acting on the person, often by naming it), mapping the problem's influence , finding unique outcomes / sparkling moments (times the person resisted the problem), re-authoring the story around those exceptions, therapeutic documents / letters , and recruiting an audience / definitional ceremony ("outsider witnesses"). Relationship. Collaborative, curious, non-expert, de-centred-but-influential; the therapist is an investigative co-author. Used for / evidence. Family work, identity and trauma narratives, oppression-linked problems; evidence largely qualitative. Criticisms. Hard to evaluate empirically; intellectually demanding; can underweight biological/severe illness. Miracle question · exception · scaling questions = SFBT (de Shazer & Berg) . Externalising the problem · re-authoring · unique outcomes = Narrative (White & Epston) . Both are postmodern/constructivist and "client-

chunks.heading: Ch 13. Feminist therapy
chunks.text: Ch 13. Feminist therapy Originators. No single founder; a movement arising from the 1960s–70s women's movement (figures include Jean Baker Miller, Carolyn Enns, Laura Brown). Often integrated with other approaches. Theory of personality / how problems develop. Psychological distress cannot be separated from the social and political context , especially gender-role socialisation and the unequal distribution of power . Much "pathology" in women is a reasonable response to oppression, sexism and trauma. The guiding slogan: "the personal is political." Goals. Symptom relief plus broader change: raise awareness of how gender-role and power dynamics shaped the client's problems; foster empowerment, self-definition, and (often) social action; value the client's own experience. Techniques. Gender-role analysis (examine how gendered expectations affected the client) and gender-role intervention ; power analysis (examine power differences and how to gain personal power); assertiveness training ; reframing and relabelling (move blame from the individual to the social cause); bibliotherapy ; self-disclosure ; demystifying therapy. Relationship. Deliberately egalitarian — minimise the power differential, share information, treat the client as an equal collaborator. Used for / evidence. Trauma, abuse survivors, identity, gender and multicultural issues; emphasises social justice. Mostly prin

chunks.heading: Ch 14. Family systems therapies
chunks.text: Ch 14. Family systems therapies The unit of treatment shifts from the individual to the system . Drawing on general systems theory and cybernetics , these models hold that a symptom in one member (the " identified patient ") expresses a dysfunction in the whole family's patterns; you change the person by changing the system. Key shared concepts: homeostasis (the system resists change), circular causality (not A→B but a mutual loop), feedback loops , boundaries , and subsystems . Sharf covers four major schools.

chunks.heading: Bowen — multigenerational / transgenerational family therapy
chunks.text: Bowen — multigenerational / transgenerational family therapy Originator. Murray Bowen . Core constructs: differentiation of self (the capacity to separate intellect from emotion and self from family fusion — the central goal), triangulation (a two-person tension pulls in a third to stabilise), the nuclear family emotional system , the family projection process , the multigenerational transmission process , emotional cutoff , and sibling position . Signature tool: the genogram (a multigenerational family map/diagram). Goal: raise differentiation and detriangulate; the therapist stays calm and de-triangled (a non-anxious presence). Insight-leaning, slower, multigenerational.

chunks.heading: Structural family therapy
chunks.text: Structural family therapy Originator. Salvador Minuchin . Focus on the family's structure : its boundaries (which range from rigid → disengaged families, to diffuse → enmeshed families, with clear boundaries in between), its subsystems (spousal, parental, sibling), hierarchy , alignments and coalitions. Pathology = a faulty structure. Techniques: joining and accommodating, mapping the structure, enactment (have the family play out the problem interaction in session so the therapist can see and reshape it), boundary-making , unbalancing , and reframing . Active, present-focused; the therapist restructures the system.

chunks.heading: Strategic family therapy
chunks.text: Strategic family therapy Originators. Jay Haley and Cloé Madanes; the MRI group (Watzlawick, Weakland) and the influence of Milton Erickson ; the Milan group nearby. Focus on solving the presenting problem via planned interventions; the therapist takes responsibility for designing a strategy. Symptoms serve a function and are maintained by the family's attempted "solutions." Techniques: directives (tasks assigned between sessions), paradoxical interventions (e.g. prescribing the symptom — instructing the family to keep doing it, so it loses its grip), reframing , ordeals , pretend techniques. Brief, directive, problem-focused; little emphasis on insight.

chunks.heading: Satir — experiential / communications (human validation)
chunks.text: Satir — experiential / communications (human validation) Originator. Virginia Satir . Warm, growth- and communication -focused; emphasises self-esteem, congruent communication and emotional experience. Her famous communication / coping stances under stress: placater, blamer, super-reasonable (computer), irrelevant (distractor) , and the healthy congruent / leveller . Techniques: family sculpting , family reconstruction , role play, touch and warmth, modelling congruent communication. Goals: raise self-esteem and honest, congruent communication. Family-theorist swaps (a top NIMHANS trap): Bowen = differentiation, triangulation, genogram , multigenerational (insight). Minuchin = structural : boundaries (enmeshed vs disengaged), subsystems, enactment , joining. Haley = strategic : directives, paradox / prescribing the symptom, problem-focused. Satir = experiential/communication: the four stress stances + congruent leveller, family sculpting. "Genogram" → Bowen; "enactment / boundaries" → Minuchin; "directive / paradox" → Haley; "sculpting / placater-blamer" → Satir. Recap Ch 14. Family systems: treat the system, not the person (identified patient, homeostasis, circular causality, boundaries). Bowen = differentiation + genogram; Minuchin = structure/boundaries + enactment; Haley = strategic directives + paradox; Satir = communication stances + sculpting.

chunks.heading: Ch 15. Transactional Analysis & a note on integrative / eclectic approaches
chunks.text: Ch 15. Transactional Analysis & a note on integrative / eclectic approaches

chunks.heading: Transactional Analysis (TA)
chunks.text: Transactional Analysis (TA) Originator. Eric Berne (1910–1970); popularised in Games People Play . Theory of personality. Personality has three ego states : Parent (taught, the internalised authority — nurturing or critical), Adult (the rational, here-and-now data processor), and Child (felt, the spontaneous or adapted child). Transactions between people occur between ego states and can be complementary (smooth), crossed (conflict), or ulterior (hidden agenda). Early decisions form a life script ; we exchange strokes (units of recognition); and we play repetitive games (e.g. "Why Don't You — Yes But") that pay off in bad feelings. A person's basic life position is one of four: I'm OK–You're OK (healthy), I'm OK–You're not OK, I'm not OK–You're OK, I'm not OK–You're not OK. Goals & techniques. Reach autonomy via awareness, spontaneity, intimacy; strengthen the Adult ; rewrite the script. Techniques: structural analysis (of ego states), transactional analysis proper (of exchanges), game analysis , script analysis ; usually contract-based and often done in groups. Criticisms. Jargon-heavy, popularised; uneven evidence.

chunks.heading: Integrative / eclectic approaches
chunks.text: Integrative / eclectic approaches Most practising counsellors are not "pure" anything. Sharf distinguishes routes to combining theories: technical eclecticism (pick whatever techniques work, regardless of theory — e.g. Lazarus's multimodal therapy , the BASIC ID), theoretical integration (blend two or more theories into a new whole — e.g. Wachtel's cyclical psychodynamics), the common-factors route (use what all therapies share — see NIMHANS box), and assimilative integration (work from one home theory while importing techniques). The aim is to fit the therapy to the client, not the client to one theory. Ego states (Parent–Adult–Child) · games · scripts · strokes · life positions = TA / Berne . Multimodal therapy / BASIC ID / technical eclecticism = Arnold Lazarus. Recap Ch 15. Berne/TA: Parent-Adult-Child ego states; complementary/crossed/ulterior transactions; games, scripts, strokes; "I'm OK–You're OK." Integration: technical eclecticism (Lazarus, BASIC ID) vs theoretical integration vs common factors vs assimilative.

chunks.heading: Ch 16. Comparison & integration — how the theories line up
chunks.text: Ch 16. Comparison & integration — how the theories line up Sharf closes by lining the theories up on the recurring axes. Reading these axes off, you can place any theory and predict its "which approach" answer. View of human nature. Determined / pessimistic at one end (psychoanalysis), free / optimistic / growth-oriented at the other (person-centred, existential, Adlerian, humanistic). Behavioural = neutral (a product of learning, neither good nor bad). Role of the past. Past-focused: psychoanalysis, Jungian, (Adlerian uses early recollections but aims forward). Present/future-focused: behavioural, cognitive, REBT, reality, Gestalt (radically here-and-now), solution-focused, narrative. Directiveness. Highly directive: behaviour therapy, REBT, reality therapy, strategic family. Non-directive: person-centred (the extreme). In between / collaborative: Beck's CT, Adlerian, solution-focused. The relationship. The cure itself: person-centred (necessary and sufficient). A collaboration: cognitive, Adlerian, the postmodern therapies. The site of the work via transference: psychoanalysis. A means to an end / working alliance: behaviour therapy, REBT. Insight vs action. Insight-based: psychoanalysis, Jungian. Action/doing-based: behavioural, reality, solution-focused, strategic. Cognitive-and-both: REBT and Beck (insight into thinking, then behavioural action). NIMHANS — the four big "fo

chunks.heading: All the MCQ traps, collected
chunks.text: All the MCQ traps, collected REBT (Ellis) vs Cognitive Therapy (Beck): Ellis = A-B-C(DE) , irrational beliefs / musturbation , disputing , directive & confrontational. Beck = automatic thoughts / cognitive distortions / schemas , collaborative empiricism , Socratic, the client tests the thought as a hypothesis. REBT predates Beck. Cognitive triad (negative self / world / future) = Beck (depression), NOT Ellis. Systematic desensitisation (Wolpe) = graded hierarchy + relaxation (reciprocal inhibition). Flooding = intense, no hierarchy, no relaxation, extinguish anxiety. Both are exposure; opposite intensities. Token economy = operant / Skinnerian. Modeling / observational learning = Bandura. Aversion therapy = pair behaviour with an unpleasant stimulus. Person-centred core triad (congruence/genuineness, unconditional positive regard, empathy) = Rogers . "Six necessary and sufficient conditions," "fully functioning person," "actualising tendency" = Rogers. Empty chair · top-dog vs under-dog · here-and-now awareness · unfinished business = Gestalt / Perls . Miracle question · exception · scaling questions = SFBT / de Shazer & Berg . (Most-tested: miracle question is de Shazer, not Gestalt.) Externalising the problem · re-authoring · unique outcomes = Narrative / White & Epston . Logotherapy · will to meaning · existential vacuum · paradoxical intention · dereflection = Frankl . The

chunks.heading: Beyond Sharf — what NIMHANS adds
chunks.text: Beyond Sharf — what NIMHANS adds Common factors & the Dodo-bird verdict (Wampold). Across the bona-fide therapies, much of the outcome is explained by common factors shared by all (the therapeutic alliance , empathy, expectancy/hope, a believable rationale + ritual, goal consensus) rather than the specific techniques. The " Dodo-bird verdict " (from Rosenzweig, championed by Luborsky and Bruce Wampold 's contextual model): "everyone has won and all must have prizes," i.e. all therapies achieve broadly comparable outcomes. The working/therapeutic alliance (Bordin: bond + goals + tasks) is the most robust predictor of outcome. Stages of change — the Transtheoretical Model (Prochaska & DiClemente). Change moves through stages: precontemplation → contemplation → preparation → action → maintenance (with relapse possible). Match the intervention to the stage; "the client isn't resistant, they're precontemplative." Motivational Interviewing (Miller & Rollnick). A client-centred but directive method to resolve ambivalence and elicit change talk . Spirit = partnership, acceptance, compassion, evocation (PACE); core skills = OARS (Open questions, Affirmations, Reflective listening, Summaries); " roll with resistance ," develop discrepancy, support self-efficacy. Pairs naturally with the stages of change. Multicultural counselling competencies (Sue & Sue). The "fourth force." A competent

chunks.text: Fast glossary (one line each, A–Z) Last-mile recall: every nameable term on this page reduced to a single line and its theory/founder, alphabetical so you can self-test by covering the right column. Term One-line definition (and who) A-B-C-D-E Activating event → Belief → Consequence → Dispute → Effective new philosophy (Ellis, REBT). Actualising tendency Innate drive of the organism to grow and enhance itself (Rogers). Active imagination Dialoguing with inner images/symbols (Jung). Archetypes Universal inherited images in the collective unconscious (Jung). Automatic thoughts Rapid, plausible negative appraisals just below awareness (Beck). BASIC ID Multimodal assessment grid: Behaviour, Affect, Sensation, Imagery, Cognition, Interpersonal, Drugs/biology (Lazarus). Boundaries (family) Rules of contact between subsystems; rigid→disengaged, diffuse→enmeshed (Minuchin). Choice theory We choose nearly all our behaviour to meet five needs (Glasser). Cognitive distortions Systematic thinking errors (all-or-nothing, overgeneralisation, catastrophising…) (Beck). Cognitive triad Negative view of self, world, future, in depression (Beck). Collaborative empiricism Client + therapist test beliefs as hypotheses with evidence (Beck). Collective unconscious Inherited layer shared by all humanity; holds archetypes (Jung). Common factors / Dodo-bird Shared ingredients (alliance, hope) drive outc

chunks.heading: Self-test (active recall, by theory)
chunks.text: Self-test (active recall, by theory) Cover the answers, ask each aloud, then check. Miss one → jump back to its chapter. Answers follow in green .

chunks.heading: Psychoanalysis, Jung, Adler
chunks.text: Psychoanalysis, Jung, Adler The defining technique and the defining relationship mechanism of psychoanalysis? Free association; the transference. Collective unconscious + individuation + amplification belong to whom? Jung (NOT Freud, who has only the personal unconscious + free association). Adler's mark of mental health, and his two assessment tools? Social interest (Gemeinschaftsgefühl); early recollections and birth order. Match the three "wills": pleasure, power, meaning. Freud (pleasure), Adler (power), Frankl (meaning).

chunks.heading: Existential & person-centred
chunks.text: Existential & person-centred Yalom's four givens? Death, freedom, isolation, meaninglessness. Name the two logotherapy techniques and their author. Paradoxical intention and dereflection (Frankl). Rogers' core triad, and how many conditions in total? Congruence/genuineness, unconditional positive regard, empathy; six necessary-and-sufficient conditions (therapist supplies three). What does the client take on that produces incongruence? Conditions of worth (Rogers).

chunks.heading: Gestalt, behaviour, REBT, cognitive
chunks.text: Gestalt, behaviour, REBT, cognitive Empty chair and top-dog/under-dog belong to whom? Perls / Gestalt. Systematic desensitisation vs flooding — the two differences? Desensitisation = graded hierarchy + relaxation (Wolpe); flooding = intense, no hierarchy, no relaxation. Spell out Ellis's model and what truly causes C. A-B-C-D-E; it's B (the belief), not A (the event), that causes C. Beck's hallmark relationship stance and his depression triad? Collaborative empiricism; the cognitive triad (negative self, world, future). One line: REBT vs Beck. Ellis disputes irrational beliefs (directive); Beck tests automatic thoughts as hypotheses (collaborative/Socratic).

chunks.heading: Reality, constructivist, feminist
chunks.text: Reality, constructivist, feminist Expand WDEP and name its author(s). Wants, Doing, Evaluation, Plan (Glasser; formalised by Wubbolding). Glasser's five needs? Survival, love/belonging, power, freedom, fun. Miracle question vs externalising — which theory and founder each? Miracle question = SFBT (de Shazer & Berg); externalising = narrative (White & Epston). The feminist slogan and signature relationship stance? "The personal is political"; an egalitarian relationship.

chunks.heading: Family systems & TA
chunks.text: Family systems & TA Genogram and differentiation = whose model? Bowen (multigenerational). Enactment and enmeshed/disengaged boundaries = whose? Minuchin (structural). Prescribing the symptom / directives = whose? Haley (strategic). The four Satir stress stances plus the healthy one? Placater, blamer, super-reasonable (computer), irrelevant (distractor); healthy = congruent/leveller. Berne's three ego states and the healthy life position? Parent, Adult, Child; "I'm OK–You're OK."

chunks.heading: NIMHANS extensions
chunks.text: NIMHANS extensions What does the Dodo-bird verdict claim, and who champions the contextual/common-factors model? All bona-fide therapies achieve roughly equal outcomes; Wampold (alliance is the top predictor). List the stages of change and their authors. Precontemplation→contemplation→preparation→action→maintenance (Prochaska & DiClemente). Spell OARS and name MI's authors. Open questions, Affirmations, Reflective listening, Summaries (Miller & Rollnick). Sue & Sue's three multicultural competencies? Awareness (of own bias), Knowledge (of the client's culture), Skills. That's the whole Sharf book on one page, chapter by chapter. Read it once top to bottom, then revise off the coloured boxes: cover the founder column → name the theory; cover the technique → name who; and for every trap box, learn both sides of the pair. chunks.text: Cranial Nerves I–XII What this is. The full I–XII table (name, type, function, common deficits) plus both mnemonics and the MCQ traps that hit every MET/NIMHANS paper. Spun out of the biopsych brain-anatomy note because you flagged it in Mock 1 and it deserves its own page. If you only memorise one biopsych side-page, make it this one. Full I–XII table Mnemonics Sensory vs motor vs both Parasympathetic carriers Brainstem nuclei map High-yield deficits MCQ traps Bedside testing

chunks.heading: Full I–XII table
chunks.text: Full I–XII table # Name Type Function Common deficit / MCQ hook I Olfactory Sensory Smell Only nerve that bypasses thalamus. Anosmia is first lost in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's. Trauma to cribriform plate shears it off. II Optic Sensory Vision CNS tract, not a true peripheral nerve (myelinated by oligodendrocytes, surrounded by meninges). Lesion at optic chiasm = bitemporal hemianopia (pituitary adenoma). III Oculomotor Motor (+parasym) Most extraocular muscles (SR, IR, MR, IO) + levator palpebrae + parasympathetic pupil constriction (Edinger-Westphal nucleus) + lens accommodation. Full palsy = ptosis + "down & out" eye + fixed dilated pupil. Uncal herniation compresses III early (blown pupil). IV Trochlear Motor Superior oblique (depresses + intorts adducted eye). Smallest CN. Only CN that decussates before exit AND only one to exit dorsally from brainstem. Vertical diplopia worse going down stairs; patient tilts head away from lesion. V Trigeminal Both Sensation of face (V1 ophthalmic, V2 maxillary, V3 mandibular) + cornea + ant ⅔ scalp + dura. Motor: muscles of mastication. Trigeminal neuralgia (tic douloureux) — V2/V3 most common. Corneal reflex afferent. Jaw deviates toward weak side on opening. VI Abducens Motor Lateral rectus (abduction). Longest intracranial course → first CN affected by raised ICP. False localising sign. Lesion = inability to abduct, horizontal diplop

chunks.heading: Mnemonics
chunks.text: Mnemonics Name mnemonic (the classic): " On Old Olympus' Towering Tops, A Finn And German Viewed Some Hops " → O lfactory, O ptic, O culomotor, T rochlear, T rigeminal, A bducens, F acial, A uditory (vestibulocochlear), G lossopharyngeal, V agus, S pinal accessory, H ypoglossal. Type mnemonic (Sensory / Motor / Both): " Some Say Marry Money, But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter More " → S, S, M, M, B, M, B, S, B, B, M, M (I–XII). Brainstem exit level: Midbrain: III, IV. Pons: V, VI, VII, VIII. Medulla: IX, X, XI, XII. (I + II are forebrain; everything else exits brainstem top-to-bottom in number order.)

chunks.heading: Sensory vs motor vs both
chunks.text: Sensory vs motor vs both Class CNs Memory hook Purely sensory I, II, VIII "1, 2, 8" — the special senses (smell, sight, hearing/balance). Purely motor III, IV, VI, XI, XII Five of them. Eye movement trio (III/IV/VI) + neck/tongue duo (XI/XII). Mixed (both) V, VII, IX, X The four "B"s in the mnemonic.

chunks.heading: Parasympathetic carriers
chunks.text: Parasympathetic carriers Only four CNs carry parasympathetic fibres. Memorise the four targets: CN Parasympathetic target Nucleus (preganglionic) Ganglion (postganglionic) III Pupil constriction + lens accommodation Edinger-Westphal Ciliary VII Lacrimal, submandibular, sublingual glands Superior salivatory Pterygopalatine + submandibular IX Parotid gland Inferior salivatory Otic X Heart, lungs, GI tract to splenic flexure Dorsal motor nucleus of X + nucleus ambiguus Intrinsic ganglia in target organs

chunks.heading: Brainstem nuclei map
chunks.text: Brainstem nuclei map Level CN nuclei present Midbrain III (oculomotor + Edinger-Westphal), IV (trochlear) Pons V (trigeminal motor + main sensory + spinal trigeminal — spinal V extends down to upper cord), VI (abducens), VII (facial motor + superior salivatory + solitary, taste), VIII (vestibular + cochlear) Medulla IX (nucleus ambiguus motor + inferior salivatory + solitary, taste/visceral), X (dorsal motor + ambiguus + solitary), XI (nucleus ambiguus + spinal accessory nucleus C1–C5), XII (hypoglossal) Sensory nuclei sit lateral, motor nuclei sit medial. Solitary nucleus (taste + visceral afferent) gets VII, IX, X.

chunks.heading: High-yield deficits to memorise
chunks.text: High-yield deficits to memorise CN III palsy — ptosis + "down and out" eye + fixed dilated pupil. Compressive cause (PCom aneurysm, uncal herniation) hits parasympathetic fibres first → pupil involved. Ischaemic cause (diabetes) often pupil-sparing. CN IV palsy — vertical diplopia, worse looking down (reading, stairs). Compensatory head tilt away from lesion (Bielschowsky sign). CN VI palsy — inability to abduct, horizontal diplopia worse on gaze to lesion side. First CN to fail in raised ICP — false localising sign. Bell's palsy (CN VII, LMN) — whole half-face including forehead, taste loss anterior ⅔ tongue, hyperacusis, dry eye. UMN (stroke) spares forehead because upper face has bilateral cortical input. Acoustic neuroma (CN VIII) — unilateral sensorineural hearing loss + tinnitus + vertigo. At cerebellopontine angle so later involves V and VII as it grows. Bulbar palsy — LMN lesion of IX, X, XI, XII (and sometimes V, VII). Flaccid, fasciculating tongue, nasal speech, dysphagia. Cause: MND (PMA variant), Guillain-Barré, brainstem stroke. Pseudobulbar palsy — UMN lesion of same CNs. Spastic tongue (can't protrude), brisk jaw jerk, emotional lability, "Donald Duck" speech. Cause: bilateral strokes, MS, MND (UMN variant). CN XII lesion — tongue deviates TOWARD lesion (LMN) — "the lick goes to the sick." UMN lesion deviates AWAY. CN X / vagus lesion — uvula deviates AWAY from l

chunks.heading: High-yield MCQ traps
chunks.text: High-yield MCQ traps "Which CN bypasses the thalamus?" — Olfactory (I). Every other sensory modality relays through thalamus. "Which CN exits dorsally from the brainstem?" — Trochlear (IV). Also the only one to decussate before exit. "First CN affected in raised ICP?" — Abducens (VI), longest intracranial course. "Which CN is most often a false localising sign?" — VI (raised ICP) and III (uncal herniation). "Bell's palsy spares the forehead?" — NO. Bell's is LMN, whole half-face. Forehead-sparing = UMN = stroke. "Tongue deviates which way in CN XII lesion?" — TOWARD the lesion (LMN). The weak side can't push the tongue out so the strong side pushes it across. "Uvula deviates which way in CN X lesion?" — AWAY from lesion. Opposite of tongue. Same logic: strong side pulls uvula across. "Gag reflex — afferent vs efferent?" — Afferent IX, efferent X. (Both, but knowing which limb is which is the trap.) "Smallest CN?" — Trochlear (IV). "Largest CN?" — Trigeminal (V). "CN with longest intracranial course?" — Abducens (VI). "Which CN carries taste from anterior ⅔ tongue?" — Facial (VII) via chorda tympani. Posterior ⅓ = IX. Epiglottis = X. "Acoustic neuroma associated with?" — NF2 (bilateral), CPA lesion, CN V/VII signs as it expands. "Argyll Robertson pupil" — accommodates but does NOT react to light. Neurosyphilis classic. "Prostitute's pupil — accommodates but doesn't react." "Marc

chunks.heading: Bedside testing (NIMHANS clinical viva)
chunks.text: Bedside testing (NIMHANS clinical viva) CN How to test I Smell coffee/cloves each nostril separately. (Often skipped in routine exam.) II Snellen chart, fields by confrontation, fundoscopy, pupillary light reflex (afferent), colour vision (Ishihara). III, IV, VI "H-pattern" eye movements, pupils (light + accommodation), look for ptosis, diplopia. V Light touch + pinprick V1/V2/V3 each side. Corneal reflex (afferent V, efferent VII). Clench teeth (masseter bulk). Jaw jerk. VII Raise eyebrows, screw eyes shut tight, show teeth, puff cheeks. Watch for forehead sparing. VIII Whisper test or finger-rub each ear. Rinne (tuning fork mastoid vs air) + Weber (forehead, lateralises to affected ear in conductive loss, away in sensorineural). IX, X Say "ahh" — uvula should rise midline. Gag reflex (touch posterior pharynx). Voice quality (hoarse = X). XI Shrug shoulders against resistance (trapezius). Turn head against resistance (SCM — turns to opposite side). XII Protrude tongue — note deviation, fasciculations, atrophy. Push against cheek from inside. One-line revision trick. The eye-movement trio (III, IV, VI) is tested together as an H-pattern, the lower-CN bulbar group (IX, X, XII) is tested together with "ahh" + tongue + voice, and VII gets its own block (eyebrows + eyes shut + teeth + cheeks). If you can run those three sub-exams from memory, you've covered 8 of the 12 CNs. Source:
