chunks.heading: General Psychology — detailed notes
chunks.text: General Psychology — detailed notes Perception · attention · memory · learning · emotion · motivation · intelligence · cognition · landmark experiments · Built 2026-05-22 What this is. The detailed standalone general-psychology notes you asked for, one section per area, each with the named theories, the people behind them, and the traps. This is the depth; the Rapid Recall block is the one-line version for the cab. Use this to read, that one to test yourself. Jump to: 1. Perception 2. Attention 3. Memory 4. Learning 5. Emotion 6. Motivation 7. Intelligence 8. Cognition 9. Landmark experiments 10. Personality 11. Social psychology 12. Developmental 13. Consciousness & sleep 14. Stress & coping 15. Schools & history

chunks.heading: 1. Perception & Sensation
chunks.text: 1. Perception & Sensation Sensation is detecting raw stimulus energy at the receptors; perception is the brain organising and interpreting it. Transduction is the conversion of stimulus energy into neural signals.

chunks.heading: Psychophysics (thresholds)
chunks.text: Psychophysics (thresholds) Concept Meaning Absolute threshold Smallest intensity detectable 50 percent of the time Difference threshold (JND) Smallest change between two stimuli that is detectable 50 percent of the time Weber's law The JND is a constant proportion of the stimulus, not a fixed amount Fechner's law Sensation grows with the logarithm of stimulus intensity Stevens' power law Sensation is a power function of intensity (often fits better than Fechner) Subliminal / priming Stimuli below the absolute threshold can still prime responses

chunks.heading: Signal detection theory
chunks.text: Signal detection theory Detection is a decision under uncertainty, not a fixed threshold. Four outcomes: hit , miss , false alarm , correct rejection . d-prime (d') measures true sensitivity; beta is the response criterion (how willing you are to say "yes"). Motivation and expectation shift beta, not sensitivity.

chunks.heading: Theories of perception
chunks.text: Theories of perception The two camps: Gibson's direct / bottom-up theory (the stimulus itself carries enough information, perception is data-driven) versus Gregory's constructivist / top-down theory (perception is an active hypothesis built from prior knowledge and inference). Most modern views combine both.

chunks.heading: Gestalt laws of organisation
chunks.text: Gestalt laws of organisation "The whole is greater than the sum of its parts." Proximity, similarity, closure, continuity (good continuation), common fate, figure-ground, pragnanz (simplicity). Founders: Wertheimer, Koffka, Kohler.

chunks.heading: Depth & constancy
chunks.text: Depth & constancy Binocular cues: retinal disparity, convergence. Monocular cues: relative size, interposition, linear perspective, texture gradient, motion parallax, aerial perspective. Perceptual constancies: size, shape, colour, brightness, the object looks stable despite changing retinal image. Feature integration theory (Treisman): a preattentive stage detects individual features in parallel, then focused attention binds them into a whole object. Failure of binding produces illusory conjunctions.

chunks.heading: Pattern recognition & perceptual set
chunks.text: Pattern recognition & perceptual set Template, prototype, and feature-detection theories of how we recognise patterns; Biederman's recognition-by-components (geons) builds objects from basic 3D primitives. Perceptual set / expectancy: context, motivation, culture, and prior knowledge bias what we perceive (top-down). Illusions: Müller-Lyer, Ponzo, Ames room, moon illusion, the Kanizsa triangle (illusory contours), the McGurk effect (vision alters what we hear). Illusions reveal the brain's interpretive shortcuts.

chunks.heading: 2. Attention
chunks.text: 2. Attention Attention is the selective allocation of limited processing capacity. The big debate: where in the stream does selection happen (early vs late), and how much capacity is there (bottleneck vs flexible resources).

chunks.heading: Bottleneck / filter models (where does selection happen?)
chunks.text: Bottleneck / filter models (where does selection happen?) Model Claim Broadbent (1958, early selection) A single filter blocks unattended input early , based on physical features (pitch, location), before meaning is processed. Based on Cherry's dichotic-listening / shadowing work. Treisman (1964, attenuation) The filter attenuates (turns down) unattended input rather than fully blocking it; high-priority words with low thresholds (your name, "fire") still break through. Deutsch & Deutsch / Norman (late selection) All input is fully processed for meaning; selection happens late , at the response/awareness stage, not at perception. Johnston & Heinz (multimode) Selection is flexible: it can occur early or late depending on task demands, but later selection costs more capacity.

chunks.heading: Capacity / resource models (how much is there?)
chunks.text: Capacity / resource models (how much is there?) Model Claim Kahneman (1973, single capacity) Attention is one limited pool of effort/resources allocated across tasks; arousal changes the size of the pool; an allocation policy decides where it goes. Wickens (multiple resources) There are several separate resource pools (e.g. visual vs auditory, verbal vs spatial). Two tasks interfere most when they draw on the same pool, which is why you can drive and listen but not read and listen. Norman & Bobrow Data-limited (limited by poor stimulus quality) vs resource-limited (limited by available attention) performance. Lavie (perceptual load theory) Under high perceptual load selection is early (no spare capacity, distractors filtered out); under low load spare capacity spills onto distractors, so selection is late. Reconciles the early/late debate.

chunks.heading: Spatial / visual attention
chunks.text: Spatial / visual attention Spotlight model (Posner): attention is a movable "spotlight" that enhances processing wherever it points. Zoom-lens (Eriksen): the spotlight can widen or narrow, trading area for resolution. Posner cueing paradigm: a valid cue speeds detection, an invalid one slows it. Endogenous (voluntary, goal-driven, central cue) vs exogenous (reflexive, stimulus-driven, peripheral cue) orienting. Phases of orienting: disengage → move → engage. Feature Integration Theory (Treisman): a preattentive stage registers features (colour, orientation) in parallel across the field; focused attention then binds them into objects. Feature search ("pop-out") is parallel and fast; conjunction search is serial. Failed binding = illusory conjunctions . Guided search (Wolfe): a refinement of FIT, top-down knowledge guides attention toward likely targets.

chunks.heading: Types & control
chunks.text: Types & control Selective (focus on one source), divided (split across tasks), sustained (vigilance over time), alternating/switching (toggle between tasks, with a switch cost). Automatic vs controlled (Schneider & Shiffrin): automatic is fast, parallel, effortless, hard to suppress (Stroop interference happens because reading is automatic); controlled is slow, serial, effortful, flexible. Practice automatises a skill. Supervisory Attentional System (Norman & Shallice): routine action runs on automatic "schemas" via contention scheduling; the SAS (frontal) intervenes only for novel or risky situations. Failures → action slips / capture errors.

chunks.heading: Key phenomena
chunks.text: Key phenomena Cocktail-party effect (Cherry): you can follow one voice in a crowd yet still detect your own name in an ignored stream. Stroop effect: naming the ink colour of a colour-word is slowed because reading is automatic. Classic interference / automaticity demo. Inattentional blindness (Simons & Chabris invisible-gorilla) and change blindness : without attention, even large changes go unnoticed, so attention is needed for conscious perception. Attentional blink: in rapid serial visual presentation, a second target is missed if it appears ~200-500 ms after the first, attention is briefly "used up". Vigilance decrement (Mackworth's clock test): sustained-attention performance declines over time, faster when signals are rare. Psychological refractory period: a second response is delayed when two stimuli arrive close together, evidence for a central bottleneck. Spatial neglect: right-parietal damage leaves patients ignoring the left side of space, a clinical breakdown of spatial attention. TRAP: Cocktail-party effect (hearing your name in an unattended conversation) supports late /attenuation selection, NOT Broadbent's early filter, this is the most common attention MCQ. Broadbent = early/physical; Treisman = attenuation; Deutsch-Norman = late/meaning; Lavie = depends on load. Feature search pops out (parallel); conjunction search is serial.

chunks.heading: 3. Memory
chunks.text: 3. Memory

chunks.heading: Multi-store model (Atkinson-Shiffrin)
chunks.text: Multi-store model (Atkinson-Shiffrin) Sensory memory → short-term/working memory → long-term memory, with attention and rehearsal as the gates. Store Capacity / duration Sensory: iconic (visual) large; about 0.25 to 1 second (Sperling's partial-report) Sensory: echoic (auditory) about 2 to 4 seconds Short-term memory 7 plus or minus 2 items (Miller), about 15 to 30 seconds; chunking expands it Long-term memory effectively unlimited, durable

chunks.heading: Working memory (Baddeley & Hitch)
chunks.text: Working memory (Baddeley & Hitch) Four parts: central executive (control), phonological loop (verbal/acoustic), visuospatial sketchpad (visual/spatial), and the episodic buffer (added 2000, integrates information across systems).

chunks.heading: Types of long-term memory
chunks.text: Types of long-term memory Explicit / declarative (conscious): episodic (events, "what I did") and semantic (facts, meanings). Implicit / non-declarative (unconscious): procedural (skills), priming, classical conditioning.

chunks.heading: Processes, forgetting & distortion
chunks.text: Processes, forgetting & distortion Encoding → storage → retrieval. Levels of processing (Craik & Lockhart): deep semantic encoding beats shallow. Forgetting: decay; interference (proactive = old disrupts new; retroactive = new disrupts old); cue-dependent / retrieval failure; encoding failure. Ebbinghaus forgetting curve: rapid early loss then levelling; spacing and overlearning slow it. Serial position effect: primacy (LTM) + recency (STM). A delay wipes recency, not primacy. Reconstructive memory: Bartlett (schemas distort recall, "War of the Ghosts"); Loftus (misinformation effect, leading questions reshape memory). Amnesia: anterograde (cannot form new memories, e.g. H.M.) vs retrograde (cannot recall old). Korsakoff = thiamine deficiency + confabulation.

chunks.heading: Retrieval, cues & enhancement
chunks.text: Retrieval, cues & enhancement Encoding specificity (Tulving): retrieval is best when cues at recall match those at encoding. Context-dependent (same place/environment) and state-dependent (same mood/physiological state) memory; mood-congruent recall. Recall vs recognition vs relearning (savings) as measures of retention; recognition is usually easier than recall. Flashbulb memories: vivid, confident memories of shocking events, felt accurate but still prone to distortion. Tip-of-the-tongue state = retrieval failure with partial access. Spacing effect and testing effect : spaced practice and active retrieval beat massed re-reading. Consolidation: the hippocampus binds new memories; sleep aids consolidation; reconsolidation makes reactivated memories briefly editable.

chunks.heading: 4. Learning
chunks.text: 4. Learning

chunks.heading: Classical conditioning (Pavlov)
chunks.text: Classical conditioning (Pavlov) A neutral stimulus paired with an unconditioned stimulus (UCS) becomes a conditioned stimulus (CS) that triggers a conditioned response (CR). Phases: acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalisation, discrimination, higher-order conditioning. Watson's Little Albert = conditioned fear. Garcia effect = taste aversion learned in one trial over long delay (biological preparedness).

chunks.heading: Operant conditioning (Thorndike, Skinner)
chunks.text: Operant conditioning (Thorndike, Skinner) Thorndike's law of effect : responses followed by satisfaction are stamped in. Skinner formalised it. Add (positive) Remove (negative) Increase behaviour (reinforcement) Positive reinforcement (give a reward) Negative reinforcement (remove an aversive) Decrease behaviour (punishment) Positive punishment (add an aversive) Negative punishment (remove a reward) Schedules of reinforcement: Fixed Ratio, Variable Ratio, Fixed Interval, Variable Interval. Variable Ratio gives the highest, steadiest response rate and is the most resistant to extinction (gambling). Ratio schedules beat interval; variable beats fixed. Shaping = reinforcing successive approximations. Premack principle = a high-frequency behaviour reinforces a low-frequency one ("eat your vegetables, then dessert").

chunks.heading: Cognitive & observational learning
chunks.text: Cognitive & observational learning Tolman: latent learning + cognitive maps (rats learned the maze without reinforcement). Kohler: insight learning (chimps solved problems suddenly, the "aha"). Bandura: observational learning / modelling (Bobo doll); steps = attention, retention, reproduction, motivation. Seligman: learned helplessness; biological constraints (preparedness) limit what can be conditioned. Rescorla-Wagner model: conditioning depends on surprise/prediction error , not mere pairing. The CS must reliably predict the UCS. Explains blocking (a new cue learns nothing if an existing cue already predicts the UCS) and the contingency (not just contiguity) requirement, Rescorla showed the CS must signal information. More terms: stimulus generalisation vs discrimination ; spontaneous recovery of an extinguished CR; overshadowing (a salient cue overshadows a weak one); latent inhibition (a pre-exposed stimulus is harder to condition). In operant work: escape vs avoidance learning, discriminative stimulus (signals when a response pays off), extinction burst , and the partial-reinforcement extinction effect (intermittently reinforced behaviour resists extinction).

chunks.heading: 5. Emotion
chunks.text: 5. Emotion Theory Sequence James-Lange Stimulus → body arousal → you label the emotion ("I tremble, therefore I am afraid") Cannon-Bard Stimulus → arousal AND emotion at the same time (thalamus routes both) Schachter-Singer (two-factor) Arousal + a cognitive label = emotion; same arousal, different label, different emotion Lazarus (appraisal) Cognitive appraisal comes first, then emotion Zajonc Some emotional reactions occur before/without cognition ("preferences need no inferences") Facial feedback hypothesis Facial expressions feed back and intensify the felt emotion Ekman: six basic universal emotions (happiness, sadness, anger, fear, surprise, disgust). Components of emotion: physiological arousal, expressive behaviour, conscious experience. Yerkes-Dodson law: performance peaks at moderate arousal (inverted U); harder tasks peak at lower arousal. Plutchik's wheel: eight primary emotions in opposing pairs that blend into secondary emotions (e.g. joy + trust = love). Dimensional models: Russell's circumplex maps emotion on valence (pleasant-unpleasant) × arousal (high-low). LeDoux's two roads to fear: a fast "low road" (thalamus → amygdala) for quick reaction and a slower "high road" (via cortex) for accurate appraisal. Cognitive appraisal detail (Lazarus): primary appraisal (is it relevant/threatening?) then secondary (can I cope?). Display rules: culturally learned norms fo

chunks.heading: 6. Motivation
chunks.text: 6. Motivation Instinct theory: behaviour driven by innate biological programs. Drive-reduction (Hull): a need creates a drive; behaviour reduces the drive to restore homeostasis. Arousal theory: we seek an optimal level of arousal (links to Yerkes-Dodson). Incentive theory: external rewards pull behaviour. Maslow's hierarchy: physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem → self-actualisation (later: cognitive, aesthetic, transcendence). Intrinsic vs extrinsic: intrinsic = for its own sake; extrinsic = for a reward. The overjustification effect : paying for an already-enjoyed activity can reduce intrinsic motivation. Self-determination theory (Deci & Ryan): autonomy, competence, relatedness. McClelland: needs for achievement, affiliation, power (measured via the TAT). ERG theory (Alderfer): Maslow condensed to Existence, Relatedness, Growth; allows movement up and down (frustration-regression). Expectancy theory (Vroom): motivation = expectancy × instrumentality × valence. Goal-setting theory (Locke & Latham): specific, challenging, accepted goals drive performance. Approach-avoidance conflict (Lewin): approach-approach, avoidance-avoidance, and approach-avoidance conflicts. Specific drives: hunger (lateral hypothalamus starts eating, ventromedial stops it; the set-point/leptin idea); arousal/sensation-seeking; achievement motivation (need for achievement vs fear of failure).

chunks.heading: 7. Intelligence
chunks.text: 7. Intelligence Theorist Model Spearman (1904) Two-factor: general intelligence g + specific s ; invented factor analysis Thurstone (1938) 7 Primary Mental Abilities (no single g) Cattell & Horn Fluid intelligence (Gf, reasoning) vs crystallised (Gc, learned knowledge) Guilford Structure of Intellect (up to 180 cells); convergent vs divergent thinking Gardner (1983) Multiple intelligences (8): linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinaesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalist Sternberg Triarchic: analytical, creative, practical Carroll / CHC Three-stratum hierarchy (g → broad → narrow); the dominant modern model Tests: Wechsler (WAIS/WISC, deviation IQ, SD 15), Stanford-Binet (SD 16, SB-5 uses 15), Raven's Progressive Matrices (culture-reduced g). Ratio IQ = (mental age / chronological age) × 100. Flynn effect = rising IQ scores across generations. Heritability estimates are population statistics, not individual destiny. Vernon's hierarchical model and Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) integrate g, broad, and narrow abilities, the basis of most modern tests. Galton (first to study individual differences, hereditary genius), Binet & Simon (first practical test, the concept of mental age), Terman (Stanford-Binet, longitudinal study of gifted "Termites"). Emotional intelligence (Goleman) and Sternberg's successful intelligence broaden the construct beyond ac

chunks.heading: 8. Cognition (thinking, problem-solving, language)
chunks.text: 8. Cognition (thinking, problem-solving, language) Concepts & prototypes: we categorise by comparison to a best example (prototype). Problem solving: algorithms (guaranteed, slow) vs heuristics (fast rules of thumb). Barriers: fixation, mental set, functional fixedness. Heuristics & biases (Tversky & Kahneman): representativeness, availability, anchoring; confirmation bias; framing effect; overconfidence. Decision making: System 1 (fast, intuitive) vs System 2 (slow, deliberate). Language: phonemes → morphemes → syntax → semantics → pragmatics. Stages: cooing, babbling, one-word (~12 mo), telegraphic (~24 mo). Chomsky: language acquisition device + universal grammar (nativist). Skinner: language is learned by reinforcement (behaviourist), demolished by Chomsky's review. Whorf: linguistic relativity (language shapes thought). Critical/sensitive period (Lenneberg); the case of Genie. Reasoning: deductive (general → specific, logically certain) vs inductive (specific → general, probabilistic); confirmation bias and belief bias distort it. More heuristics & effects: gambler's fallacy, sunk-cost fallacy, hindsight bias, base-rate neglect, the conjunction fallacy (Linda problem), loss aversion and prospect theory (Kahneman & Tversky). Mental imagery: Shepard & Metzler's mental rotation, imagery is analog and spatial. Concept structure: classical (defining features) vs prototype vs ex

chunks.heading: 9. Landmark experiments (the detail)
chunks.text: 9. Landmark experiments (the detail) Study Method & finding Milgram (1963) obedience Participants gave what they thought were escalating shocks on an experimenter's orders; 65 percent went to the maximum 450 V. Obedience to authority over conscience. Asch (1951) conformity Line-judgement task with confederates giving wrong answers; about 75 percent conformed at least once. Normative social influence. Zimbardo (1971) Stanford Prison Students randomly assigned guard/prisoner roles; the situation produced abusive behaviour, stopped early. Power of roles and situation (deindividuation). Darley & Latane (1968) bystander The more bystanders present, the less likely and slower any one person helps. Diffusion of responsibility (sparked by the Kitty Genovese case). Festinger & Carlsmith (1959) dissonance People paid 1 dollar to lie about a boring task later rated it more enjoyable than those paid 20 dollars. Less external justification → more attitude change. Sherif (1954) Robbers Cave Boys' camp; competition created intergroup hostility, shared superordinate goals reduced it. Realistic conflict theory. Tajfel (1971) minimal group Arbitrary group labels alone produced in-group favouritism. Social identity theory. Bandura (1961) Bobo doll Children who watched an adult hit a doll imitated the aggression. Observational learning. Harlow (1958) monkeys Infant monkeys preferred a soft cloth "

chunks.heading: 10. Personality
chunks.text: 10. Personality Full version: this is the compact pass. The dedicated Personality Theories page has all of it in depth — every defence mechanism, the neo-Freudians side by side, type theories, assessment pairings, and the collected MCQ traps.

chunks.heading: Psychodynamic (Freud)
chunks.text: Psychodynamic (Freud) Structure: id (pleasure principle), ego (reality principle), superego (morality/conscience). Topographic: conscious, preconscious, unconscious. The iceberg. Psychosexual stages: oral → anal → phallic (Oedipus/Electra) → latency → genital. Fixation at a stage shapes the adult personality. Defence mechanisms: repression, denial, projection, displacement, reaction formation, rationalisation, sublimation, regression. (Anna Freud catalogued these.)

chunks.heading: Neo-Freudians
chunks.text: Neo-Freudians Jung: collective unconscious, archetypes, introversion/extraversion. Adler: inferiority complex, striving for superiority, birth order. Horney: basic anxiety, womb envy (countered Freud). Erikson: psychosocial stages (see Development).

chunks.heading: Trait theories
chunks.text: Trait theories Theorist Model Allport Cardinal, central, secondary traits Cattell 16 Personality Factors (16PF), via factor analysis Eysenck Three dimensions: extraversion, neuroticism, psychoticism (PEN) Costa & McCrae Big Five / OCEAN: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism

chunks.heading: Humanistic & social-cognitive
chunks.text: Humanistic & social-cognitive Rogers: self-concept, congruence (real vs ideal self), unconditional positive regard, the fully functioning person. Maslow: self-actualisation (see Motivation). Bandura: reciprocal determinism (behaviour ↔ person ↔ environment), self-efficacy. Rotter: locus of control (internal vs external). Assessment: projective tests (Rorschach inkblots, TAT) tap the unconscious; objective inventories (MMPI, 16PF, NEO-PI) are self-report and standardised.

chunks.heading: 11. Social psychology (concepts)
chunks.text: 11. Social psychology (concepts) Attribution: dispositional vs situational. Fundamental attribution error = overweighting disposition for others' behaviour. Actor-observer bias , self-serving bias (credit success, blame the situation). Attitudes & persuasion: ABC components (affective, behavioural, cognitive). Elaboration Likelihood Model (Petty & Cacioppo): central route (argument quality) vs peripheral route (cues). Cognitive dissonance (Festinger): conflicting cognitions create discomfort that drives attitude change. Conformity & obedience: normative (to fit in) vs informational (to be right) influence. Compliance techniques: foot-in-the-door, door-in-the-face, low-balling. Group processes: social facilitation (others improve easy tasks, worsen hard ones), social loafing, deindividuation, groupthink (Janis), group polarisation, risky shift. Prejudice: stereotype (cognitive), prejudice (affective), discrimination (behavioural). Realistic conflict theory; social identity theory (Tajfel); contact hypothesis (Allport) reduces it. Prosocial & aggression: bystander effect + diffusion of responsibility; altruism vs reciprocity. Frustration-aggression hypothesis; social learning of aggression. Attraction: proximity, similarity, mere-exposure effect, reciprocity, physical attractiveness; matching hypothesis; Sternberg's triangular theory of love (intimacy, passion, commitment). Self

chunks.heading: 12. Developmental psychology
chunks.text: 12. Developmental psychology Theorist Stages / idea Piaget (cognitive) Sensorimotor (0-2, object permanence) → preoperational (2-7, egocentrism, no conservation) → concrete operational (7-11, conservation) → formal operational (11+, abstract). Schemas, assimilation, accommodation. Erikson (psychosocial) 8 stages, each a crisis: trust v mistrust → autonomy v shame → initiative v guilt → industry v inferiority → identity v role confusion → intimacy v isolation → generativity v stagnation → integrity v despair. Kohlberg (moral) Preconventional (punishment/reward) → conventional (social approval, law and order) → postconventional (social contract, universal ethics). Vygotsky (sociocultural) Zone of proximal development, scaffolding, the social origin of thought (more-knowledgeable other). Freud (psychosexual) See Personality. Attachment (Bowlby; Ainsworth's Strange Situation): secure, insecure-avoidant, insecure-resistant/ambivalent, and disorganised (Main & Solomon). Harlow = contact comfort. Temperament (Thomas & Chess): easy, difficult, slow-to-warm-up. Nature vs nurture & epigenetics; maturation vs learning; continuous vs stage (discontinuous) views; critical vs sensitive periods. Theory of mind (false-belief / Sally-Anne task, ~4 yrs); Vygotsky vs Piaget on private speech and the social origin of thought. Parenting styles (Baumrind): authoritative, authoritarian, permissive, n

chunks.heading: 13. States of consciousness & sleep
chunks.text: 13. States of consciousness & sleep Sleep stages: NREM 1 (theta, hypnagogic) → NREM 2 (sleep spindles, K-complexes) → NREM 3 (delta, deep/slow-wave) → REM (paradoxical: brain active, body paralysed, dreaming). ~90-minute cycles; REM lengthens toward morning. Circadian rhythm: ~24-hour cycle, governed by the suprachiasmatic nucleus; melatonin from the pineal gland. Dream theories: Freud (wish fulfilment, manifest vs latent content); activation-synthesis (Hobson & McCarley, brain makes sense of random REM activity); information-processing/consolidation. Sleep disorders: insomnia, narcolepsy, sleep apnoea, night terrors (NREM) vs nightmares (REM), somnambulism. Altered states: hypnosis, meditation, and psychoactive drugs (depressants, stimulants, hallucinogens, opioids) altering consciousness via neurotransmitters. Theories of hypnosis: Hilgard's neodissociation ("hidden observer") vs the social-cognitive/role-enactment view. Functions of sleep: restoration, energy conservation, memory consolidation; sleep deprivation effects. Drug concepts: tolerance, dependence, withdrawal, the reward pathway (dopamine, nucleus accumbens). Consciousness debates: the "hard problem"; the cognitive unconscious; global workspace theory.

chunks.heading: 14. Stress, coping & health
chunks.text: 14. Stress, coping & health Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome: alarm → resistance → exhaustion. Lazarus & Folkman: primary appraisal (is it a threat?) then secondary appraisal (can I cope?). Problem-focused coping (change the stressor) vs emotion-focused coping (manage the feeling). Physiology: the HPA axis and sympathetic "fight-or-flight" (Cannon); cortisol as the chronic-stress hormone. Type A (competitive, hostile, time-urgent) vs Type B; hostility links to heart disease. Buffers: social support, perceived control, optimism, hardiness (Kobasa: commitment, control, challenge). Stressors: Holmes & Rahe Social Readjustment Rating Scale (life-change units); daily hassles vs uplifts (Lazarus); acute vs chronic stress. Tend-and-befriend (Taylor): an alternative to fight-or-flight, oxytocin-linked, more often described in women. Health: psychoneuroimmunology (stress suppresses immunity); the biopsychosocial model; learned optimism (Seligman).

chunks.heading: 15. Schools & history of psychology
chunks.text: 15. Schools & history of psychology School Core idea & figures Structuralism Break consciousness into elements via introspection. Wundt (first lab, 1879), Titchener. Functionalism What is the mind for ? Adaptive function of behaviour. William James, influenced by Darwin. Psychoanalysis Unconscious drives and early experience. Freud. Behaviourism Only observable behaviour; learning by conditioning. Watson, Pavlov, Skinner. Gestalt The whole differs from the sum of parts. Wertheimer, Koffka, Kohler. Humanistic ("third force") Free will, growth, self-actualisation. Maslow, Rogers. Cognitive Mental processes as information processing; the "cognitive revolution" (1950s-60s). Neisser, Miller. Biological / evolutionary Behaviour rooted in the brain, genes, and adaptation. Companion: the one-line testable version of all of this is in the textbook's Section 9, Rapid Recall . Read this page once for understanding, then drill the Rapid Recall block. Sihan MET 2026 + NIMHANS prep · /notes/general-psych/

chunks.heading: The Goldmine — clean revision notes
chunks.text: The Goldmine — clean revision notes One clean pass over the exact clusters that keep coming up in your prep: disorders (DSM-5-TR vs ICD-11, dissociative, psychotic spectrum, neurodevelopmental), assessment scales (Vineland, Vanderbilt, BPAQ + the scale table), stats & research methods (factor analysis, biserial vs point-biserial, t-tests, sampling distributions, regression), and therapy (CBT, operant, behaviour mod). There's a dedicated box at the end tying the aggression literature straight into your dissertation for the 11 Jun interview. Read the prose, not just the tables. Trap boxes flag the exact confusions MCQs are built on; NIMHANS boxes flag where the clinical entrance digs deeper than MET. 1 DSM vs ICD 2 Dissociative 3 Psychotic spectrum 4 Neurodevelopmental 5 Assessment scales 6 Factor analysis 7 Biserial / point-biserial 8 t-tests 9 Sampling distributions 10 Regression 11 CBT / operant / behaviour mod 12 Dissertation: porn & aggression

chunks.heading: 1 · DSM-5-TR vs ICD-11
chunks.text: 1 · DSM-5-TR vs ICD-11 Both are diagnostic systems; they classify the same disorders but differ in author, purpose and structure . Know the contrasts, not just the names. DSM-5-TR ICD-11 Author APA (American Psychiatric Assoc.) WHO Scope US-centric, research / clinical Global, billing + clinical, all health conditions Released DSM-5 2013; 5-TR text revision 2022 Adopted 2019, in force Jan 2022 Structure Mostly categorical , detailed criteria sets More dimensional (esp. personality) Personality d/o Keeps 10 categorical types (Sec II) Abolished types → one PD dx + severity (mild/mod/severe) + trait domains High-yield contrasts • PTSD: ICD-11 is tighter — only re-experiencing in the here-and-now , avoidance, and a sense of current threat . ICD-11 also adds Complex PTSD (PTSD + disturbances in self-organisation: affect dysregulation, negative self-concept, relationship problems). • Schizophrenia duration: DSM-5 needs 6 months (incl. prodrome/residual); ICD-11 needs 1 month of active symptoms. • New in ICD-11: Gaming disorder, prolonged grief disorder, compulsive sexual behaviour disorder. New in DSM-5-TR: prolonged grief disorder (added too), unspecified mood/suicidal-behaviour codes. • Bereavement: DSM-5 removed the bereavement exclusion for MDD (you can diagnose depression even during grief). Trap: "Which system is dimensional for personality?" → ICD-11 . DSM-5's main text is sti

chunks.heading: 2 · Dissociative disorders
chunks.text: 2 · Dissociative disorders Core theme: a disruption of the normal integration of consciousness, memory, identity, emotion, perception or body representation. DSM-5 recognises three: Dissociative Identity Disorder (DID) — two or more distinct personality states + recurrent gaps in recall. (Formerly "multiple personality disorder".) Dissociative Amnesia — inability to recall important autobiographical info, usually traumatic. With dissociative fugue = amnesia + purposeful travel/bewildered wandering. Depersonalization/Derealization Disorder — persistent detachment, with intact reality testing. Trap: Depersonalization = detachment from your own self (feeling unreal, robotic, watching yourself). Derealization = detachment from surroundings (the world feels dreamlike, foggy, unreal). Reality testing stays intact — that's what separates it from psychosis.

chunks.heading: 3 · Schizophrenia spectrum & other psychotic disorders
chunks.text: 3 · Schizophrenia spectrum & other psychotic disorders Disorder Key marker Brief psychotic disorder < 1 month, full return to function Schizophreniform 1–6 months Schizophrenia ≥ 6 months (DSM); active phase ≥ 1 month Schizoaffective Mood episode + psychosis, but ≥ 2 wks psychosis without mood symptoms Delusional disorder Non-bizarre delusion(s) ≥ 1 month, function otherwise OK Positive vs negative symptoms. Positive = added on (delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech/behaviour). Negative = taken away (the 5 A's: Avolition, Alogia, Anhedonia, Affective flattening, Asociality ). Negative symptoms predict worse prognosis and respond least to antipsychotics. NIMHANS: Know Schneider's first-rank symptoms (thought insertion/withdrawal/broadcasting, audible thoughts, running commentary, delusional perception, passivity). DSM-5 dropped the classic subtypes (paranoid, catatonic, hebephrenic, residual) — they're now specifiers/dimensions, not separate diagnoses.

chunks.heading: 4 · Neurodevelopmental disorders
chunks.text: 4 · Neurodevelopmental disorders Onset in the developmental period. The DSM-5 cluster: Intellectual Disability, Communication disorders, Autism Spectrum Disorder, ADHD, Specific Learning Disorder, Motor disorders (incl. tics / Tourette's). DSM-5 changes to know: Asperger's, autistic disorder and PDD-NOS were merged into one ASD with severity levels 1–3 (1 = "requiring support", 3 = "requiring very substantial support"). ID severity is now set by adaptive functioning , not IQ score alone. Trap: ADHD presentations are predominantly inattentive / predominantly hyperactive-impulsive / combined — not "subtypes". Onset of several symptoms must be before age 12 (DSM-5 raised it from 7).

chunks.heading: 5 · Assessment scales — Vineland, Vanderbilt, BPAQ
chunks.text: 5 · Assessment scales — Vineland, Vanderbilt, BPAQ Scale Measures Notes Vineland (VABS) Adaptive behaviour : Communication, Daily Living, Socialization, Motor Caregiver/teacher semi-structured interview. Central to ID & ASD diagnosis (the "adaptive functioning" half). Vanderbilt (NICHQ) ADHD rating scale; also screens ODD, conduct, anxiety/depression Parent + teacher versions, ages ~6–12. Free, used in primary-care ADHD assessment. BPAQ Aggression : Physical, Verbal, Anger, Hostility Buss–Perry Aggression Questionnaire, 29 items. Revision of the Buss–Durkee Hostility Inventory. (Your dissertation measure — see §12.) Quick recall: Vineland → adaptive behaviour (not IQ). Vanderbilt → ADHD. BPAQ → 4 factors of aggression. Don't confuse the BPAQ (trait aggression) with the Buss–Durkee (its older parent) or with the STAXI (state-trait anger only). NIMHANS: Keep the bigger scale map straight — adaptive : Vineland, ABAS; intelligence : WAIS-IV/WISC-V, Binet-Kamat, MISIC, Bhatia; development : DDST, BSID, DST/Gesell; ADHD : Conners, Vanderbilt; aggression/anger : BPAQ, STAXI, OAS.

chunks.heading: 6 · Factor analysis
chunks.text: 6 · Factor analysis A data-reduction technique: takes many correlated variables and finds a smaller set of underlying latent factors that explain the shared variance. EFA (exploratory) — you don't know the structure, you let the data reveal it. CFA (confirmatory) — you test a hypothesised structure (a measurement model, via SEM). Extraction: Kaiser criterion keeps factors with eigenvalue > 1 ; cross-check with the scree plot (keep factors above the "elbow"). Factor loadings = correlation of a variable with a factor (≥ .30–.40 is meaningful). Rotation: Varimax = orthogonal (factors assumed uncorrelated); Oblimin/Promax = oblique (factors allowed to correlate). Rotation makes loadings interpretable, it doesn't change fit. Adequacy checks: KMO (> .60 ok) and Bartlett's test of sphericity (must be significant). Trap: Factor analysis vs PCA — PCA explains total variance and is pure data reduction; factor analysis models only the shared (common) variance and assumes latent causes. Exams love this distinction.

chunks.heading: 7 · Biserial vs point-biserial correlation
chunks.text: 7 · Biserial vs point-biserial correlation Point-biserial (r pb ) Biserial (r b ) One variable is… a true dichotomy (genuinely two categories: pass/fail, male/female) an artificial dichotomy (a continuous trait chopped into two: "high/low", "pass mark on a continuum") Other variable continuous continuous Assumes nothing extra an underlying normal continuum behind the dichotomy Classic use Item analysis — item (right/wrong) vs total test score = item discrimination same idea, when the dichotomy is really continuous Trap: If the split is real (you can't be "a bit male"), use point-biserial . If you've forced a cut on something continuous, use biserial . Don't mix up either with phi (two true dichotomies) or tetrachoric (two artificial dichotomies).

chunks.heading: 8 · t-tests
chunks.text: 8 · t-tests Compares two means and asks whether the difference is bigger than you'd expect by chance. Three flavours: One-sample — sample mean vs a known/hypothesised value. df = n − 1 . Independent-samples — two separate groups. df = n₁ + n₂ − 2 . Paired / dependent — same people twice (pre/post) or matched pairs. df = n − 1 (n = number of pairs). Assumptions: interval/ratio data, normality , homogeneity of variance (Levene's test; if violated use Welch's t), independence of observations. Violate them badly → use the non-parametric cousin (Mann–Whitney U for independent, Wilcoxon signed-rank for paired). Trap: ≥ 3 groups → not a t-test, use ANOVA (running many t-tests inflates Type I error). A t-test is just ANOVA with two groups (t² = F).

chunks.heading: 9 · Sampling distributions
chunks.text: 9 · Sampling distributions The distribution of a statistic (usually the mean) over all possible samples of size n from a population. It's the bridge from one sample to a probability statement about the population. Standard error (SE) = SD / √n — the SD of the sampling distribution. Bigger n → smaller SE → more precise estimate. Central Limit Theorem: as n grows, the sampling distribution of the mean approaches normal regardless of the population's shape (rule of thumb n ≥ 30). This is why parametric tests work even on non-normal data with big samples. Trap: Don't confuse SD (spread of raw scores) with SE (spread of sample means). SE is always smaller and shrinks with √n; SD doesn't shrink as you collect more data.

chunks.heading: 10 · Regression
chunks.text: 10 · Regression Predicts a continuous outcome (Y) from one (simple) or more (multiple) predictors (X), via the least-squares line that minimises the squared residuals. Equation: Ŷ = a + bX — a = intercept, b = slope (change in Y per 1-unit change in X). R² = proportion of variance in Y explained by the model (the coefficient of determination; = r² in simple regression). Standardised β lets you compare predictors' strength on a common scale. Assumptions (LINE): L inearity, I ndependence of errors, N ormality of residuals, E qual variance (homoscedasticity). Multiple regression adds: no severe multicollinearity (check VIF). Trap: Correlation ≠ causation, and a high R² doesn't mean the model is causal or that predictions extrapolate beyond the data range.

chunks.heading: 11 · CBT · operant conditioning · behaviour modification
chunks.text: 11 · CBT · operant conditioning · behaviour modification

chunks.heading: CBT
chunks.text: CBT Targets the link between thoughts → feelings → behaviour ; change maladaptive cognitions and you change the emotion and behaviour. Two roots: Beck (Cognitive Therapy): the cognitive triad (negative views of self, world, future ), cognitive distortions (catastrophising, all-or-nothing, overgeneralisation, mind-reading), automatic thoughts, schemas. Technique: cognitive restructuring, thought records, behavioural experiments. Ellis (REBT): the ABC model — A ctivating event → B elief (irrational) → C onsequence. Dispute the irrational belief (D) to a new effect (E).

chunks.heading: Operant conditioning (Skinner)
chunks.text: Operant conditioning (Skinner) Add (positive) Remove (negative) Increase behaviour (Reinforcement) + give a reward − take away something aversive Decrease behaviour (Punishment) + apply something aversive − remove something pleasant (response cost) Schedules of reinforcement: Ratio (per responses) vs Interval (per time); Fixed vs Variable. Variable Ratio (VR) = highest, steadiest response rate and most resistant to extinction (gambling). Fixed Interval gives the "scalloped" pattern. Trap: Negative reinforcement is NOT punishment. Negative reinforcement increases behaviour by removing something nasty (taking a painkiller to stop pain). Punishment decreases behaviour.

chunks.heading: Behaviour modification
chunks.text: Behaviour modification The applied use of operant/classical principles to change behaviour: token economy , contingency management , shaping (reinforcing successive approximations), extinction , time-out (from positive reinforcement), and the Premack principle (a high-frequency behaviour reinforces a low-frequency one — "eat your veg, then dessert"). Sits under the umbrella of ABA (Applied Behaviour Analysis). NIMHANS: Keep the classical-conditioning techniques distinct from operant ones — systematic desensitisation , flooding , aversion therapy are based on classical (Pavlovian + reciprocal inhibition / Wolpe); token economy and shaping are operant .

chunks.heading: 12 · Dissertation thread — pornography & aggression (for 11 Jun)
chunks.text: 12 · Dissertation thread — pornography & aggression (for 11 Jun) This is the box for your interview. It ties §5 (BPAQ) and §10 (regression) straight to your dissertation. Be ready to state your research question, design, measure and the framework you're situating it in .

chunks.heading: The frameworks to name-drop
chunks.text: The frameworks to name-drop General Aggression Model (GAM — Anderson & Bushman, 2002): media/situational inputs → internal state (cognition, affect, arousal) → appraisal → aggressive behaviour. Repeated exposure builds aggression-related knowledge structures/scripts . The dominant integrative model. Confluence Model of sexual aggression (Malamuth): two converging paths — hostile masculinity and impersonal sex — predict sexual aggression; pornography use interacts with (doesn't single-handedly cause) these risk factors. Sexual script theory: repeated media exposure shapes the cognitive "scripts" people bring to real encounters. Desensitisation vs the catharsis hypothesis : evidence supports desensitisation/priming; the old "porn releases the urge so it lowers aggression" catharsis idea is largely unsupported .

chunks.heading: What the evidence actually says
chunks.text: What the evidence actually says Meta-analyses (e.g. Wright, Tokunaga & Kraus, 2016) link pornography consumption — especially violent content — to attitudes supporting aggression and to actual sexual aggression, with effects stronger for verbal than physical aggression and stronger for violent than non-violent material. The relationship is correlational and moderated (by trait hostility, content type), not a simple cause.

chunks.heading: Measurement & method (own your limitations)
chunks.text: Measurement & method (own your limitations) Measure: BPAQ for trait aggression (4 subscales) — you can correlate subscale scores with consumption frequency/type. Analysis: correlation → multiple regression with porn-use variables predicting BPAQ, controlling for confounds (trait hostility, sensation-seeking, prior victimisation). Limitations to pre-empt: self-report & social-desirability bias, the third-variable problem (a confound drives both), cross-sectional ≠ causal , ecological validity, sampling. One-line answer if they ask "so does porn cause aggression?": "The evidence is a consistent but modest association , strongest for violent content and aggression-supportive attitudes; it's moderated by individual risk factors and the design is correlational, so I'm careful to claim a link, not direct causation." One pass tomorrow morning, only the red TRAP boxes and the tables. Anything you blank on, mark it and re-read the corresponding cheatsheet section. Don't try to memorize this in one sitting, target the gaps.

chunks.heading: 1. Abnormal Psychology
chunks.text: 1. Abnormal Psychology

chunks.heading: 1.1 The 4 Ds (definition of abnormality)
chunks.text: 1.1 The 4 Ds (definition of abnormality) Deviance — statistical or social norm violation Distress — subjective suffering Dysfunction — impairs daily life / role functioning Danger — risk to self or others TRAP: Deviance alone ≠ abnormal. A genius IQ is statistically deviant but not pathological. Always need distress or dysfunction with it.

chunks.heading: 1.2 Historical conceptions, one-line
chunks.text: 1.2 Historical conceptions, one-line Era Model Key name Ancient Supernatural (demons, possession) Trephination Greek Biological, four humors Hippocrates Middle Ages Demonological return, witch trials Malleus Maleficarum Renaissance Asylum reform begins Pinel (moral treatment), Tuke 19th c. Biological / classification Kraepelin (dementia praecox), Bleuler (renamed schizophrenia) 20th c. Psychological Freud (psychoanalysis), Watson (behaviorism), Beck (CBT)

chunks.heading: 1.3 DSM-5 vs ICD-11, must-knows
chunks.text: 1.3 DSM-5 vs ICD-11, must-knows DSM-5 (2013) / DSM-5-TR (2022) ICD-11 (2019) Publisher APA, US WHO, global Sections 3 sections, 22 chapters, no axes (axes dropped from DSM-IV) Chapter 6 = mental, behavioral, neurodev OCD Own chapter (separated from anxiety) Own chapter too PTSD Own chapter (Trauma-related) Own chapter, adds Complex PTSD Schizophrenia subtypes Removed in DSM-5 (no more paranoid/catatonic/etc.) Removed in ICD-11 too Mental Retardation Renamed Intellectual Developmental Disorder Disorders of Intellectual Development Asperger's Folded into ASD Folded into ASD Bereavement exclusion (MDD) Removed Still cautious TRAP: Multi-axial system was DSM-IV. DSM-5 dropped it. If a question says "Axis I disorder" it is testing pre-DSM-5 vocabulary.

chunks.heading: 1.4 Mental Status Examination (MSE), order matters
chunks.text: 1.4 Mental Status Examination (MSE), order matters ABS-MTPCIJ : Appearance, Behavior, Speech, Mood/affect, Thought (form + content), Perception, Cognition, Insight, Judgment. Mood = subjective ("how do you feel"). Affect = observed (range, congruence). Thought form = how thoughts flow (loose, tangential, flight of ideas, circumstantial). Thought content = what (delusions, suicidal, obsessions). Insight = awareness of illness. Judgment = decision-making in real situations.

chunks.heading: 1.5 Approaches to psychopathology
chunks.text: 1.5 Approaches to psychopathology Approach Cause Treatment Biological Genes, neurotransmitters, brain Meds, ECT Psychodynamic Unconscious conflict, early experience Psychoanalysis, free association Behavioral Maladaptive learning Conditioning, exposure, reinforcement Cognitive Distorted thoughts, schemas CBT, cognitive restructuring (Beck, Ellis) Humanistic Blocked self-actualization Person-centered (Rogers), Gestalt (Perls) Sociocultural Family, culture, stigma Family therapy, community Biopsychosocial All three interact (Engel, 1977) Integrative

chunks.heading: 1.6 Anxiety disorders, distinguishing features
chunks.text: 1.6 Anxiety disorders, distinguishing features Disorder Core feature Time GAD Excessive worry, multiple domains, hard to control ≥ 6 months Panic Disorder Recurrent unexpected panic attacks + worry about more Attack peaks in 10 min Specific Phobia Fear of one object/situation ≥ 6 months Social Anxiety Fear of scrutiny, judgment in social situations ≥ 6 months Agoraphobia Fear of places where escape is hard (≥ 2 of 5 situations) ≥ 6 months Separation Anxiety Excessive fear of separation from attachment figure ≥ 4 wks (kids), 6 mo (adults) TRAP: OCD is NOT in the anxiety chapter in DSM-5. It has its own chapter (OCD and related). Same for PTSD (Trauma- and stressor-related).

chunks.heading: 1.7 OCD and related, hoard the list
chunks.text: 1.7 OCD and related, hoard the list OCD Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD) Hoarding Disorder (new in DSM-5) Trichotillomania (hair-pulling) Excoriation (skin-picking, new in DSM-5)

chunks.heading: 1.8 Mood disorders
chunks.text: 1.8 Mood disorders Disorder Episode Duration MDD ≥ 5 of 9 SIG-E-CAPS, must include depressed mood OR anhedonia ≥ 2 weeks Persistent Depressive Disorder (Dysthymia) Chronic low-grade depression ≥ 2 yrs (1 yr kids) Bipolar I ≥ 1 manic episode (depression not required) Mania ≥ 1 wk Bipolar II Hypomania + at least one MDE, no full mania ever Hypomania ≥ 4 days Cyclothymia Hypomanic + depressive symptoms, never full episode ≥ 2 yrs PMDD Severe mood symptoms premenstrually Most cycles in last yr Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder Severe temper outbursts in kids Onset before 10, dx 6-18 SIG-E-CAPS for MDD: Sleep, Interest (anhedonia), Guilt, Energy, Concentration, Appetite, Psychomotor, Suicidal ideation. + depressed mood = 9 total. DIG-FAST for mania: Distractibility, Indiscretion, Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity increase, Sleep decrease, Talkativeness.

chunks.heading: 1.9 Suicide risk, SAD PERSONS
chunks.text: 1.9 Suicide risk, SAD PERSONS S ex (male), A ge (<19 or >45), D epression, P revious attempt, E thanol/drugs, R ational thinking loss, S ocial supports lacking, O rganized plan, N o spouse, S ickness. TRAP: Strongest single predictor of completed suicide = previous attempt . Most common method globally = hanging. Highest-risk diagnosis = MDD with comorbid substance use.

chunks.heading: 1.10 Schizophrenia (Schneider, Bleuler, DSM-5)
chunks.text: 1.10 Schizophrenia (Schneider, Bleuler, DSM-5) Bleuler's 4 As : Associations (loose), Affect (flat), Ambivalence, Autism (withdrawal). Schneider's First-Rank Symptoms : thought insertion/withdrawal/broadcasting, audible thoughts, voices commenting/arguing, made impulses/actions, somatic passivity, delusional perception. Suggestive but not diagnostic alone. Positive symptoms : hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior. Negative symptoms : flat affect, alogia, avolition, anhedonia, asociality. DSM-5 criteria : ≥ 2 of (delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized/catatonic behavior, negative symptoms), at least one from first three. Active phase ≥ 1 month, total disturbance ≥ 6 months. Disorder Duration Brief Psychotic Disorder 1 day to < 1 month Schizophreniform 1 month to < 6 months Schizophrenia ≥ 6 months Schizoaffective Mood episode + psychosis, but ≥ 2 wks of psychosis without mood symptoms Delusional Disorder ≥ 1 month delusions only, no other psychotic symptoms TRAP: Kraepelin coined dementia praecox . Bleuler renamed it schizophrenia (split mind, not split personality). Don't confuse with DID.

chunks.heading: 1.11 Dissociative disorders
chunks.text: 1.11 Dissociative disorders Dissociative Amnesia — gaps in autobiographical memory, often after trauma. Specifier: with dissociative fugue. DID (Dissociative Identity Disorder) — ≥ 2 distinct identities, recurrent gaps in recall. Strongly linked to severe early trauma. Depersonalization / Derealization Disorder — feeling unreal/detached from self or surroundings, reality testing intact.

chunks.heading: 1.12 Somatic symptom and related (DSM-5 renamed from somatoform)
chunks.text: 1.12 Somatic symptom and related (DSM-5 renamed from somatoform) Somatic Symptom Disorder — distressing somatic symptoms + excessive thoughts/behaviors about them. Illness Anxiety Disorder — preoccupation with having illness, few/no somatic symptoms (replaces hypochondriasis). Conversion Disorder (Functional Neurological Symptom) — neuro symptoms without medical explanation. La belle indifférence is a soft sign. Factitious Disorder — intentional faking for sick role. Munchausen = on self; Munchausen by proxy = on another. Malingering — faking for external gain (money, avoiding work). NOT a mental disorder, V-code. TRAP: Conversion + factitious + malingering are easy to mix. Conversion = unconscious, no gain. Factitious = conscious symptom production, sick role gain. Malingering = conscious, external gain.

chunks.heading: 1.13 Personality disorders (3 clusters)
chunks.text: 1.13 Personality disorders (3 clusters) Cluster Theme Disorders A Odd / eccentric Paranoid, Schizoid, Schizotypal B Dramatic / emotional Antisocial, Borderline, Histrionic, Narcissistic C Anxious / fearful Avoidant, Dependent, Obsessive-Compulsive PD TRAP: OCPD ≠ OCD. OCPD = perfectionism, rigid, ego-syntonic personality style. OCD = ego-dystonic obsessions/compulsions. Different chapters in DSM-5.

chunks.heading: 1.14 Substance use disorder (DSM-5)
chunks.text: 1.14 Substance use disorder (DSM-5) ≥ 2 of 11 criteria in 12 months. Severity: 2-3 mild, 4-5 moderate, ≥ 6 severe. DSM-5 collapsed abuse + dependence into one spectrum (no more "abuse vs dependence").

chunks.heading: 1.15 Childhood / neurodevelopmental disorders
chunks.text: 1.15 Childhood / neurodevelopmental disorders IDD (Intellectual Developmental Disorder) — onset in dev period, deficits in intellectual + adaptive functioning. Severity by adaptive function, not just IQ. ASD — social communication deficits + restricted/repetitive behaviors. DSM-5 merged Asperger's, PDD-NOS, autistic disorder into one spectrum. ADHD — inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity ≥ 6 months, onset before 12, ≥ 2 settings. Specific Learning Disorder — reading (dyslexia), writing (dysgraphia), math (dyscalculia). Tic disorders — Tourette's = motor + vocal tics ≥ 1 yr, onset before 18.

chunks.heading: 2. Developmental Psychology
chunks.text: 2. Developmental Psychology

chunks.heading: 2.1 Principles of development
chunks.text: 2.1 Principles of development Cephalocaudal — head to toe Proximodistal — center to periphery Continuity vs discontinuity (gradual vs stages) Nature vs nurture (genes vs environment, now interactionist consensus) Critical periods (rigid window) vs sensitive periods (preferred but flexible window)

chunks.heading: 2.2 Piaget, 4 stages
chunks.text: 2.2 Piaget, 4 stages Stage Age Achievement Sensorimotor 0-2 Object permanence (~8 mo), goal-directed action Preoperational 2-7 Symbolic thought, egocentrism, animism, lacks conservation Concrete Operational 7-11 Conservation, reversibility, classification, seriation Formal Operational 11+ Abstract, hypothetico-deductive reasoning Sensorimotor 6 substages : Reflexes (0-1mo) → Primary circular reactions (1-4mo, on body) → Secondary CR (4-8mo, on objects) → Coordination of secondary (8-12mo, intentional, object permanence) → Tertiary CR (12-18mo, experimentation) → Mental representation (18-24mo, deferred imitation). TRAP: Conservation ≠ object permanence. Object permanence = sensorimotor (~8mo). Conservation = concrete operational (~7yr). Easy mix-up.

chunks.heading: 2.3 Piaget key concepts
chunks.text: 2.3 Piaget key concepts Schema — mental framework Assimilation — fitting new info into existing schema Accommodation — modifying schema for new info Equilibration — drive to balance assimilation + accommodation Egocentrism — preoperational, can't take others' view (Three Mountains task) Animism — preoperational, attributing life to objects Centration — focus on one feature, blocks conservation

chunks.heading: 2.4 Vygotsky, sociocultural
chunks.text: 2.4 Vygotsky, sociocultural ZPD (Zone of Proximal Development) — gap between what child can do alone vs with help Scaffolding — temporary support from more knowledgeable other (MKO) Private speech — self-talk that becomes inner speech, guides thinking Tools of thought — language is the master tool, internalized from social interaction TRAP: Scaffolding term is Bruner's , applied to Vygotsky's ZPD. Vygotsky himself talked about MKO and ZPD, didn't use "scaffolding" word.

chunks.heading: 2.5 Erikson, 8 psychosocial stages
chunks.text: 2.5 Erikson, 8 psychosocial stages Age Conflict Virtue 0-1.5 Trust vs Mistrust Hope 1.5-3 Autonomy vs Shame/Doubt Will 3-6 Initiative vs Guilt Purpose 6-12 Industry vs Inferiority Competence 12-18 Identity vs Role Confusion Fidelity 18-40 Intimacy vs Isolation Love 40-65 Generativity vs Stagnation Care 65+ Integrity vs Despair Wisdom

chunks.heading: 2.6 Freud, 5 psychosexual stages
chunks.text: 2.6 Freud, 5 psychosexual stages Age Stage Erogenous zone / fixation 0-1 Oral Mouth, dependency, smoking, eating 1-3 Anal Bowel control; anal-retentive (orderly) or anal-expulsive (messy) 3-6 Phallic Genitals; Oedipus / Electra; superego forms 6-12 Latency Sexual urges dormant, same-sex friends 12+ Genital Mature sexuality

chunks.heading: 2.7 Kohlberg, moral development
chunks.text: 2.7 Kohlberg, moral development Level Stages Driver Preconventional 1. Punishment-obedience 2. Instrumental exchange Self-interest Conventional 3. Good boy / good girl 4. Law and order Social approval, rules Postconventional 5. Social contract 6. Universal ethical principles Abstract principles TRAP: Gilligan's critique = Kohlberg's stages reflect male "justice" orientation; women often reason via "ethics of care." Don't say Gilligan replaced Kohlberg, she added a parallel orientation.

chunks.heading: 2.8 Attachment, Bowlby + Ainsworth
chunks.text: 2.8 Attachment, Bowlby + Ainsworth Bowlby phases : Pre-attachment (0-6 wk) → Attachment-in-the-making (6 wk - 8 mo) → Clear-cut attachment (8 mo - 18 mo, separation anxiety + stranger anxiety peak) → Reciprocal relationships (18-24 mo+). Ainsworth's Strange Situation (4 styles): Style Behavior on separation Behavior on reunion Caregiver pattern Secure (B, ~60%) Distressed Easily comforted, returns to play Sensitive, responsive Avoidant (A, ~20%) Little distress Avoids/ignores caregiver Rejecting, unresponsive Resistant / Ambivalent (C, ~10%) Very distressed Seeks + resists contact, can't be soothed Inconsistent Disorganized (D, Main & Solomon) Confused, freezing, contradictory Approach + avoid, dazed Frightening / abusive / unresolved trauma TRAP: Disorganized was added by Main & Solomon, not Ainsworth. Ainsworth's original three were A/B/C.

chunks.heading: 2.9 Baumrind's parenting styles (2 axes)
chunks.text: 2.9 Baumrind's parenting styles (2 axes) High demand Low demand High warmth Authoritative (best outcomes) Permissive / Indulgent Low warmth Authoritarian Neglectful / Uninvolved (Maccoby & Martin added this 4th) TRAP: Authoritative ≠ Authoritarian. Authoritative = high warmth + high demand (the good one). Authoritarian = low warmth + high demand (the harsh one).

chunks.heading: 2.10 Language development, milestones
chunks.text: 2.10 Language development, milestones Age Milestone 0-2 mo Crying, reflexive sounds 2-4 mo Cooing (vowels) 6 mo Babbling (consonants + vowels) 10-14 mo First word; holophrastic speech (one word = whole thought) 18-24 mo Two-word / telegraphic speech ("more milk") 2-3 yr Vocab burst, simple sentences, overregularization ("goed", "foots") 3-5 yr Complex grammar, ~2000 words by 5 Theories : Skinner = behaviorist (operant, imitation). Chomsky = nativist (LAD, Universal Grammar, poverty of stimulus). Vygotsky / Bruner = social-interactionist. Piaget = cognitive (thought before language).

chunks.heading: 2.11 Theorists, 1-line hooks
chunks.text: 2.11 Theorists, 1-line hooks Theorist Hook Piaget 4 cognitive stages, schemas, equilibration Vygotsky ZPD, scaffolding, sociocultural, language as tool Erikson 8 psychosocial conflicts across life Freud 5 psychosexual stages, unconscious, id/ego/superego Bowlby Attachment as biological survival system, internal working model Ainsworth Strange Situation, A/B/C styles Main & Solomon Added disorganized (D) Harlow Wire vs cloth mother, contact comfort > food Lorenz Imprinting in geese, critical period Kohlberg 3 levels, 6 stages of moral reasoning, Heinz dilemma Gilligan Ethics of care, gendered critique of Kohlberg Baumrind Parenting styles (3, then 4) Bandura Social learning, observation, Bobo doll, self-efficacy Bronfenbrenner Ecological systems (micro/meso/exo/macro/chrono) Thomas & Chess Temperament, easy / difficult / slow-to-warm Marcia Identity statuses (diffusion, foreclosure, moratorium, achievement) Gesell Maturation, normative milestones Hall Adolescence as "storm and stress"

chunks.heading: 2.12 Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems
chunks.text: 2.12 Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems Full exam-grade primer: Bronfenbrenner, Ecological Systems Theory . Microsystem — direct, face-to-face settings (family, school, peers). Bidirectional influence. Mesosystem — interactions between microsystems (parent-teacher meetings, home-school link). Not a setting itself. Exosystem — settings the child isn't in but which still affect them (parent's workplace, school board, mass media). Macrosystem — cultural blueprint (ideology, laws, religion, SES, customs). Chronosystem — the time dimension (divorce, pandemic, sociohistorical era). Added later , originally 4 systems. 1979 Ecological Systems Theory → 1994 Bioecological Model with PPCT : P roximal P rocesses (engine of development, regular reciprocal interactions over time), P erson (demand / resource / force traits), C ontext (the 5 systems), T ime (micro / meso / macro time). TRAP: Exosystem ≠ no influence. Child isn't in it, but it shapes them via the microsystem (e.g. dad loses job → stress at home). If the stem mentions: nested environments, cultural context, parent's workplace affecting child, indirect influence → answer is Bronfenbrenner .

chunks.heading: 2.13 Marcia's identity statuses (Erikson stage 5 expansion)
chunks.text: 2.13 Marcia's identity statuses (Erikson stage 5 expansion) Crisis explored? Commitment made? Diffusion No No Foreclosure No Yes (handed down) Moratorium Yes (in progress) No Achievement Yes (resolved) Yes

chunks.heading: 3. Top 20 MCQ Traps, mixed
chunks.text: 3. Top 20 MCQ Traps, mixed Object permanence vs conservation, different stages. OCD is NOT in the anxiety chapter (DSM-5). Authoritative ≠ Authoritarian. Conversion (unconscious) ≠ Factitious (conscious, sick role) ≠ Malingering (conscious, external gain). OCPD ≠ OCD. Bipolar I needs mania ≥ 1 wk; Bipolar II is hypomania + MDE, never full mania. Schizophrenia = Bleuler. Dementia praecox = Kraepelin. Schizophrenia ≠ DID (split personality). Disorganized attachment was Main & Solomon, not Ainsworth. Scaffolding is Bruner's term (applied to Vygotsky). Schizophreniform = 1-6 mo. Brief Psychotic = < 1 mo. Schizophrenia = ≥ 6 mo. DSM-5 dropped axes; multi-axial is DSM-IV. Strongest predictor of completed suicide = previous attempt. MDD needs ≥ 5 of 9 SIG-E-CAPS, must include depressed mood OR anhedonia. Egocentrism is preoperational (Piaget), not narcissism. Critical period (rigid) vs sensitive period (flexible). Gilligan added "ethics of care," didn't replace Kohlberg. Asperger's no longer a separate dx (folded into ASD in DSM-5). Hoarding and Excoriation are NEW disorders in DSM-5. Bereavement exclusion was REMOVED in DSM-5 (you can dx MDD even within 2 mo of loss). Sheet built 2026-05-04 for last 19 days before MET. Pair with the abnormal and dev cheatsheets for the full picture. Papers (full primers) coming next. Sihan MET 2026 + NIMHANS Prep

chunks.heading: HPA Axis — Stress Endocrinology
chunks.text: HPA Axis — Stress Endocrinology Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal axis · Built 2026-05-16 Why this matters. HPA shows up in MET + NIMHANS papers under at least four hats: (1) biopsych "draw the axis," (2) abnormal psych "HPA in MDD/PTSD/Cushing's," (3) stress/health psych "Selye + allostatic load," (4) assessment "dexamethasone suppression test." One page, all four. Three things to know cold: CRH → ACTH → cortisol, the negative feedback loop, and which psychiatric disorder shows what kind of HPA dysregulation.

chunks.heading: 1. The axis in one diagram
chunks.text: 1. The axis in one diagram STRESSOR (physical, psychological, immune) ↓ HYPOTHALAMUS (paraventricular nucleus, PVN) → releases CRH (Corticotropin-Releasing Hormone) + AVP (vasopressin, synergistic) ↓ (via portal blood, infundibular stalk) ANTERIOR PITUITARY (corticotroph cells) → releases ACTH (Adrenocorticotropic Hormone) from POMC precursor ↓ (via systemic circulation) ADRENAL CORTEX — zona fasciculata → releases CORTISOL (glucocorticoid) + small DHEA, weak aldosterone ↓ TARGET TISSUES : liver, muscle, fat, immune, brain NEGATIVE FEEDBACK : cortisol inhibits both hypothalamus (↓CRH) and pituitary (↓ACTH). This loop shuts the response off when the stressor ends. In MDD and PTSD it breaks.

chunks.heading: 1.1 Anatomy details to memorise
chunks.text: 1.1 Anatomy details to memorise Paraventricular nucleus (PVN) of hypothalamus — the brain origin of stress. CRH = 41-amino-acid peptide, half-life ~60 min. Co-secreted with AVP (potentiates). Anterior pituitary corticotrophs make POMC → cleaved to ACTH + β-endorphin + MSH. Adrenal cortex layers (outside in): G lomerulosa (aldosterone), F asciculata (cortisol), R eticularis (androgens — DHEA). Memory: " GFR , salt-sugar-sex deeper you go". Adrenal medulla (inner) makes adrenaline / noradrenaline via SAM axis — fast, "fight-or-flight". HPA is the slower, sustained arm.

chunks.heading: 2. The two stress systems (compare and contrast)
chunks.text: 2. The two stress systems (compare and contrast) SAM (Sympatho-Adrenal Medullary) HPA Onset Seconds Minutes Hormones Adrenaline, noradrenaline Cortisol (with CRH, ACTH) Source Adrenal medulla, sympathetic neurons Adrenal cortex, via hypothalamus + pituitary Effect ↑HR, ↑BP, pupil dilation, bronchodilation, blood to muscle ↑glucose, ↑BP sustained, ↓immune, ↑gluconeogenesis, ↑lipolysis Role Immediate fight-or-flight Sustained mobilisation + recovery Cannon vs Selye Cannon's "fight or flight" Selye's GAS, "stress" coined

chunks.heading: 3. Cortisol — what it actually does
chunks.text: 3. Cortisol — what it actually does Metabolic : ↑gluconeogenesis, ↑glycogenolysis, ↑lipolysis, ↑proteolysis (catabolic). Raises blood glucose. Immune : suppresses inflammation, decreases lymphocytes, neutrophilia. That's why glucocorticoids are anti-inflammatory drugs. Cardiovascular : maintains vascular tone, permissive for catecholamines. CNS : alertness, attention. At chronic high levels: hippocampal atrophy, memory deficits, mood changes. GI : ↑gastric acid (chronic stress → ulcers). Bone : ↑resorption, ↓formation → osteoporosis with chronic excess.

chunks.heading: 3.1 Cortisol's diurnal rhythm
chunks.text: 3.1 Cortisol's diurnal rhythm Peak : ~30 min after waking ("cortisol awakening response", CAR). Trough : around midnight. Tightly tied to SCN (suprachiasmatic nucleus) circadian rhythm via the hypothalamus. Disrupted in shift workers, depression, chronic insomnia, jet lag.

chunks.heading: 4. HPA dysregulation in psychiatric disorders
chunks.text: 4. HPA dysregulation in psychiatric disorders

chunks.heading: 4.1 Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)
chunks.text: 4.1 Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) Hyperactive HPA axis is one of the most replicated biological findings in MDD. Elevated baseline cortisol; blunted diurnal variation; flattened cortisol awakening response. Enlarged adrenal glands on imaging. Dexamethasone Suppression Test (DST) : give 1 mg dex at 11 pm, measure cortisol next morning. In healthy subjects → cortisol suppressed. In ~50% of melancholic / psychotic depression → non-suppression . Sensitivity ~40-50%, specificity ~80-90%, not used diagnostically but historically big in NIMHANS papers (Carroll DST). Mechanism: impaired glucocorticoid receptor feedback → cortisol cannot turn the axis off → sustained CRH drive. Reduces hippocampal BDNF, contributes to volume loss. SSRIs and CBT both normalise HPA over weeks of treatment.

chunks.heading: 4.2 PTSD — paradox
chunks.text: 4.2 PTSD — paradox PTSD shows low basal cortisol (often) but enhanced negative feedback (super-suppression on low-dose DST). Elevated CRH in CSF. Theory: hypersensitive glucocorticoid receptors → over-suppression of cortisol after stressor. Contrast with MDD: depressed = hypercortisolaemic with failed feedback; PTSD = hypocortisolaemic with exaggerated feedback. Frequent MCQ trap.

chunks.heading: 4.3 Cushing's syndrome / disease
chunks.text: 4.3 Cushing's syndrome / disease Excess cortisol from any cause. Cushing's disease = pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma (most common endogenous cause). Cushing's syndrome = the broader phenotype, often iatrogenic (exogenous steroids). Physical: central obesity, moon face, buffalo hump, purple striae, hirsutism, hypertension, hyperglycaemia, thin skin, easy bruising. Psychiatric: depression in 50-80% , irritability, anxiety, insomnia, occasional psychosis or mania. Treating the Cushing's often resolves the depression — pure example of endocrine psychiatry.

chunks.heading: 4.4 Addison's disease
chunks.text: 4.4 Addison's disease Primary adrenal insufficiency — cortisol and aldosterone deficient. Fatigue, weight loss, hyperpigmentation (high ACTH stimulates MSH), hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia. Psychiatric: apathy, depression, occasional psychosis. Reverses with hydrocortisone replacement.

chunks.heading: 4.5 Anxiety disorders, panic, OCD
chunks.text: 4.5 Anxiety disorders, panic, OCD Findings are mixed. Panic disorder shows mild HPA activation during attacks but normal baselines. GAD: subtle blunting of CAR, elevated evening cortisol. OCD: no clear HPA signature — less examinable than mood / PTSD.

chunks.heading: 4.6 Schizophrenia
chunks.text: 4.6 Schizophrenia HPA hyperactivity at first episode, especially with poor outcome. Cortisol rises before psychotic relapse in some prospective studies. Linked to dopamine sensitisation theory ("threat → cortisol → mesolimbic DA").

chunks.heading: 4.7 Eating disorders
chunks.text: 4.7 Eating disorders Anorexia nervosa: hypercortisolaemia, loss of diurnal variation, often DST non-suppression even without depression. Restoration of weight partly normalises HPA.

chunks.heading: 4.8 Early life stress / abuse
chunks.text: 4.8 Early life stress / abuse Childhood maltreatment → durable HPA dysregulation in adulthood (often blunted reactivity + altered glucocorticoid receptor methylation). Mediator for later depression, PTSD, addiction risk. McGowan / Meaney rat studies — maternal licking ↑ glucocorticoid receptor in hippocampus → calmer adult. Classic epigenetics MCQ.

chunks.heading: 5. Stress theory — Selye and beyond
chunks.text: 5. Stress theory — Selye and beyond

chunks.heading: 5.1 Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS)
chunks.text: 5.1 Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) Stage What happens HPA state Alarm "Fight or flight": SAM activation first, then HPA kicks in Cortisol rises sharply Resistance Body adapts, mobilises resources, performance can rise Cortisol elevated and sustained Exhaustion Resources depleted, disease onset (ulcers, infection, depression) HPA dysregulation — high or low Memory: A-R-E (Alarm, Resistance, Exhaustion). Selye called the non-specific response to demand "stress" and the trigger "stressor". His rat experiments (1936) launched the field.

chunks.heading: 5.2 Cannon — "fight or flight" (1915)
chunks.text: 5.2 Cannon — "fight or flight" (1915) Walter Cannon coined "fight or flight" — the immediate SAM response. Predates Selye; describes the acute phase only. " Homeostasis " is also Cannon's term — keeping internal milieu constant.

chunks.heading: 5.3 Allostasis and allostatic load (McEwen, 1993+)
chunks.text: 5.3 Allostasis and allostatic load (McEwen, 1993+) Allostasis = achieving stability through change (active adaptation, not just returning to a setpoint). Allostatic load = the wear-and-tear from chronic activation of adaptive systems (HPA, SAM, immune). Allostatic overload = the load becomes pathology: cardiovascular disease, depression, metabolic syndrome, immune dysfunction. Updates Selye's "exhaustion" with a cumulative, multi-system model. Bruce McEwen — high-yield name for any "modern stress theory" MCQ.

chunks.heading: 5.4 Lazarus & Folkman — cognitive appraisal (1984)
chunks.text: 5.4 Lazarus & Folkman — cognitive appraisal (1984) Stress is the relationship between person and environment appraised as exceeding resources . Primary appraisal : is this event harmful/threatening/challenging? Secondary appraisal : can I cope with it? Coping styles: problem-focused vs emotion-focused . Transactional model — bridges biology with cognition; what activates HPA depends on appraisal, not the event alone.

chunks.heading: 6. Measuring the HPA axis
chunks.text: 6. Measuring the HPA axis Salivary cortisol — non-invasive, captures diurnal rhythm and CAR. Used in research. 24-hour urinary free cortisol — best for Cushing's screening. Midnight serum cortisol — should be low; non-suppression suggests Cushing's. Dexamethasone Suppression Test (DST) : Low-dose (1 mg overnight) — screen for Cushing's; non-suppression abnormal. High-dose (8 mg) — distinguishes pituitary Cushing's (suppresses) from ectopic ACTH (no suppression). In psychiatry: Carroll DST in depression — non-suppression suggests melancholic depression. CRH stimulation test — distinguishes hypothalamic vs pituitary defects. Trier Social Stress Test (TSST) — laboratory stressor (mock interview + arithmetic). Reliably activates HPA in healthy controls; blunted in many psychiatric groups. Highly cited.

chunks.heading: 7. HPA + neuroplasticity — why chronic cortisol matters
chunks.text: 7. HPA + neuroplasticity — why chronic cortisol matters Hippocampus is densely packed with glucocorticoid receptors. Chronic cortisol → dendritic atrophy in CA3, suppression of neurogenesis in dentate gyrus, hippocampal volume loss (MRI in MDD, PTSD, Cushing's). Cortisol ↓ BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) → less synaptic plasticity. Antidepressants reverse this over weeks. Prefrontal cortex also atrophies; amygdala often hypertrophies or hyperreacts → fear bias. This biology underpins the "neurotrophic hypothesis of depression" : stress → ↑cortisol → ↓BDNF → ↓hippocampal plasticity → depressive phenotype. Reversed by antidepressants and exercise.

chunks.heading: 8. One-page exam summary
chunks.text: 8. One-page exam summary Element Answer in 1 line Source of CRH Paraventricular nucleus of hypothalamus Source of ACTH Anterior pituitary corticotrophs (from POMC) Source of cortisol Adrenal cortex, zona fasciculata Feedback target Hypothalamus + pituitary (negative) Cortisol peak / trough Peak 30 min post-waking (CAR), trough ~midnight Fast vs slow stress SAM (seconds, adrenaline) vs HPA (minutes, cortisol) Selye's stages Alarm → Resistance → Exhaustion Allostatic load McEwen — wear and tear of chronic adaptation MDD HPA Hyper-cortisol, blunted rhythm, DST non-suppression PTSD HPA Hypo-cortisol, exaggerated feedback (paradox) Cushing's ↑cortisol, depression in 50-80%, central obesity, striae Addison's ↓cortisol, hyperpigmentation, apathy/depression Hippocampal effect Chronic cortisol → atrophy, ↓BDNF, ↓neurogenesis Test for HPA in research Salivary CAR, TSST, low-dose DST

chunks.heading: 9. Top 10 MCQ traps
chunks.text: 9. Top 10 MCQ traps "Releasing hormone for cortisol" → CRH , not ACTH. ACTH is the pituitary hormone downstream of CRH. Adrenal cortex layers: GFR → glomerulosa (aldosterone) / fasciculata (cortisol) / reticularis (androgens). Medulla = adrenaline. MDD = hyper -cortisol with failed suppression. PTSD = hypo -cortisol with super-suppression. Don't mix these up. DST non-suppression has poor sensitivity — not diagnostic, only suggestive of melancholic depression. Cushing's disease = pituitary adenoma. Cushing's syndrome = any cause of hypercortisolism (often iatrogenic steroids). Addison's hyperpigmentation is from MSH (made from same POMC precursor as ACTH). "Stress" was coined by Selye , "fight or flight" by Cannon , "allostatic load" by McEwen , "cognitive appraisal" by Lazarus & Folkman . Cortisol awakening response peaks ~30 minutes after waking , not at waking. Chronic cortisol → hippocampal atrophy (memory complaints in depression, Cushing's). Glucocorticoid receptor methylation (Meaney) is the headline epigenetics finding linking early life care to adult stress reactivity.
