chunks.heading: Your Therapeutic Style — interview-ready
chunks.text: Your Therapeutic Style — interview-ready This is your clinical voice, pulled straight from your own YourDOST session work. Every quote in a purple box is something you actually typed or said to a real client; every blue box is an answer you can give out loud in an interview, built from that same material. Nothing here is textbook-borrowed. When they ask "what's your therapeutic approach?" you don't have to perform a school you don't practise: you have a real, distinctive style and the language to describe it. Source + method are at the bottom. The one-line answer: you're an integrative, state-driven therapist with a person-centred relational base and a CBT / behavioural spine : you stabilise before you explore, validate before you intervene, and you pick the technique off the client's emotional state in the moment rather than off a manual. Your caseload line (say this with confidence): "I've carried hundreds of clients over the past year on YourDOST." That is your real number, and now it's documented, not a guess. The whole export was re-read end to end this time, every chat in the YD project, and 254 distinct named clients were individuated from it (plus another 79 real client sessions where the platform didn't preserve a usable name), across 473 session-instances. The earlier "~30" was never your caseload; it was just how many the first quick pass could separate. The real, ev

chunks.heading: 1 · Your approach / modality, as the sessions actually show it
chunks.text: 1 · Your approach / modality, as the sessions actually show it You are not a single-school therapist, and that's a strength, not a hedge: the sessions show a deliberate, repeatable logic for when you use what . The spine is cognitive-behavioural (you name automatic thoughts, loops, triggers, and you set small behavioural homework), the relational stance is person-centred (validate first, collaborative, never directive), and you reach for ACT/compassion/solution-focused moves when they fit the moment. The defining feature: you're state-driven, not modality-driven. You don't run "CBT clients" and "person-centred clients." You read the client's level of overwhelm and switch: • Overwhelmed / flooded → containment + supportive holding • Stuck in a thought → gentle CBT / ACT reframing • Ambivalent about change → motivational interviewing (roll with resistance) • Functionally stuck → behavioural activation + problem-solving • Self-critical → compassion-focused ("what would you tell a friend?") You've actually codified this. Your own session framework is built on two named gears: A) DEFAULT MODE (use when client is stable enough to talk) … B) CONTAINMENT MODE (override default when client is overwhelmed) … Goal: Stabilize the nervous system, not solve the problem. your YD session framework, written out for yourself The CBT spine is unmistakable in your own words to clients: Sometimes o

chunks.heading: 2 · Your go-to interventions
chunks.text: 2 · Your go-to interventions These are the moves that recur in almost every session, in roughly the order you deploy them.

chunks.heading: Validation + normalisation (your most frequent move)
chunks.text: Validation + normalisation (your most frequent move) You lead with it, every time, in plain undramatic language. Thats completely understandable… anyone in that situation would feel tired. recurring across clients The care and responsibility you showed during such a difficult period speaks about your empathy and strength to the marriage-distress client

chunks.heading: Strength-spotting / restoring agency
chunks.text: Strength-spotting / restoring agency You consistently hand the client back evidence of their own competence, and you reframe "failures" as data. The relapse is actually evidence that you can change the pattern, and one relapse doesn't erase that progress. to Akashdeep I don't see those six years as foolish. You stayed because you believed it would work. to Nuzhat (breakup) despite loss and pressure, you still have a strong drive for self improvement and growth, that part of you hasn't disappeared, it's just been waiting. to the identity/career client

chunks.heading: Psychoeducation — simple, relevant, never a lecture
chunks.text: Psychoeducation — simple, relevant, never a lecture You translate the mechanism into everyday language so the symptom stops feeling like a personal failing. Sometimes when burnout and depression last a long time, our brain's reward system becomes a bit "numb," but it seems that you have been able to function so far for this long which shows a lot of strength. to Steve (burnout) Health anxiety often stays strong because the body has learned to panic fast, not because there is real danger.. to the health-anxiety client

chunks.heading: Behavioural activation / one small step
chunks.text: Behavioural activation / one small step You end on a single, low-pressure, collaborative action ("would it feel okay to…?"), never a homework dump. For this week, you dont have to perform or commit to anything. Just choose one very low pressure action to Vaisakh For this week, keep it simple: make a short list of things you want to add to your life, and spend just 15-20 minutes learning about one administrative institution around you. That's enough for now. to the identity/career client

chunks.heading: Harm-reduction over abrupt cessation
chunks.text: Harm-reduction over abrupt cessation A real signature in your habit/urge cases: you refuse white-knuckle abstinence and build an alternative coping system first. entirely stopping masturbation may be difficult and create more anxiety without having an alternate coping system in place… Goal is not to stop it abruptly but to be able to manage anxiety or these triggers healthily. to Akashdeep It's not that we'll stop it entirely, but … just uska effect reduce karne ke liye. [we're trying to reduce its effect on your life] to a compulsion client, switching to Hindi for comfort

chunks.heading: 3 · Specific techniques you reach for
chunks.text: 3 · Specific techniques you reach for Technique What you actually do One-question pacing You almost always close a turn with a single open question, so the chat never becomes an interrogation. It's a written rule in your framework: "Ask ONE soft, natural question." ".. / ..." pacing Your signature on text: ellipses to slow the conversation and signal attentive silence — "I see.. Im listening.. Please go on.." Labelling / defusion Name the thought, delay the action, don't fight it. "label it as 'anxiety thought' and delay any checking by 10 minutes." Cognitive defusion of the inner critic "this is him trying to trigger me and not a fact about me" / "This is my old critical voice, not reality." Containment when flooded Stop exploring, hold, give permission not to answer. "You've already shared a lot, it's okay to not say more." Self-compassion prompt "What would you tell someone who you care about if they are in the exact same position as you right now?" 5-4-3-2-1 grounding + paced breathing Your standing crisis/anxiety tool: name 5 see / 4 touch / 3 hear / 2 smell / 1 taste, paired with inhale 4 · hold 2 · exhale 6. Risk screening built into the frame Every session opens with the confidentiality-limit line; you screen for self-harm warmly and directly when flags appear, then safety-plan. Self-diagnosis handling "explore phenomenology before pathology" — you steer from labels bac

chunks.heading: The containment move, in your own words
chunks.text: The containment move, in your own words For now it would be very important for us to slow down.. it would be important to not rush this… 3 years of being together can definitely make things more difficult to end to Yedik You've already shared a lot, it's okay to not say more. / We can just sit with what's here. / You don't need to figure anything out in this moment. your containment phrasebook

chunks.heading: Risk screening, in your own words
chunks.text: Risk screening, in your own words before we talk about more.. I want to check something important because you mentioned earlier that you "feel like you better die." Right now, do you ever get thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life? to a low-mood client is there someone at home who can be with you in the same room for a while, a parent, relative, or anyone nearby? You don't have to tell them anything, just not be alone for the moment. safety-planning, same client You also know your scope and hold it cleanly: I wouldnt able to prescribe any medication as I am a psychologist… Have you consulted a psychiatrist in the past? scope boundary + referral

chunks.heading: Handling the over-informed / self-diagnosing client
chunks.text: Handling the over-informed / self-diagnosing client One of your sharper clinical instincts. When a client arrived narrating themselves in textbook labels (ADHD, hypomania, depression), your read was: there might be a tendency to overreport or falsely self-diagnose. Do not take all of the words at face value. your note to yourself mid-session …and you redirect to behaviour, not labels: "When you say ADHD symptoms, what does that usually look like for you during class?" That's mature, NIMHANS-level thinking and a great interview anecdote.

chunks.heading: Your named techniques — the actual mechanics, your real example, the PI line
chunks.text: Your named techniques — the actual mechanics, your real example, the PI line This is the part that has to be sharp. For each technique you get three things: the real clinical mechanics (the actual steps, the ratings, the named sub-parts — what separates a clinician from someone who memorised the word), your own verbatim move from a YD session , and the concrete line to say in the interview ("here's exactly what I did and why", not a textbook sentence). Don't recite all of these. Know the mechanics cold, then for a given case pick two or three and walk the interviewer through the steps.

chunks.heading: 1 · Cognitive restructuring
chunks.text: 1 · Cognitive restructuring The actual mechanics — the 5 moves Catch the automatic thought. The moment mood drops, get the exact thought in the client's own words ("I'm going to fail and everyone will see") — not a paraphrase. Pin the situation, the thought, the emotion. Rate it. Belief in the thought 0–100%, intensity of the emotion 0–100. This is what makes the change measurable: you re-rate at the end. Name the cognitive distortion driving it. You're labelling the type of thinking error, which itself loosens it: all-or-nothing (black/white) catastrophising mind-reading overgeneralisation mental filter (only the negatives) discounting the positive emotional reasoning "should" statements labelling personalisation fortune-telling Test the evidence. Evidence for vs. evidence against; the double-standard question ("would you hold a friend to this?"); de-catastrophise (worst case / best case / most likely, and "could you cope if it happened?"). Build the balanced alternative — a believable, more accurate thought (not a fake positive affirmation), then re-rate belief and emotion to show the shift. Often set as a written thought record for homework. It would be important to identify certain automatic thoughts that we may have that doesnt allow us to accept these thoughts. to Levi For now, the goal is not to stop the voice, but to change your response to it. When it shows up, pause a

chunks.heading: 2 · Graded exposure (with a fear hierarchy + SUDS)
chunks.text: 2 · Graded exposure (with a fear hierarchy + SUDS) The actual mechanics Build a fear/avoidance hierarchy. List the avoided situations and rate each on SUDS — Subjective Units of Distress, 0 (calm) to 100 (worst panic imaginable). Order them low → high into a ladder. Start low. Begin on a rung around SUDS 40–50 — challenging but doable. Too easy does nothing; too hard and they flee. Stay until it drops. Remain in the situation until SUDS falls by roughly half ( habituation ). Escaping at the peak is the one thing that strengthens the fear, because relief reinforces avoidance. Repeat the same rung until it reliably triggers low distress, then climb to the next. Drop safety behaviours (reassurance-seeking, checking, gripping). The new learning — "the feared thing didn't happen, and I coped" — only lands when the safety crutch is gone (inhibitory learning). entirely stopping … may be difficult and create more anxiety without having an alternate coping system in place… Goal is not to stop it abruptly but to be able to manage anxiety or these triggers healthily. to Akashdeep (graded, not abrupt) Say it in the PI: "For avoidance and anxiety I use graded exposure. We build a hierarchy of the feared situations and rate each one on SUDS, 0 to 100, then order them into a ladder. We start on a rung around 40–50 — hard but doable — and the key rule is to stay in it until the SUDS drops by a

chunks.heading: 3 · Behavioural activation (activity scheduling + mastery/pleasure)
chunks.text: 3 · Behavioural activation (activity scheduling + mastery/pleasure) The actual mechanics Monitor first. Have the client log activity hour by hour for a few days and rate each one on two scales: Mastery (sense of achievement, 0–10) and Pleasure (enjoyment, 0–10). Read the pattern. Low mood tracks withdrawal and avoidance; the log shows which activities still give any M or any P, and where the dead zones are. Schedule activities at specific times — deliberately mixing mastery and pleasure tasks, graded easy → hard , and tied to the client's values , not just "keeping busy". Act from the schedule, not the mood. The principle is action-before-motivation: you do the activity first and the feeling follows, instead of waiting to feel like it. Review the M/P logs, troubleshoot what blocked a task, and grade up. For this week, you dont have to perform or commit to anything. Just choose one very low pressure action to Vaisakh keep it simple: make a short list of things you want to add to your life, and spend just 15-20 minutes learning about one administrative institution around you. That's enough for now. to the identity/career client Say it in the PI: "For low mood I use behavioural activation. I start by having them monitor their activities and rate each one for mastery and pleasure, 0 to 10, so we can see that mood is tracking avoidance. Then we schedule specific activities — a mix o

chunks.heading: 4 · Stimulus control
chunks.text: 4 · Stimulus control The actual mechanics Find the antecedent cues that reliably set off the behaviour — the time, place, object, mood, or person that precedes it. Change the environment, not the willpower. Remove or limit the cues for the problem behaviour (put the object out of reach, change the route/time, leave the phone in another room) and add cues for the wanted behaviour. Narrow the context. Classic example is insomnia — bed used only for sleep so the bed re-cues sleep, not wakeful rumination. Same logic for any habit: shrink the situations where the behaviour can be triggered. Pair it with an alternative response so the cue, when it does fire, routes to a coping action instead. entirely stopping … may be difficult … without having an alternate coping system in place… Goal is … to be able to manage anxiety or these triggers healthily. to Akashdeep — alternative system before removal Say it in the PI: "I lean on stimulus control rather than relying on willpower at the peak of an urge, because willpower fails right when it's needed. We map the cues that trigger the behaviour — the time, place, object, the mood — and then change the environment: get the cue out of reach, change the route or the timing, and pre-load an alternative response so when the trigger does fire it routes somewhere healthier. It's the same principle as telling an insomniac to use the bed only for sle

chunks.heading: 5 · Response prevention (ERP) & urge-surfing
chunks.text: 5 · Response prevention (ERP) & urge-surfing The actual mechanics Expose to the trigger/urge, then deliberately block the compulsive response (the checking, the reassurance, the behaviour) instead of acting on it. Urge-surf. Teach the client that an urge is a wave — it rises, peaks, and falls on its own, usually within ~20–30 minutes — if you don't feed it. You ride it out rather than fight it. Each blocked response weakens the loop. The urge→act→relief cycle only survives because the relief reinforces it; prevent the response and the urge gradually loses its grip. Build the alternative coping skill first (harm-reduction), then extend the delay — 10 minutes, then longer — rather than demanding zero overnight. label it as 'anxiety thought' and delay any checking by 10 minutes. health-anxiety client — graded response delay Say it in the PI: "With compulsive behaviour I use exposure and response prevention. The client faces the trigger and we block the compulsion rather than letting them act on it, and I teach urge-surfing — an urge is a wave that peaks and falls within about twenty, thirty minutes if you don't feed it. Every time the response is prevented, the urge-relief loop weakens. I do it inside a harm-reduction frame though — I won't ask someone to white-knuckle to zero overnight, we build an alternative coping skill first and extend the delay, ten minutes then longer."

chunks.heading: 6 · Cognitive defusion (ACT)
chunks.text: 6 · Cognitive defusion (ACT) The actual mechanics Change the relationship to the thought, not its content. You don't argue whether it's true — you create distance so it stops dictating action. The defusion moves: add the frame " I'm having the thought that… "; label it ("that's an anxiety thought"); thank the mind for it; leaves-on-a-stream (watch the thought float past); or repeat the hot word until it loses its charge. Pair with an action delay — once unhooked, the urge the thought was driving can be delayed rather than obeyed. label it as 'anxiety thought' and delay any checking by 10 minutes. health-anxiety client this is him trying to trigger me and not a fact about me defusing a thought from its content Say it in the PI: "When a thought is sticky I use defusion rather than debate, because arguing with a thought keeps you hooked to it. We name it — 'that's an anxiety thought', 'I'm having the thought that…' — so the client steps back and sees it as a mental event rather than a fact, and then delays the urge it was driving. It takes the power out of the thought without me having to prove it wrong, which matters because you usually can't win that argument."

chunks.heading: 7 · Behavioural chain analysis (chaining)
chunks.text: 7 · Behavioural chain analysis (chaining) The actual mechanics Reconstruct the chain link by link, in order: vulnerability factors (poor sleep, stress, hunger, low mood that lowered the threshold) → prompting event (the trigger) → the links (every thought, body sensation, emotion and action between the trigger and the behaviour) → problem behaviour → consequences (short-term relief, longer-term cost). Find the weak links. Walk the chain with the client and locate the points where a different thought, a delay, a coping skill or a changed environment could have broken the path — the earlier the better. Insert a skill at each link and reframe the short-term relief as the reinforcer that maintains the whole chain. the relief you feel after testing is actually what keeps the anxiety alive and not solving it. health-anxiety client — the relief is the reinforcer Say it in the PI: "I do a behavioural chain analysis — I walk the whole sequence with the client: the vulnerability factors that lowered the threshold, the prompting event, then every thought, sensation and urge that linked the trigger to the behaviour, and finally the consequence. The point is to find the weak links, the earliest spot where a delay or a different response could have broken the chain, and put a skill there. And I show them the short-term relief is exactly what's reinforcing the loop — with a health-anxiety cli

chunks.heading: 8 · Contingency management
chunks.text: 8 · Contingency management The actual mechanics Behaviour follows its consequences. Identify what currently reinforces the problem behaviour (relief, escape, attention) and reduce it. Attach reinforcement to the target behaviour instead — a self-reward for a completed step, tracking a streak, social reinforcement (genuine praise, handing back evidence of competence). Make rewards immediate and achievable, and shape by reinforcing successive approximations — reward the small step now, raise the bar gradually. The relapse is actually evidence that you can change the pattern, and one relapse doesn't erase that progress. to Akashdeep — reinforcing the effort, not the slip For this week, you dont have to perform or commit to anything. Just choose one very low pressure action to Vaisakh — a step small enough to be reinforced Say it in the PI: "I use contingency management — behaviour is shaped by what follows it. So I figure out what's currently reinforcing the problem behaviour, usually the relief or escape, and then attach reinforcement to the behaviour I want instead: an immediate, achievable reward, tracking a streak, or just genuine social reinforcement for the attempt. I deliberately set the first step small enough that it gets reinforced, and I shape it up from there rather than demanding the whole change at once."

chunks.heading: 9 · Relapse-prevention planning
chunks.text: 9 · Relapse-prevention planning The actual mechanics (Marlatt model) Map the high-risk situations — the emotional states, people, places and times when a slip is most likely. Separate a lapse from a relapse. A lapse is one slip; a relapse is a full return. The danger is the Abstinence Violation Effect — "I've already blown it, so I may as well go all in" — and you pre-empt that thinking directly. Build a coping plan for each high-risk situation, plus early-warning signs and an if-then plan ("if I notice X, I do Y"). Reframe a lapse as data, not failure — what was the trigger, what link broke, what would change next time. The relapse is actually evidence that you can change the pattern, and one relapse doesn't erase that progress. to Akashdeep — exactly the abstinence-violation reframe Say it in the PI: "I build a relapse-prevention plan. We map the high-risk situations — the moods, people, times when a slip is most likely — and we plan a coping response for each, with early-warning signs and an if-then plan. The crucial part is separating a lapse from a relapse: I prep the client for the abstinence-violation effect, that 'I've already slipped so I may as well give up' thought, because that thought is what turns one slip into a full relapse. I treat a lapse as data — what triggered it, which link broke — not as failure. With one client I framed a relapse as evidence he can chang

chunks.heading: 10 · Functional analysis (the loop, ABC)
chunks.text: 10 · Functional analysis (the loop, ABC) The actual mechanics ABC. Antecedent (trigger) → Behaviour → Consequence — extended in your work to Trigger → Thought → Urge → Action → Relief → Guilt → repeat. Locate the intervention at the earliest link, where there's still a real choice, instead of fighting the behaviour at its peak. Expose the maintaining consequence — name how the short-term relief is the very thing that keeps the loop alive. the relief you feel after testing is actually what keeps the anxiety alive and not solving it. health-anxiety client Say it in the PI: "I do a functional analysis — antecedent, behaviour, consequence — and with my clients I map it as trigger, thought, urge, action, relief, guilt, and back round. Then we intervene at the earliest link, right when the first thoughts start, because that's where there's still a choice. And I make the maintaining consequence explicit: the relief is what's reinforcing the loop, so chasing relief is feeding the problem."

chunks.heading: 11 · Socratic questioning / guided discovery
chunks.text: 11 · Socratic questioning / guided discovery The actual mechanics Don't tell, ask. Use questions that lead the client to their own conclusion rather than supplying it — it sticks because they reached it themselves. The question types: clarifying ("what does that look like exactly?"), evidence ("what makes you think that?"), alternative-perspective ("how else could you read it?"), consequence ("what would it mean if that were true?"), and the summary/synthesis question that ties it together. Move from label to phenomenology — from "I have ADHD" to what actually happens, when, and for how long. When you say ADHD symptoms, what does that usually look like for you during class? to a self-diagnosing client Say it in the PI: "I use Socratic questioning — guided discovery — rather than telling the client what to think, because an insight they reach themselves actually sticks. If someone self-diagnoses, say 'I have ADHD and hypomania', I don't confirm it and I don't argue. I ask what it actually looks like for them, when it happens, how long it lasts — clarifying and evidence questions — so we explore the phenomenology before the pathology and it stays clinical instead of becoming a debate."

chunks.heading: 12 · Motivational interviewing
chunks.text: 12 · Motivational interviewing The actual mechanics Spirit: collaboration, evocation, autonomy — you draw the client's own reasons for change out, you don't install them. OARS — Open questions, Affirmations, Reflective listening, Summaries. Develop discrepancy between the behaviour and the client's own goals/values; roll with resistance rather than confronting it (arguing for change makes them argue against it). Listen for and reinforce change talk ("DARN-CAT": Desire, Ability, Reasons, Need → Commitment, Activation, Taking steps). Tools: a scaling/readiness ruler (0–10, "why a 4 and not a 2?") and a decisional balance. You have mentioned … studies … Another would be … managing the urges. What would you like to focus on in todays session? to Vaisakh — evoking the client's own agenda Say it in the PI: "When a client is ambivalent about change I use motivational interviewing. I work in the spirit of it — collaboration and drawing out their own reasons rather than installing mine — using OARS: open questions, affirmations, reflective listening, summaries. I roll with the resistance instead of arguing for change, because the moment I argue the change side they argue the other. I develop the discrepancy between the behaviour and what they actually want, and I listen for their change talk and build on it. I'll let them set the session agenda, which is itself MI — pushing change befor

chunks.heading: 13 · Compassion-focused work
chunks.text: 13 · Compassion-focused work The actual mechanics Map the three systems (CFT): the threat system (the harsh inner critic), the drive system, and the under-developed soothing system — the goal is to strengthen the soothing/self-compassion system. The friend reframe — route the self-talk through "what would you say to someone you love in exactly this spot?" to access a kinder, more reasonable voice they'd never aim at themselves. Soothing-rhythm breathing + a compassionate-self stance, then re-write the critical message in that voice. What would you tell someone who you care about if they are in the exact same position as you right now? self-compassion prompt, recurring Say it in the PI: "For a self-critical client I use compassion-focused work. The frame is that the threat system — the harsh inner critic — is overdeveloped and the soothing system is starved, so we build the soothing one. The move I lean on is the friend reframe: 'what would you say to someone you love in this exact spot?' It gives them access to a kinder, more reasonable voice they'd never turn on themselves, and we rewrite the critical message in that voice and build from there."

chunks.heading: 14 · Grounding & arousal regulation
chunks.text: 14 · Grounding & arousal regulation The actual mechanics Body before mind. A flooded nervous system can't do cognitive work, so you down-regulate arousal first. 5-4-3-2-1 sensory grounding — name 5 things you see, 4 you touch, 3 you hear, 2 you smell, 1 you taste — pulls attention out of the spiral and into the present. Paced breathing with a long exhale — inhale 4, hold 2, exhale 6 . The longer exhale engages the parasympathetic (vagal) brake and physically lowers arousal; that's why exhale > inhale, not the other way round. name 5 things you can see, 4 you can touch, 3 you can hear, 2 you can smell, 1 you can taste … inhale for 4, hold 2, exhale for 6. 5-4-3-2-1 grounding + paced breathing Say it in the PI: "When someone's highly activated I regulate the body before the mind, because you can't do cognitive work on a flooded nervous system. I use 5-4-3-2-1 grounding — five things you see, four you touch, and so on — to pull them out of the spiral and into the present, paired with paced breathing where the exhale is longer than the inhale, inhale four, hold two, exhale six. The long exhale is deliberate: it engages the vagal brake and physically brings the arousal down. Once the body's settled, we can think." How to use this in the room: don't recite the list — that reads as memorised. Know the mechanics cold, then for the case they hand you pick two or three, name the techniqu

chunks.heading: 3c · Your most difficult case — the full clinical walkthrough
chunks.text: 3c · Your most difficult case — the full clinical walkthrough This is the answer that actually wins a PI. Anyone can name a school. What separates you is being able to take your hardest, most-stuck client and walk the panel through the real reasoning: what you were seeing , which technique you reached for and why that one , the specific moves in order, and how the client shifted . Below are your two strongest cases from the YD work — one a months-long stuck case that finally broke, one an acute late-night crisis — plus the one that went wrong and what it taught you. Pick the one that fits the question; know the arc cold.

chunks.heading: Case A · The client who was stuck for months — and finally broke the loop
chunks.text: Case A · The client who was stuck for months — and finally broke the loop hardest / most stuck · ~9 / 10 OCD-spectrum + scrupulosity passive SI flagged documented breakthrough Who: a young man, ego-dystonic intrusive sexual imagery (violent, deeply shameful to him) that had generalised into a fear of any sexual feeling — he was afraid that seeing someone would "get impressed in my brain" and turn him into someone who acts on it. Layered on top: rigid moral/purity perfectionism ("money is deception," self-punishment around food) and passive suicidal ideation ("I would commit suicide in a month or two" if forced into a corporate job). He had abruptly ended his first call, called psychologists "stupid," and came in hostile. Why it was the hardest: three things made this the most stuck case you carried. (1) Risk on the table — the suicide statement had to be assessed as active until ruled out. (2) A hostile rupture from the start — sessions ended abruptly, the alliance kept breaking. (3) The loop was eating the therapy itself — your own note was that "he has been repeating the same things every session in loops" ; the talking had become a compulsion, so every insight-chasing session was quietly reinforcing the rumination instead of breaking it. This is the trap: the case feels like it's progressing because he's engaged, but the engagement is the symptom. 1 · What you were seeing —

chunks.heading: Case B · Under acute pressure — a real-time crisis you contained
chunks.text: Case B · Under acute pressure — a real-time crisis you contained acute crisis · ~10 / 10 live self-harm + SI chat-only, ~2 AM de-escalated by next session Who: a young man who'd just discovered his long-distance partner was emotionally cheating. Who he was stuck on: within ~15 minutes of a chat-only session, near 2 AM, it escalated from breakup grief to active self-harm in real time and suicidal ideation — "I feel worthless… useless," "cut my hands," "maybe I should also not exist" — while he kept trying to redirect you to "should I go to her place" instead of his own safety. The bind: no voice, middle of the night, an actively self-harming, help-rejecting client. 1 · What you were seeing You correctly re-classified the session on the spot. This was no longer relationship counselling — it was crisis containment . Risk over reasoning. The "should I visit her" question was a distraction from the only thing that mattered in the room: is he safe. 2 · The moves, in order (a) Validate the pain, reframe the self-blame — don't argue him out of it, take the "stupid / obsessed" self-attack off the table first: Its not obsession or stupidity but something you valued a lot. What matters right now is caring for yourself, not proving anything… How have you been managing your anxiety lately? to Indranil (typed, verbatim) (b) The direct safety question. The moment self-harm surfaced you didn't

chunks.heading: Case C · The one that went wrong — and the rule it gave you
chunks.text: Case C · The one that went wrong — and the rule it gave you documented bad outcome negative client rating → became your containment rule If they ask for a mistake rather than a win, this is the honest one, and it pairs perfectly with Cases A and B because it's why you now contain. A film student came in carrying three colliding things at once — a creative block on his graduation film, unresolved domestic-violence history , and a new queer identity he was trying to put into his work. He left a negative rating . Your own after-action read was unsparing and exactly right: • You over-talked — filled the session with metaphors and analogies (pink elephants, breakups, good-time-vs-bad-time) and gave lectures, not therapy. • You chased every thread — identity → writing → career → DV history → authenticity → coming out — and let it sprawl until he stopped feeling helped. • You gave general wisdom instead of containment — "he needed containment, not commentary." • You didn't validate or stabilise before explaining , and you left him with no single concrete step . The fix you built from it is the spine of how you now work — and it's the same discipline you can show firing correctly in Case A (refusing the loop) and Case B (switching to containment): validate before you explain, every time; one theme per session; one tiny concrete step; and the moment a client is flooded, contain and stab

chunks.heading: 4 · Therapeutic relationship + case formulation
chunks.text: 4 · Therapeutic relationship + case formulation

chunks.heading: How you open (your standard frame, verbatim)
chunks.text: How you open (your standard frame, verbatim) You run the same warm, consent-based, time-boxed opening every time — this is your rapport-and-safety move: Hi, welcome to YourDOST! I am Sihan, one of the psychologists here. We have 45 minutes today, and you're free to talk about whatever's on your mind. Everything stays confidential unless there's a risk of harm to you or someone else. Before we begin, would you mind sharing a little about yourself - like your name, age, gender, what you do, or anything else you'd like me to know? your opening, near-identical across every session You're transparent about time and boundaries throughout — "Unfortunately, I have an appointment coming up, so this will be a shorter session of 30 minutes. Would that be alright?" — and you greet returning clients by name ("Hello Akashdeep. Its good to see you again.").

chunks.heading: The relational stance: permission-giving, never rushing
chunks.text: The relational stance: permission-giving, never rushing You dont have to explain everything at once to an overwhelmed client Take your time, Vaisakh. I'm here and listening to Vaisakh Many people who are strong and self reliant struggle with sharing at first so thats completely okay normalising reluctance

chunks.heading: How you formulate a case
chunks.text: How you formulate a case Your working model is consistently a loop , and you locate the intervention at the earliest link. You also separate the automatic/biological driver from the psychological one and sequence treatment accordingly (break the automatic pattern first, then go after deeper triggers). Your recurring formulation: Trigger → Thought → Urge → Action → Relief → Guilt → repeat. You teach the client to step in "right when we start having the first few thoughts," and you reframe the relief as the thing that maintains the problem: "the relief you feel after testing is actually what keeps the anxiety alive and not solving it." You set agendas collaboratively rather than imposing them: You have mentioned … studies … Another would be … managing the urges. What would you like to focus on in todays session? to Vaisakh — collaborative agenda-setting And you reformulate when the referral label is wrong — e.g. you rejected a platform's "gaming disorder" tag and re-read it as post-bereavement anxiety and executive dysfunction after the client lost his father and sister. That's diagnostic flexibility worth naming in an interview.

chunks.heading: Your documentation house-style
chunks.text: Your documentation house-style After each session you produce a fixed format (good to mention — it shows structure): Session Summary — one formal, neutral paragraph: demographics, duration/frequency of concern, key emotions + issues, coping attempted, one direct client quote , any progress/insight, plus a risk line. Next Session Plan — 3–5 action-oriented, symptom-focused bullets: review homework → reassess triggers → deepen one area → introduce the next technique → monitor functioning (sleep/appetite/mood).

chunks.heading: Modality nudge
chunks.text: Modality nudge You routinely invite chat clients toward audio/video for depth — "it may help us progress faster" — while deferring to their comfort. A small but real relationship instinct: you're managing the format to serve the work.

chunks.heading: 5 · Strengths & growth edges (be honest, it reads as insight)
chunks.text: 5 · Strengths & growth edges (be honest, it reads as insight)

chunks.heading: Strengths — well evidenced
chunks.text: Strengths — well evidenced • Validation-first, genuinely warm, non-judgmental , especially on shame-loaded topics (porn/urges, relapse, cheating). "It takes courage to do this and I appreciate you for it." • Disciplined one-question pacing + ellipsis holding — keeps text sessions therapeutic, not interrogative. • Strong reframes around shame and loss ("the relapse is evidence you can change the pattern"). • Harm-reduction maturity — alternative coping before abstinence. • Good risk awareness — confidentiality framing every session, warm SI screening, safety planning, psychiatric referral, knows scope. • Conscientious continuity — formal formulation + next-session plan every time; carries personal threads forward. • Diagnostic humility — handles self-diagnosis well, reformulates wrong referral labels, rules cases out of psychology when they're medical.

chunks.heading: Growth edges — own these as "what I'm working on"
chunks.text: Growth edges — own these as "what I'm working on" • Over-talking / chasing every thread when a client needs containment. Your honest self-critique on one tough session: you "chased every thread instead of anchoring … he needed containment, not commentary." The fix you already know: anchor one target, talk less. • Over-psychoeducating — your longest turns can tip from collaborative into lecturing. You catch it yourself ("this sounds very preachy. talk in my style"). • Stock phrasing — "I understand..", "That makes sense.." can pile up before any intervention; some clients want something concrete sooner. • Pacing toward solutions vs. exploration under a 45-min cap — efficient, but can short-change depth. • Formal outcome tracking is light — progress is narrative; a standardised measure (even a quick scale) would strengthen it. Interview tip: a growth edge you can name and show a fix for is worth more than a fake weakness. "Early on I'd chase every thread when a client was overwhelmed; I've learned to anchor one target and contain first" is a strong, true answer.

chunks.heading: 6 · Interview answers, built from your own work
chunks.text: 6 · Interview answers, built from your own work Each of these is concrete on purpose: a named technique, the actual steps, and a real moment. That's what reads as a clinician. Say them in your own voice. "What is your therapeutic approach?" "I'd call myself integrative but state-driven. My base is person-centred — I validate and build safety before anything else — and my working spine is cognitive-behavioural: I work with automatic thoughts, run functional analyses of the maintaining loop, and use graded behavioural steps. But I don't apply one school to every client. I read where the person is and switch: if they're flooded I regulate arousal first with grounding and paced breathing; if they're stuck in a thought I do cognitive restructuring or defusion; if they're ambivalent I use motivational interviewing; if they're shut down and avoidant I use behavioural activation. The rule underneath all of it is regulate before you explore, validate before you intervene, and pick the technique off the client's state in the moment, not off a manual." "Give an example of how you handle a client in distress." "I run a two-gear model. Default gear: validate, one focused question, one small step. But the moment a client floods — 'I don't know', 'nothing helps', or they start looping — I switch into containment. Concretely: I stop exploring and stop problem-solving, and I regulate the body f

chunks.heading: 7 · Source & method (so you can trust every line)
chunks.text: 7 · Source & method (so you can trust every line) This profile was built only from your "YD sessions" ChatGPT project (confirmed as yours in the export — "In this folder 'YD sessions' there must be 100s of session transcripts"). The rest of the 933-chat export was ignored, as you asked. What was read (full re-ingest): the entire export was re-processed end to end. 454 YD-related chats, ~27.6M characters , every file read in full by a fleet of parallel readers, one client record built per session, then deduplicated by client name. That produced 254 distinct named clients plus 79 more real client sessions where no usable name survived in the export, across 473 session-instances; 176 of those involved risk content you handled (suicidal ideation, self-harm, crisis or abuse). 79 framework/style chats and 9 gambling-platform chats were set aside as non-clinical.
